div.p: I was well aware, Brutus, that when I committed to Latin what philosophers of the highest genius and the most exquisite learning had treated in the Greek tongue, this labour of mine would meet with various criticisms. For there are some — and not unlearned men at that — to whom the whole business of philosophizing is distasteful. Others do not so much object to it, provided it is pursued with restraint, but think that so much zeal and so much labour ought not to be expended upon it. There will also be men learned in Greek letters and contemptuous of Latin who will say that they prefer to spend their effort on reading Greek. And finally I suspect there will be some who summon me to other kinds of writing, declaring that this style, however elegant, is yet beneath my character and standing.

When each of them had looked at me and signified that they were ready to listen, 'First of all,' said I, 'I beg you not to suppose that I shall expound to you some lecture, as a philosopher might — a thing which I never greatly approved even in the philosophers themselves. For when did Socrates, who may rightly be called the parent of philosophy, ever do anything of the sort? That was the practice of those who were then called sophists, of whose number Gorgias of Leontini first dared, in an assembly, to call for a question — that is, to bid someone state on what subject he wished to hear him speak. A bold undertaking, I should call it shameless, had not this practice afterward been transferred to our philosophers.

Pleasure indeed, Brutus, if it should plead for itself and not have such obstinate advocates, would, I think, yield to dignity, convicted as it was in the previous book. For it would be shameless if it should resist virtue any longer, or set the pleasant before the honourable, or contend that the sweetness of the body, or the gladness born of it, is worth more than gravity and steadfastness of mind. Wherefore let us dismiss it, and bid it keep within its own bounds, lest the strictness of our argument be hindered by its blandishments and enticements.

When he had said this, he made an end. But I: 'Indeed, Cato,' said I, 'you have set forth those things — so many, from memory, and so obscure — clearly. And so let us either give up wishing to say anything against them at all, or take time to think; for it is not easy to learn thoroughly a doctrine so diligently — even if less truly (for I do not yet dare to say that), yet so carefully — not only founded, but built up.' Then he: 'Do you say so indeed?' said he; 'when I see you, by this new law, answer your accuser on the same day and finish your plea in three hours, do you think you will gain delay in this cause? — which yet will be pleaded by you no better than those which you sometimes win. Wherefore attack this question too — especially as it has been handled both by others and often by yourself — so that words cannot fail you.'

When I had heard Antiochus, Brutus, as I was wont, with Marcus Piso, in that gymnasium which is called the Ptolemaeum, and together with us my brother Quintus and Titus Pomponius and Lucius Cicero — my cousin by kinship, my brother in affection — we settled among ourselves to take our afternoon walk in the Academy, chiefly because that place at that hour was free from all crowd. And so at the appointed time we all came to Piso's house. Thence, in varied talk, we completed those six stades from the Dipylon gate. But when we had come into the walks of the Academy, not without cause renowned, there was that solitude which we had wished for.

To all these I think a brief reply must be made. As for the disparagers of philosophy, answer enough has been given in that book in which philosophy was defended and praised by me when it had been accused and reviled by Hortensius. Since that book seemed to win the approval both of yourself and of those whom I judged capable of forming a judgment, I have undertaken more, fearing that I might seem to rouse men's enthusiasm but be unable to hold it. As for those who, even if they thoroughly approve of philosophy, would yet have it pursued more moderately, they demand a difficult sort of self-control in a matter which, once admitted, cannot be checked or held back — so that we might almost find more reasonable those who would call us away from philosophy altogether than those who set a limit to things that are boundless and, in a pursuit that is the better for being the greater, look for moderation.

But both the man I have named, and the other sophists, we see, as may be understood from Plato, made sport of by Socrates. For by questioning and interrogating he used to draw out the opinions of those with whom he discoursed, so that he might say something, if it seemed good, in answer to what they had replied. Since this practice was not kept up by his successors, Arcesilas revived it, and established that those who wished to hear him should not ask questions of him, but should themselves say what they thought; and when they had said it, he argued against it. But his hearers defended their own opinion as far as they could. With the other philosophers, however, the man who has asked a question keeps silence; which indeed is now done even in the Academy. For when the man who wishes to hear has said, 'Pleasure seems to me to be the highest good,' the argument is conducted against it in a continuous discourse, so that it may easily be understood that those who say something seems true to them do not themselves hold that opinion, but wish to hear the contrary. We proceed more conveniently.

For we must inquire where that highest good lies which we wish to find, since both pleasure has been removed from it, and much the same things can be said against those who would have freedom from pain to be the end of goods; nor indeed ought any highest good to be approved which lacks virtue, than which nothing can be more excellent. And so, although in that discussion which was held with Torquatus we were not slack, yet this struggle prepared with the Stoics is keener. For the things said about pleasure are argued neither very acutely nor abstrusely; for neither are those who defend it skilful in argument, nor do those who speak against it repel a difficult case.

Then I: 'Not, by Hercules,' said I, 'am I wont rashly to speak against the Stoics — not that I altogether assent to them, but I am hindered by modesty; for they say many things which I can hardly understand.' 'Some things are obscure, I confess,' said he, 'nor yet are they said by them so on purpose, but the obscurity lies in the things themselves.' 'Why, then,' said I, 'when the Peripatetics say the same things, is there no word that is not understood?' 'The same things?' said he. 'Have I argued too little that the Stoics differ from the Peripatetics not in words, but in the whole substance and the entire opinion?' 'And yet, Cato,' said I, 'if you make that good, you may carry me over wholly to your side.' 'I thought,' said he, 'that I had said enough. So to those points first, if you please; but if you wish anything else, afterward.' 'Nay, that indeed,' said I, 'as to in what place I treat each thing — unless I ask what is unfair — at my own discretion.' 'As you please,' said he; 'although that other course was the more fitting, to grant each man his right.'

Then Piso said: 'Shall I say that this is given us by nature, or by some illusion, that, when we see those places in which we have learned that men worthy of remembrance much frequented, we are more moved than when at any time we either hear of their very deeds or read some writing of theirs? As I now am moved. For Plato comes into my mind, who, we have learned, was the first wont to dispute here; and those little gardens of his, close by, not only bring me the memory of him, but seem to set the man himself before my sight. Here was Speusippus, here Xenocrates, here his hearer Polemo — whose very seat that was which we see. For my part, gazing too at our senate-house — the Hostilia, I mean, not this new one, which seems to me smaller since it has been made larger — I used to think of Scipio, Cato, Laelius, and above all of my own grandfather; so great is the force of admonition in places, that not without cause the art of memory has been derived from them.

For if wisdom can be attained, then we must not only acquire it but enjoy it; or if this is difficult, still there is no limit to the search for truth short of finding it, and to grow weary of seeking is shameful, since the object of the search is the fairest of all things. Indeed, if we take delight in writing, who is so grudging as to draw us from it? Or if we toil at it, who would set a limit to another man's industry? For just as Terence's Chremes is not inhumane when he is unwilling that his new neighbour should 'dig or plough or carry anything at all' — since it is not from industry but from servile drudgery that he deters him — so these meddlesome critics are offended by a labour that is to me by no means unwelcome.

For not only did Torquatus say what he thought, but also why. Yet I judge — though I was much delighted by his continuous discourse — that it is more convenient, when you halt at single points and understand what each man grants and what he denies, to draw from the points conceded the conclusion you intend, and so come to the end. For when discourse rushes on like a torrent, however much of every kind it sweeps along, yet you hold nothing, you grasp nothing; nowhere can you check the rushing speech. Now every discourse which is conducted by some method and reasoning in inquiry ought first to lay down, as in certain legal formulas, the terms on which the matter shall be handled, so that those between whom the discussion is held may agree what the thing is about which the discussion turns.

Epicurus himself even says that there is no need to argue about pleasure, because its judgment is placed in the senses, so that it is enough for us to be reminded, and there is no need to be taught. Wherefore that discussion of ours was a simple one on both sides. For there was nothing intricate or tortuous in Torquatus's speech, and ours, as it seems to me, was a clear discourse. But you are not unaware how subtle, or rather thorny, is the Stoics' kind of argument — both for the Greeks, and still more for us, who must even bring words to birth and impose new names on new things. And no moderately learned man will wonder at this, considering that in every art whose use is not vulgar and common there is much novelty of names, since the terms of those things must be established which are handled in each art.

'I think, then, Cato,' said I, 'that those old hearers of Plato — Speusippus, Aristotle, Xenocrates, and then their successors, Polemo, Theophrastus — had a doctrine sufficiently and copiously and elegantly established, so that there was no cause for Zeno, when he had heard Polemo, why he should differ both from that very man and from his predecessors. Their teaching was as follows, in which I should like you to mark what you think must be changed, and not to wait until I speak to all the things which were said by you; for I think we must clash with their whole system against the whole of yours.

Then Quintus said: 'It is plainly so, Piso, as you say. For just now, as I came hither, that Colonean spot turned me toward itself, whose inhabitant Sophocles dwelt before my eyes — Sophocles, whom you know how I admire and how I delight in him. Indeed a certain vision moved me toward the deeper memory of Oedipus coming hither, and asking in that most tender song what these very places were — vainly, of course, but yet it moved me.' Then Pomponius: 'But I, whom you are wont to pursue as devoted to Epicurus, am much indeed with Phaedrus, whom I love uniquely, as you know, in the gardens of Epicurus, which we just now passed; but, warned by the old proverb, I remember the living — and yet I cannot forget Epicurus, even if I should wish, whose likeness our friends have not only in pictures, but even on cups and on rings.'

It is therefore harder to satisfy those who say they despise writings in Latin. In them the first thing I wonder at is why their native tongue should not delight them in the gravest matters, when the same men read without reluctance Latin plays rendered word for word from the Greek. For who is so hostile, almost, to the very name of Rome as to scorn or reject the Medea of Ennius or the Antiopa of Pacuvius, on the ground that, though he delights in the same plays of Euripides, he hates Latin letters? 'Am I,' says he, 'to read the Synephebi of Caecilius or the Andria of Terence rather than both plays of Menander?' From such men I so far dissent that, although Sophocles wrote his Electra with the utmost excellence, I yet think the poor translation by Atilius worth my reading — Atilius of whom Lucilius says,

This rule, laid down by Plato in the Phaedrus, Epicurus approved, and felt that it ought to be done in every discussion. But the next step he did not see. For he says it is not his pleasure that a thing be defined — without which it is sometimes impossible that those who dispute should agree what the thing is about which they are arguing, as in this very matter we are now discussing. For we are inquiring into the end of goods. Can we know here what it is, unless we have agreed among ourselves, when we have spoken of the end of goods, what 'end' is, and what the 'good' itself is?

And so both the dialecticians and the natural philosophers use words which are not known even to Greece itself; the geometers, moreover, and the musicians, and the grammarians too speak after a certain fashion of their own. The very arts of the rhetoricians, which are wholly forensic and popular, yet use in teaching words, as it were, private and their own. And, to pass over these elegant and liberal arts, not even craftsmen could maintain their crafts unless they used words unknown to us but familiar to themselves. Nay, even agriculture, which shrinks from all the finer refinement, has yet marked the things with which it is concerned by new names. So much the more must this be done by the philosopher; for philosophy is the art of life, and discoursing of it he cannot snatch his words from the forum.

When they saw that we were so born that we were fitted, in common, for those virtues which are well known and illustrious — I mean justice, temperance, and the rest of that kind, all of which are like the other arts, differing only in their material toward the better part, and in their handling — and when they saw that we seek those very virtues more grandly and more ardently, and that we have, too, a certain implanted, or rather inborn, desire of knowledge, and were born for the gathering together of men and for the society and community of the human race, and that these things shine forth most in the greatest geniuses, they divided the whole of philosophy into three parts — which partition we see was retained by Zeno.

Here I: 'Our Pomponius indeed,' said I, 'seems to jest, and perhaps by his own right. For he has so settled himself at Athens that he is almost one of the Attic men — so that he seems likely even to have that surname. But I assent to you, Piso, that it comes about by experience that we think somewhat more keenly and attentively of famous men at the reminder of places. For you know that I once came with you to Metapontum, and did not turn aside to my host before I had seen that very spot where Pythagoras had ended his life, and his seat. But at this time, although in every part of Athens there are many marks of the greatest men in the very places, yet I am moved by that exedra. For just now it was the seat of Carneades, whom I seem to see — for his likeness is well known — and I think that very seat, bereaved of so great a magnitude of genius, longs for that voice.'

'a writer of iron' — yet a writer, in my opinion, and one worth reading. For to be utterly unread in our own poets is the mark either of the most slothful idleness or of the most fastidious daintiness. To me, at least, no men seem learned enough who are ignorant of our own literature. Do we not read the line 'Would that in the grove [...]' no less than this same passage in Greek? And shall it not, then, be permitted to set forth in Latin the discussions of Plato upon living well and happily?

And yet this laying open, as it were, of hidden things, when it is revealed what each thing is, is definition; which you yourself sometimes unwittingly employed. For you were defining this very thing — whether 'end' or 'uttermost' or 'last' — as that to which all things rightly done are referred, while it itself is referred to nothing. Excellently said. And the good itself, too — what it was — you would perhaps have defined, if there had been need: either as what is by nature to be sought, or as what is profitable, or what helps, or what merely pleases. Now then, since defining does not altogether displease you, and you do it when you will, I should like you, if it is not troublesome, to define what pleasure is, on which this whole inquiry turns. 'Who, pray,' said he, 'is there who does not know what pleasure is, or who, the better to understand it, would want any definition?'

Although of all the philosophers the Stoics have coined the most new words, and Zeno, their chief, was not so much an inventor of things as of new words. But if, in that language which most men think the richer, it was granted by Greece that the most learned men should use unfamiliar words about uncommon things, how much more should this be granted to us, who now first dare to touch these matters? And since I have often said — and that with some complaint, not only of the Greeks, but even of those who wish to be held Greeks rather than ours — that we are not only not surpassed by the Greeks in abundance of words, but are even superior in it, I must take pains to attain this not only in our own arts, but even in theirs. Although those words which by the usage of the ancients we use as Latin — such as 'philosophy' itself, 'rhetoric,' 'dialectic,' 'grammar,' 'geometry,' 'music' — though they could be said in Latin, yet, since they have been taken into use, let us count them as ours.

Since one of these is that by which morals are thought to be shaped, I defer that part, which is, as it were, the root of this question. What the end of goods is, presently; in this place I say only this much — that by the old Peripatetics and Academics, who agreed in substance but differed in terms, that subject which we may rightly call the civil (the Greeks politikon) was treated gravely and copiously. How many things did they write about the commonwealth, how many about the laws! How many precepts they left, not only in their arts, but also examples in their orations of speaking well! For first, those very things which had to be argued subtly they expressed politely and aptly, now defining, now partitioning, as your school too does; but you do it more squalidly, while you see how their discourse shines.

Then Piso said: 'Since, then, we all have said something, what of our Lucius?' said he. 'Does he gladly visit that place where Demosthenes and Aeschines were wont to contend with each other? For each man is led most by his own pursuit.' And he, when he had blushed, said: 'Do not ask me, who have even gone down to the Phaleric shore, in which place they say Demosthenes was wont to declaim against the surf, that he might accustom himself to overcome the roar with his voice. Just now too I turned a little to the right off the road, that I might approach the tomb of Pericles. Although that indeed is endless in this city; for wherever we walk, we set our foot upon some history.'

And what if I do not perform the office of a translator, but defend the doctrines spoken by those whom I approve, and add to them my own judgment and my own order of exposition? What ground have they for preferring the Greek to what has been both splendidly expressed and not translated from the Greek? For if they say these matters have been treated by the Greeks, then there is no reason for them to read even so many of the Greeks themselves as ought to be read. What has Chrysippus left out among the Stoics? And yet we read Diogenes, Antipater, Mnesarchus, Panaetius, and many others, and above all our friend Posidonius. Again — does Theophrastus give us only middling pleasure when he treats topics treated before him by Aristotle? Again — do the Epicureans cease to write at their own discretion on the very subjects on which Epicurus and the ancients had already written? If, then, Greeks are read by Greeks on the same subjects arranged in another fashion, what reason is there why our own writers should not be read by our own people?

'I should say it was myself,' said I, 'did I not seem to myself to have a good knowledge of pleasure, and to have conceived and grasped it firmly enough in my mind. But as it is, I say that Epicurus himself does not know, and wavers in this; and that he who often says that the force underlying words ought to be carefully expressed sometimes does not understand what this word \"pleasure\" sounds — that is, what thing is placed beneath this word.' Then he, laughing, said: 'This indeed is excellent! — that he who says pleasure is the end of things to be sought should not know what that last, that uttermost of goods, is, or of what kind!' 'And yet,' said I, 'either Epicurus does not know what pleasure is, or all mortals everywhere do not.' 'How so?' said he. 'Because all men feel that this is pleasure, which, received by the sense, sets it in motion and floods it with a certain delight.' 'What then?'

And so much for the names of things. But about the things themselves, Brutus, I often fear that I shall be blamed, when I write these things to you, who have made such progress both in philosophy and in the best kind of philosophy. And if I were doing this as though instructing you, I should rightly be blamed. But I am very far from that, nor do I send these things to you that you may learn what is most familiar to you, but because I rest most easily in your name, and because I have you as the fairest appraiser and judge of those studies which I share with you. You will attend, then, as you are wont, diligently, and will judge that controversy which I had with your uncle, a divine and singular man.

Then those things which required ornate and grave discourse — how magnificently were they spoken by them, how splendidly! Of justice, of temperance, of fortitude, of friendship, of the conduct of life, of philosophy, of taking part in the commonwealth — speaking, not like men plucking thorns, as the Stoics do, nor laying bare bones, but like men who wished to say great things with ornament, and lesser things with precision. And so what consolations are theirs, what exhortations, what admonitions and counsels written to the greatest men! For with them, as is the very nature of the things, so the exercise of speaking was twofold. For whatever is inquired into has a controversy either of the kind itself, without persons and times, or, these being joined, of fact, or of right, or of name. In both, therefore, they exercised themselves, and that training produced in them so great an abundance in both kinds of speaking.

Then Piso: 'And yet, Cicero,' said he, 'those studies, if they look to imitating the greatest men, are the mark of the gifted; but if only to learning the records of ancient memory, of the merely curious. But we all exhort you — running already, as I hope — that you should wish to imitate those whom you wish to have known.' Here I: 'Although this one indeed, Piso,' said I, 'does, as you see, the things you advise, yet your exhortation is pleasing to me.' Then he, most kindly, as was his wont, said: 'Let us all indeed bring all things to bear on this young man's youth, and especially that he impart something of his pursuits to philosophy too — whether to imitate you, whom he loves, or that he may be able to pursue that very thing he studies the more elegantly. But are you to be exhorted by us, Lucius,' said he, 'or are you of your own accord inclined? To me, at least, you seem to attend prettily well to Antiochus, whom you hear.' Then he, timidly, or rather modestly, said: 'I do indeed; but did you hear just now about Carneades? I am carried off thither; but Antiochus calls me back, and there is no one besides whom we may hear.'

And yet, if I were to translate Plato or Aristotle plainly, in the way our poets translated the plays, I should, I believe, deserve ill of my fellow citizens by importing those divine geniuses into our knowledge. But this I have not done so far, nor do I think myself forbidden to do so. Certain passages I shall translate, if it seems good — chiefly from those I have just named, when occasion arises that it may be aptly done, as Ennius is wont to draw from Homer, and Afranius from Menander. Nor will I, like our Lucilius, decline to have all men read what I write. Would that the famous Persius were alive — and Scipio and Rutilius far more so — out of dread of whose judgment Lucilius said he wrote for the people of Tarentum, Consentia, and Sicily! Wittily said, as much else of his; but there were not in those days such learned men to whose judgment he might labour to conform, and his own writings are of a lighter cast, so that the wit is supreme but the learning ordinary.

'Is Epicurus ignorant of that pleasure?' said he. 'Not always,' said I; 'for sometimes he knows it only too well, since he testifies that he cannot even understand where any good lies, or what it is, apart from that which is taken in food and drink, the delight of the ears, and obscene pleasure. Or are these things not said by him?' 'As though,' said he, 'I were ashamed of those things, or could not show in what sense they are said!' 'I do not doubt,' said I, 'that you can do it easily; nor is there cause for you to be ashamed to assent to a wise man — the one man who, so far as I know, has dared to profess himself wise. For Metrodorus, I think, did not himself make the profession, but, being so styled by Epicurus, was unwilling to reject so great a kindness; and those famous seven were named wise not by their own, but by the vote of all peoples.'

For when I was at my Tusculan villa, and wished to use certain books from the library of young Lucullus, I came to his villa, that I might myself, as I was wont, take them out. When I had come there, I saw Marcus Cato, whom I had not known to be there, sitting in the library, surrounded by many books of the Stoics. For there was in him, as you know, an avidity for reading, nor could he be sated; since, not even fearing the empty censure of the crowd, he was wont often to read in the senate-house itself, while the senate was being assembled, taking nothing away from his service to the commonwealth. So much the more, then, in the deepest leisure and the greatest abundance, he seemed, as it were, to gorge himself on books — if this word may be used in so honourable a matter.

This whole kind Zeno and those who are of his school either could not maintain or would not; at any rate they abandoned it. Although Cleanthes wrote an art of rhetoric, and Chrysippus too, but in such a way that, if anyone should long to be struck dumb, he need read nothing else. And so you see how they speak. They coin new words, they desert the customary ones. But how great are the things they attempt! That this whole world is our city! You see, then, how they fire those who hear them. How great a matter do you bring about, that he who dwells at Circeii should think this whole world his own township? 'Does that man, then, fire them?' He will rather quench them, if he receives them already burning. Those very things which you stated briefly — that the wise man alone is king, dictator, rich — by you indeed aptly and roundly; quite so, for you have it from the rhetoricians; but those very things, in them, how meagre about the force of virtue! — which they would have to be so great that it can of itself produce happiness. They prick, as it were with little stings, by narrow questionings, by which even those who assent are in no way changed in mind, and depart the same men as they had come. For the things, perhaps true, certainly weighty, are not handled as they ought to be, but somewhat too minutely.

Then Piso: 'Although this perhaps cannot so pass off, since he is present' — he meant me — 'yet I shall dare to call you from this New Academy to that old one, in which, as you heard Antiochus say, are counted not those alone who are called Academics — Speusippus, Xenocrates, Polemo, Crantor, and the rest — but also the old Peripatetics, whose chief is Aristotle, whom, except Plato, I know not whether I might rightly call the chief of philosophers. Turn yourself, then, I pray, to them. For from their writings and institutions both all liberal learning, all history, all elegant discourse can be drawn, and there is so great a variety of arts that no one, without that equipment, can come sufficiently adorned to any more illustrious matter. From these came orators, from these commanders and leaders of commonwealths. And, to come to lesser things, mathematicians, poets, musicians, finally physicians, set out from this workshop, as it were, of all craftsmen.' And I:

But what reader need I fear, when I dare to write on philosophy addressed to you, who yield not even to the Greeks in it? And yet in this very thing I act at your own provocation, by reason of that most welcome book on virtue which you sent me. But from this, I believe, it comes about that some take an aversion to Latin works — because they have lighted upon certain crude and rough productions, things written worse in Latin than bad Greek. To these men I assent, provided they do not think that the same subjects need not be read in Greek either. But who would not read good matter expressed in choice words with weight and ornament? — unless it be one who wishes to be called outright a Greek, as Albucius was hailed by Scaevola when he was praetor at Athens.

But in this passage I take it, by these words, that Epicurus at least knows the same force of pleasure as the rest. For all men call that pleasant motion by which the sense is gladdened — in Greek hedone, in Latin voluptas. 'What is it, then,' said he, 'that you would inquire after?' 'I will tell you,' said I, 'and that rather for the sake of learning than because I wish you or Epicurus to be censured.' 'I too,' said he, 'should more gladly learn, if you bring forward anything, than censure you.' 'Do you recall, then,' said I, 'what Hieronymus of Rhodes says is the highest good, to which he thinks all things ought to be referred?' 'I recall,' said he, 'that the end seems to him to be freedom from pain.' 'What, then,' said I, 'does this same man think about pleasure?'

And when it had happened that we saw each other unexpectedly, he at once rose. Then those first words which we are wont to use at meeting: 'What brings you here?' said he; 'from your villa, I suppose'; and, 'Had I known you were there, I should have come to you myself.' 'Yesterday,' said I, 'when the games had begun, I set out from the city and arrived toward evening. But my reason for coming hither was to take out certain books from here. And indeed, Cato, this whole store must soon be known to our friend Lucullus; for I would rather he were delighted by these books than by the rest of the villa's adornment. For it is of great care to me — although this indeed is your proper office — that he be so educated as to answer to his father, and to our Caepio, and to you, who are so near to him. And I take pains not without cause; for I am moved both by the memory of his grandfather — for you are not unaware how highly I esteemed Caepio, who, as my opinion bears, would now be among the foremost, were he alive — and Lucullus rises before my eyes, a man excelling in all virtues, and joined to me both by friendship and by every wish and opinion.'

There follows the method of arguing and the knowledge of nature; for about the highest good, presently, as I said, we shall see, and to explaining it we shall bring our whole discussion. In these two parts, then, there was nothing that Zeno was eager to change. For the matter stood admirably, and that in both parts. For what was left out by the ancients of that kind which avails for arguing? — who both defined very many things and left arts of defining; and that which is joined to definition, that a thing be divided into parts, this both is done by them and is handed down how it ought to be done; likewise of contraries, from which they came to the genera and forms of genera. Now of the chain of reasoning concluded by argument they make the head to be those things which they call evident, then they follow the order, and last, the final conclusion is what is true in each particular.

'You know,' said I, 'that I feel that very same thing, Piso; but your mention of it is opportune. For my Cicero is eager to hear what is the opinion of that old Academy of which you speak, and of the Peripatetics, about the ends of goods. And we think that you can most easily explain it, since you both had Stasea of Naples with you for many years, and we see you for several months now at Athens seeking out these very things from Antiochus.' And he, smiling, said: 'Come, come' — for cleverly enough you wished me to be the beginning of our discourse — 'let us set forth for the young man, if perchance we can, anything. For this solitude grants us that which, if some god should say it, I should never have thought — that I should dispute in the Academy like a philosopher. But let me not, while I humour him, be troublesome to you.' 'To me?' said I, 'who asked you this very thing?' Then, when Quintus and Pomponius had said that they wished the same, Piso began. Attend, I pray, to his discourse, Brutus, whether it seems sufficiently to have embraced the opinion of Antiochus — which I judge most approved by you, who have frequently heard his brother Aristus.

This very theme Lucilius adorns with much charm and all his salt, where Scaevola speaks admirably: 'You preferred, Albucius, to be called a Greek rather than a Roman and a Sabine, a fellow townsman of Pontius and Tritanus, of centurions, of illustrious men and chiefs and standard-bearers. So, as praetor at Athens, since that is what you preferred, I greet you in Greek when you approach me: "Chaere, Titus!" I say; and the lictors, the whole squadron, and all the company, "Chaere, Titus!" Hence Albucius is my foe, hence my enemy.' But Mucius was in the right.

'He denies,' said he, 'that it is to be sought for its own sake.' 'He thinks, then, that to rejoice is one thing, and not to be in pain another.' 'And indeed,' said he, 'he is greatly mistaken; for, as I showed a little before, the limit of increasing pleasure is the removal of all pain.' 'As for \"not to be in pain,\"' said I, 'what force that has I will see later; but that the force of pleasure is one thing, and that of freedom from pain another, you must needs grant, unless you are very obstinate.' 'And yet,' said he, 'you will find me obstinate on this point; for nothing can be said more truly.' 'Tell me, pray,' said I, 'is there pleasure for a thirsty man in drinking?' 'Who could deny it?' said he. 'Is it the same as when the thirst is quenched?' 'No, of another kind; for the quenched thirst has the steadiness of pleasure,' said he, 'but that other pleasure, of the quenching itself, is in motion.' 'Why, then,' said I, 'do you call things so unlike by the same name?' 'Do you not remember,' said he, 'what I said a little before — that when all pain is removed, pleasure is varied, not increased?'

'You do admirably,' said he, 'in that you both keep the memory of those, each of whom commended his children to you by will, and love the boy. As for what you call my office, I do not refuse it, but I join you as my partner. I add this too: that the boy already gives me many signs both of modesty and of genius; but you see his age.' 'I see indeed,' said I; 'but still he ought now to be steeped in those arts which, if he drinks them in while he is tender, he will come the better prepared to greater things.' 'So, and indeed more carefully and more often we will talk of these matters between ourselves, and act in common. But let us sit down,' said he, 'if you please.' And so we did.

And how great a variety of arguments concluded by reasoning is there in them, and how unlike to captious questionings! What of this, that in very many places they, as it were, give warning that we should seek the credit of the senses neither without reason, nor that of reason without the senses, and that we should not separate the one from the other? What? Those things which the dialecticians now hand down and teach — were they not instituted or invented by them? Concerning which, although it was most laboured at by Chrysippus, yet by Zeno much less than by the ancients; and by him some things not better than the old men, some things wholly left untouched.

He spoke, then, thus: How great an ornament there is in the doctrine of the Peripatetics, has been said by me, as briefly as I could, a little while ago. But the form of that doctrine, as nearly of the rest, is threefold: one part is of nature, the second of arguing, the third of living. Nature was so investigated by them that no part of heaven, sea, earth — to speak poetically — was passed over; nay even, when they had spoken of the beginnings of things and the whole world, so that they concluded many things not only by probable argumentation, but even by the necessary reasoning of the mathematicians, they brought the greatest material from things investigated for their own sake to the knowledge of hidden things.

For my part, I cannot wonder enough at the source of this strange disdain for things of our own household. This is not at all the place to teach the point; but I both feel and have often argued that the Latin language is not only not poor — as is commonly supposed — but actually richer than the Greek. For when has any ornament of speech, whether copious or elegant, been lacking to us — or rather to our good orators and poets — once there was a model for them to imitate? Indeed, since by my labours, toils, and perils in public life I think I have not deserted the post in which the Roman people stationed me, I surely owe it, so far as I am able, to labour at this too: that my fellow citizens may be made more learned by my work, my zeal, my toil; and not to contend so fiercely with those who prefer to read Greek, provided they actually read it and do not merely pretend, but rather to serve those who wish to use both literatures, or who, having their own, do not greatly miss the other.

'I remember indeed,' said I; 'but you said that in good Latin, yet not very clearly. For \"variety\" is a Latin word, and is properly used of differing colours, but is transferred to many differing things: a varied poem, a varied speech, varied manners, varied fortune; and pleasure too is often called varied, when it is perceived from many unlike things producing unlike pleasures. If you spoke of that variety, I should understand — as indeed I understand even when you do not say it. But what that variety of yours is I do not sufficiently perceive, when you say that, when we are free from pain, we are then in the highest pleasure, but when we feed on things that bring a sweet motion to the senses, then there is pleasure in motion, which makes a variety of pleasures — yet that this pleasure of not being in pain is not increased, which I know not why you call pleasure at all.' 'Can anything,' said he, 'be sweeter than to feel no pain?'

Then he: 'But you, when you have so many books yourself, what, pray, do you seek here?' 'Certain commentaries of Aristotle,' said I, 'which I knew to be here, I came to carry off, that I might read them while I am at leisure — which indeed does not often fall to us.' 'How I wish,' said he, 'that you had inclined toward the Stoics! For it was yours, if anyone's, surely, to count nothing among goods except virtue.' 'Take care,' said I, 'lest it were rather yours, when you thought the same as I in substance, not to impose new names on things. For our reasoning agrees; it is our language that contends.' 'By no means, indeed,' said he, 'does it agree. For whatever you shall say is to be sought, besides what is honourable, and shall count among goods, you both extinguish the honourable itself, as it were the light of virtue, and overthrow virtue utterly.' 'These things are said magnificently, Cato,' said I; 'but do you see that the glory of words is common to you with Pyrrho and with Aristo, who level all things?

And since there are two arts by which reason and discourse are perfectly completed — one of finding, the other of arguing — this latter both the Stoics and the Peripatetics handed down; but the former the Peripatetics excellently, while the Stoics did not even touch it at all. For from what topics, as from treasuries, arguments might be drawn, your school did not even suspect; but the older men handed it down by art and method. And this indeed brings it about that it is not necessary always to chant the same things, as it were, by rote about the same matters, nor to depart from one's little notebooks. For he who knows where each thing is placed, and by what way one comes to it, he, even if something be buried, will be able to dig it out, and will always be his own master in arguing. And although certain men endowed with great talents attain abundance of speaking without method, yet art is a surer guide than nature. For it is one thing to pour out words after the manner of the poets, another to distinguish what you say by method and art.

Aristotle followed out the origins, modes of life, and shapes of all living creatures; Theophrastus, the natures of plants and the causes and reasons of almost all things which are born from the earth; from which knowledge the investigation of the most hidden things was made easier. And of arguing, precepts were handed down by the same men not only dialectically, but also rhetorically; and by Aristotle, as chief, the exercise of speaking on both sides about single matters was instituted — not so that he always spoke against everything, like Arcesilas, and yet so that in all matters he brought out whatever could be said on either side.

And those who would have me write on other subjects ought to be fair, for many works of mine have been written — more than by anyone among us — and perhaps more will be written, if life holds out. And still, whoever has accustomed himself to read attentively what I commit to writing concerning philosophy will judge that there is nothing better worth reading than these. For what is so worth pursuing in life as philosophy in general, and in particular this question pursued in these books: what is the End, the uttermost, the ultimate, to which all our plans of living well and acting rightly are to be referred; what Nature pursues as the highest of things to be sought, and what she shuns as the last of evils? Since on this matter there is the deepest disagreement among the most learned men, who would think it foreign to that dignity, whatever it be, which each man grants me, to inquire what in every duty of life is best and truest?

'Why, let nothing be better,' said I — 'for I do not yet inquire into that — but is pleasure on that account the same thing as, so to speak, painlessness?' 'Plainly the same,' said he, 'and indeed the greatest, than which none greater can be.' 'Why, then, do you hesitate,' said I, 'now that you have so set up the highest good that it lies wholly in not being in pain, to hold to this one thing, to guard it, to defend it?

Of whom I long to know what you think.' 'Do you ask me,' said he, 'what I think? Those good men, brave, just, temperate, whom we have either heard to have been in the commonwealth, or ourselves have seen, who, without any teaching, following nature herself, did many praiseworthy things — these, I say, were better trained by nature than they could have been trained by philosophy, had they approved any other than that which holds nothing among goods but the honourable, nothing among evils but the base. And the other schools of philosophers — altogether some more, some less, but yet all of them — which count any thing devoid of virtue either among goods or among evils, these I think not only do not help at all, nor strengthen us to be better, but corrupt nature itself. For unless this be maintained, that that alone is good which is honourable, the happy life can in no way be proved to be produced by virtue. And if it be so, I know not why effort should be given to philosophy. For if any wise man could be wretched, then truly I should think that glorious and memorable virtue of yours not to be highly esteemed.'

The like can be said of the explanation of nature, which both these men and yours use — and not indeed for two reasons only, as Epicurus thinks, that the fear of death and of religion may be driven off, but also the knowledge of the heavenly things brings a certain modesty to those who see how great is the moderation even among the gods, how great the order, and brings greatness of mind to those who discern the works and deeds of the gods, and justice too, when you have come to know what is the will of the supreme ruler and master, what his counsel, what his purpose; to whose nature the reason fitted is said by the philosophers to be that true and supreme law.

But when the third part sought the precepts of living well, that too was by the same men referred not only to the plan of private life, but also to the governance of commonwealths. We have learned from Aristotle the manners, institutions, and disciplines of nearly all states, not of Greece only, but also of the barbarian world; from Theophrastus, even their laws. And since each of them had taught what kind of leader it was fitting to be in a commonwealth, and had moreover written in many books what was the best condition of a commonwealth, Theophrastus did this further: what were the inclinations of affairs in a commonwealth, and the turning-points of the times, which had to be controlled however the matter demanded. But the plan of leading life pleased them most that was quiet, placed in the contemplation and knowledge of things; which, because it was most like the life of the gods, seemed most worthy of the wise man. And about these matters their discourse is both splendid and illustrious.

Shall the question whether the offspring of a slave-girl is to be reckoned among the produce be debated among the leading men of the state — Publius Scaevola and Manius Manilius, from whom Marcus Brutus dissents (a keen kind of inquiry, and not without use for the affairs of citizens, and I both read such writings, and the rest of that sort, gladly, and shall read them) — and shall these questions, which embrace the whole of life, be neglected? For though those subjects are more saleable, these are surely the richer. Yet that judgment may be left to those who read. As for me, I think this whole inquiry concerning the ends of goods and evils has been pretty fully set forth by me in these volumes, in which, so far as I could, I have followed out not only what I myself approve, but also what is said by each of the schools of philosophy.

For what need is there to bring pleasure into the council of the virtues, as one might bring a courtesan into a gathering of matrons? The name is hateful, infamous, suspect. And so it is frequently said by you that we do not understand what Epicurus means by pleasure. And whenever this is said to me — and it is said not seldom — although I am gentle enough in debate, yet I am sometimes wont to grow a little angry. Do I not understand what hedone is in Greek, voluptas in Latin? Which of the two languages, pray, do I not know? And further, how comes it that I do not know, while all those who have chosen to be Epicureans do? For your school indeed argues very well that there is no need for one who is to be a philosopher to know letters. And so, just as our ancestors brought Cincinnatus from the plough to be dictator, so you gather from all the villages those men — good, indeed, but assuredly not very learned.

'The things which you have said so far, Cato,' said I, 'you could say the same, if you followed Pyrrho or Aristo. For you are not unaware that to these men that honourable seems not only the highest but even, as you would have it, the only good. And if it is so, it follows — the very thing which I see you wish — that all wise men are always happy. Do you, then, praise these men, and think that we ought to follow this opinion of theirs?' 'By no means, indeed theirs,' said he. 'For since it is the property of virtue to have a choice among the things that are according to nature, those who have so levelled all things that they made them equal on both sides, so as to use no selection — these have done away with virtue itself.'

There is in this same explanation of nature a certain insatiable pleasure from the knowing of things, in which alone, when necessary affairs are done, we can, free from business, live honourably and liberally. Therefore in this whole reasoning, about the greatest matters almost, the Stoics followed those men, so as to say both that the gods exist and that all things consist of four elements. But when a very difficult thing was asked — whether there seemed to be a certain fifth nature, from which reason and intelligence arose, in which there was also the inquiry as to of what kind the souls might be — Zeno said this was fire; then certain things otherwise, but those few; on the greatest matter, however, in the same way, that the whole universe and its greatest parts are administered by a divine mind and nature. But the material and abundance of things we shall find in these men meagre, in those most rich.

But about the highest good — because there are two kinds of books, one written in a popular way, which they called exoteric, the other more polished, which they left in their commentaries — they do not always seem to say the same thing; nor yet in the sum itself is there any variety among these men, at least whom I have named, or disagreement among themselves. But since the happy life is the thing sought, and this is the one thing which philosophy ought to regard and follow, whether it is wholly placed in the power of the wise man, or can be either shaken or snatched away by adverse circumstances, in this they seem sometimes to vary and to doubt. Which is chiefly brought about by Theophrastus's book on the happy life, in which a great deal indeed is given to fortune. But if it be so, wisdom cannot guarantee the happy life. This seems to me a softer, so to speak, and more effeminate reasoning than the force and gravity of virtue demands. Wherefore let us hold to Aristotle and his son Nicomachus, whose carefully written books on morals are said indeed to be Aristotle's — but I do not see why the son could not have been like the father. Let us yet use Theophrastus for very many things, provided we hold in virtue more firmness and strength than he held. Let us, then, be content with these.

But, to begin with the easiest, let the theory of Epicurus come first into the open, since to most men it is the most familiar. You will find it set forth by me in such a way as is not usually expounded more accurately even by those who approve that doctrine; for I wish to find the truth, not to confute some adversary. Now once upon a time the opinion of Epicurus concerning pleasure was carefully defended by Lucius Torquatus, a man versed in every branch of learning, and I made answer to him, while Gaius Triarius, a young man of the gravest character and most learned, was present at that discussion.

Do they, then, understand what Epicurus says, and I do not? That you may know I understand, first I say that pleasure is the same as what he calls hedone. And indeed we often seek a Latin word equal to the Greek and of the same value; here there was nothing to seek. No word can be found which declares the same in Latin as voluptas declares in Greek. Beneath this word all men everywhere who know Latin place two things: gladness in the mind, and a sweet stirring of delight in the body. For both the man in Trabea calls excessive gladness of mind 'pleasure' — the same as that Caecilian character who tells that he is glad with all gladnesses. But there is this difference, that pleasure is spoken of also in the mind — a faulty thing, as the Stoics think, who define it thus: an unreasoning elation of the mind that fancies it is enjoying some great good — whereas gladness and joy are not spoken of in the body.

'That indeed,' said I, 'you say very well; but I ask whether you must not do the same, you who say that nothing is good which is not right and honourable, and who do away with all distinction of the other things.' 'If indeed I did away with it,' said he; 'but I leave it.' 'In what way?'

How many things were sought out and gathered by them about the whole kind of living creatures, their origin, their limbs, their ages! How many things about those things which are produced from the earth! How many, and about how various matters, both causes why each thing comes to be, and demonstrations how each thing comes to be! From all which abundance very many and most certain arguments are taken for explaining the nature of each thing. Therefore so far, as I at least understand, there seems to have been no cause for changing the name. For if Zeno did not follow them in all things, it was not on that account that he had not arisen from them. Indeed I think Epicurus too, in physics at least, a follower of Democritus. He changes a few things, or even many, granted; but when he says the same about very many, then certainly about the greatest. And since your school does the same, they do not render gratitude enough to the discoverers.

For their successors are better indeed, in my opinion, than the philosophers of the other schools, but they so degenerate that they seem to have sprung from themselves. First, the successor of Theophrastus, Strato, chose to be a natural philosopher; in which, although he is great, yet very many of his views are novel, and very few are about morals. His successor, Lyco, is rich in language, but rather meagre in the things themselves. Then his successor, Aristo, is neat and elegant; but that gravity which is desired in a great philosopher was not in him; his writings, indeed, are both many and polished, but somehow his discourse has no authority.

For when both had come to me at my house near Cumae to pay their respects, after a few words at first about literature, in which the zeal of each was supreme, Torquatus said: 'Since we have at last found you at leisure, I shall certainly hear why it is that you do not exactly hate our Epicurus — as those generally do who dissent from him — but at any rate do not approve of him, the one man who in my judgment saw the truth, freed men's minds from the greatest errors, and handed down all that pertains to living well and happily. But I suppose that you, like our Triarius, take less pleasure in him because he neglected those ornaments of style proper to Plato, Aristotle, and Theophrastus. For as to the other charge, I can scarcely be brought to believe that what he held seems untrue to you.'

Now, in the usage of all who speak Latin, pleasure is placed in this: when that delight is perceived which moves some sense. This delight too, if you will, transfer to the mind; for 'to help' is said of both, and from this comes 'pleasant' — provided you understand that between the man who says, 'I am increased with such gladness that I cannot contain myself,' and the man who says, 'Now at last my heart is on fire,' of whom the one exults with gladness and the other is tortured with grief, there is a third, midway: 'Although this acquaintance between us is but lately formed' — one who neither rejoices nor is vexed; and likewise that between him who possesses the sought-for pleasures of the body and him who is tortured with the greatest pains, there is one who lacks both.

said I. 'If virtue is one thing, this one thing which you call honourable, right, praiseworthy, becoming — for it will be better known of what sort it is when it is marked by several terms declaring the same thing — this, then,' said I, 'if it is the only good, what will you have besides which you may follow? Or, if nothing is evil except what is base, dishonourable, unbecoming, crooked, infamous, foul — that we may make this too conspicuous by several names — what will you say is besides to be shunned?' 'You are not ignorant,' said he, 'of what I am about to say; but, since you desire, as I suspect, to snatch something from my brief reply, I will not answer point by point, but will rather set forth — since we are at leisure, unless you think it out of place — the whole opinion of Zeno and the Stoics.' 'By no means out of place,' said I; 'and that exposition of yours will profit much toward what we seek.'

But so much for these things. Now let us see, I pray, about the highest good, which contains philosophy, what, pray, he brought forward, for which he should differ from his discoverers as from his parents. In this place, then — although it has been carefully explained by you, Cato, what this end of goods which contains philosophy is, and how it is stated by the Stoics — yet I too will set it forth, that we may perceive, if we can, what new thing was brought in by Zeno. For when the earlier men — of whom most plainly Polemo — had said that the highest good is to live according to nature, the Stoics say that three things are signified by these words: one of this sort, to live applying knowledge of those things which happen by nature. This very thing they say is the end of Zeno, declaring that which was said by you, to live agreeably with nature.

I pass over many, and among them a learned and agreeable man, Hieronymus — whom now I know not why I should call a Peripatetic. For he set forth freedom from pain as the highest good; but whoever disagrees about the highest good disagrees about the whole system of philosophy. Critolaus wished to imitate the ancients, and indeed is nearest in gravity, and his discourse overflows; and yet not even he abides in his country's institutions. Diodorus, his hearer, joins freedom from pain to honourableness. He too is his own man, and, disagreeing about the highest good, cannot truly be called a Peripatetic. But the opinion of the ancients our Antiochus seems to me to pursue most diligently — the same which he teaches was held by Aristotle and Polemo.

'See, Torquatus,' said I, 'how greatly you are mistaken. The style of that philosopher does not offend me; for he both grasps in words what he means and says plainly what I can understand. And yet I would not reject eloquence in a philosopher if he offered it, nor would I greatly demand it if he had it none. It is in substance that he does not equally satisfy me — and that in several places. But there are as many opinions as there are men; so I may be mistaken.' 'Why, then, does he not satisfy you?' he said. 'For I count you a fair judge, provided you know well what he says.'

Do I seem, then, to grasp the force of words sufficiently, or am I still to be taught to speak either Greek or Latin? And yet take care lest, if I do not understand what Epicurus says — though I know Greek, as it seems, brilliantly — there be some fault in him who so speaks that he is not understood. This happens without blame in two ways: either if you do it on purpose, as Heraclitus, 'surnamed the Obscure, because he wrote of nature too darkly,' or when the obscurity of the matter, not of the words, makes the discourse not understood, as is the case in Plato's Timaeus. But Epicurus, as I think, neither is unwilling, if he can, to speak plainly and openly, nor speaks of an obscure matter, like the natural philosophers, or a technical one, like the mathematicians, but of a matter clear and easy and already spread abroad among the common people. And yet you do not deny that we understand what pleasure is, but only what he means by it. From which it follows, not that we do not understand the force of that word, but that he speaks in his own fashion and disregards ours.

'Let us make the attempt, then,' said he, 'although this theory of the Stoics has something rather difficult and obscure. For when in Greek speech these very names of new things once seemed [strange], which now long custom has worn smooth, what do you think will happen in Latin?' 'That indeed is most easy,' said I. 'For if it was lawful for Zeno, when he had found some unusual thing, to impose on it also an unheard-of name, why should it not be lawful for Cato? Nor yet will it be necessary to render word for word, as unskilful translators are wont, when there is a word more in use which declares the same. For my part, I am even wont, when the Greeks have a thing in one word, if I cannot otherwise, to set it forth in several. And yet I think it ought to be conceded to us that we use a Greek word, if ever a Latin one is less ready — lest this be granted to ephippia and acratophora rather than to proegmena and apoproegmena; although these indeed it will be right to call \"things preferred\" and \"things rejected.\"'

The second is signified the same, as if it were said, to live preserving all or most of the middle duties. This, so set forth, is unlike the former. For the former is right — what you called katorthoma — and falls to the wise man alone; but this is of a certain inchoate duty, not perfected, which can fall to some of the unwise. The third, however, is to live enjoying all, or the greatest, of those things which are according to nature. This is not placed in our own action. For it is filled out both from that kind of life which enjoys virtue, and from those things which are according to nature and are not in our power. But this highest good, which is understood in the third signification, and that life which is led from the highest good — because virtue is joined to it — falls to the wise man alone; and this end of goods, as we see written by the Stoics themselves, was established by Xenocrates and by Aristotle. And so by them that first constitution of nature, from which you too set out, is set forth in nearly these words:

Our Lucius, then, does prudently, who would rather hear about the highest good; for this being established, all things in philosophy are established. For in other matters, if anything has been passed over or unknown, there is no more of harm than is the worth of each of those things in which something has been neglected. But if the highest good be unknown, the plan of living must be unknown; from which so great an error follows that men cannot know into what harbour they may betake themselves. But the ends of things being known — when it is understood what is both the uttermost of goods and of evils — the road of life is found, and the shaping of all duties, when it is inquired to what each thing is to be referred;

'Unless you suppose,' said I, 'that Phaedrus or Zeno lied to me — and I heard them both, though they recommended to me nothing at all beyond their diligence — all the opinions of Epicurus are sufficiently known to me. And those whom I have named I heard frequently along with our Atticus, who admired them both, but loved Phaedrus besides; and daily we compared between ourselves what we had heard, nor was there ever any dispute about what I understood, but only about what I approved.'

For if he says the same as Hieronymus, who holds that the highest good is to live without any annoyance, why does he prefer to say 'pleasure' rather than 'freedom from pain,' as Hieronymus does, who understands what he says? But if he thinks that pleasure must be added — that which is in motion (for so he calls this sweet kind, 'in motion,' and the other, of one feeling no pain, 'in steadiness') — what is he aiming at? Since he cannot bring it about that to anyone who is known to himself — that is, who has perceived his own nature and feeling — freedom from pain and pleasure should seem the same thing. This is to do violence, Torquatus, to the senses, to wrench from our minds the meanings of words with which we have been imbued. For who is there who does not see that there are in the nature of things these three states? One, when we are in pleasure; another, when in pain; this third, in which now indeed I am, and you also, I believe — neither in pain nor in pleasure: so that the man who feasts is in pleasure, the man who is tortured in pain. But do you not see, between these, so great a multitude of men set in the middle, neither rejoicing nor grieving?

'You do well,' said he, 'in helping me; and indeed those words which you just now spoke I will rather use the Latin; in the rest you will come to my aid, if you see me sticking.' 'I will do it diligently,' said I; 'but \"fortune favours the bold\"; so make the attempt, I pray. For what can we do more divine than this?' 'It is the view,' said he, 'of those whose reasoning I approve, that as soon as a living creature is born — for here we must begin — it is reconciled to itself and commended to itself, for its own preservation and for the love of its own state, and of those things which preserve that state; but is estranged from destruction and from those things which seem to bring destruction. That this is so they prove by the fact that, before pleasure or pain has touched them, infants seek what is wholesome and spurn the contrary — which would not happen unless they loved their own state and feared destruction. But it could not be that they should seek anything unless they had a sense of themselves, and thereby loved themselves. From which it ought to be understood that the principle is derived from self-love.

Every nature wishes to be the preserver of itself, that it may be safe and be preserved in its own kind. To this end, they say, arts too were sought, which might help nature; among which is counted in the first place that which is the art of living, that it may guard what has been given by nature, and acquire what is lacking. And they divided the nature of man into mind and body. And since they had said that each of these is to be sought for its own sake, they said that the virtues too of each of them are to be sought for their own sake; and since they set the mind before the body with a certain infinite praise, they also set the virtues of the mind before the goods of the body.

from which the plan of living happily — that which all men seek — can be found and procured. But since there is great disagreement as to in what this lies, we must employ the Carneadean division, which our Antiochus is wont gladly to use. He, then, saw not only how many opinions of philosophers about the highest good there had been so far, but how many altogether there could be. He denied, then, that there is any art which proceeds from itself; for always that which is comprehended by the art is outside it. There is no need to make this longer by examples. For it is plain that no art is concerned with itself, but that the art itself is one thing, and what is set before the art another. Since, then, as medicine is the art of health, steering of navigation, so prudence is the art of living, it is necessary that it too be established and proceed from some thing.

'What, then, is it?' said he; 'for I long to hear what you do not approve.' 'First,' said I, 'in physics, on which he prides himself most, he is wholly unoriginal. He repeats the doctrines of Democritus, changing very little, but in such a way that what he means to correct he seems to me rather to spoil. Those bodies which he calls atoms — that is, particles indivisible by reason of their solidity — he holds to be carried through the infinite void, in which there is nothing highest nor lowest, nothing middle, last, or outermost, in such a way that by their collisions they cling together, and from this are produced all the things that exist and are perceived; and this motion of the atoms, he thinks, must be understood as having no beginning, but as existing from eternity.

'Not at all,' said he; 'and I say that all who are without pain are in pleasure, and that the highest pleasure too.' 'Then you put in the same pleasure the man who, not being thirsty himself, mixes mead for another, and the man who, being thirsty, drinks it?' Then he said: 'An end of questioning, if you please — which indeed I said from the first I preferred, foreseeing this very thing, the captious snares of dialectic.' 'Do you, then,' said I, 'prefer that we argue rhetorically rather than dialectically?' 'As though,' said he, 'continuous discourse belonged to the rhetoricians only, and not also to the philosophers.' 'This is the Stoic Zeno's saying,' said I: 'that the whole faculty of speech (as Aristotle had said before) is divided into two parts, and that rhetoric is like the open palm, dialectic like the closed fist, because the rhetoricians speak more broadly, the dialecticians more compressed. I shall therefore yield to your wish, and speak, if I can, rhetorically — but with this rhetoric of the philosophers, not that forensic kind of ours, which, since it speaks to the people, must needs be at times a little blunter.

But most of the Stoics do not think that pleasure should be placed among the first natural principles of self-love. With whom I strongly agree, lest, if nature should seem to have placed pleasure among the things first sought, many base consequences should follow. But it seems argument enough why we love those things which are first taken on by nature, that there is no one who, when either is allowed, would not rather have all the parts of his body fit and whole than, with the same use, maimed or distorted. But the cognitions of things — which we may call comprehensions or perceptions, or, if these words please less or are less understood, katalepseis — these very things, then, we judge to be taken on for their own sake, because they have in them something that, as it were, embraces and contains truth. And this can be understood in infants, whom we see delighted, even though it be of no interest to them, if they have found out anything by reason of themselves.

But since they would have wisdom to be the guardian and manager of the whole man, as one that was the companion and helper of nature, they said this was the office of wisdom: that, since it watched over him who consisted of mind and body, it should aid and sustain him in both. And so, the matter being first simply set down, in pursuing the rest more subtly, they thought the goods of the body had a certain easy account; about the goods of the mind they inquired more carefully, and in the first place they found that there were in them the seeds of justice, and they were the first of all the philosophers to teach that it is granted by nature that those who are begotten should be loved by their begetters; and — which in order of time is more ancient — that the unions of husbands and wives are joined by nature, from which stock the friendships of kinship arise. And setting out from these beginnings, they pursued both the origin and the progress of all the virtues. From which greatness of mind also arose, by which one could easily resist and withstand fortune, because the greatest matters were in the power of the wise man. But the changes and injuries of fortune a life ordered by the precepts of the old philosophers easily overcame.

But it has been pretty well agreed among all that that in which prudence is concerned, and which it wishes to attain, ought to be fitted and accommodated to nature, and such that of itself it invites and allures the appetite of the mind, which the Greeks call horme. But what it is that so moves and is so sought by nature at the first origin is not agreed, and about it is all the disagreement among the philosophers when the highest good is sought out. For of that whole question which is held about the ends of goods and evils — when it is inquired what in these is the uttermost and last — the source must be found, in which are the first invitations of nature; and this being found, the whole discussion about the highest good and evil is drawn from it as from a head. Some think the first appetite is for pleasure, and the first repelling for pain. Others judge that freedom from pain is first taken on, and pain first turned away.

Now Epicurus does not greatly err in the points where he follows Democritus. Yet, while there is much in both of them that I do not approve, this above all: that whereas in the nature of things two questions must be asked — one, what is the matter out of which each thing is made; the other, what is the force which makes each thing — they discoursed about matter, but left aside the force and cause of making. But this is a fault common to both; the following ruins are peculiar to Epicurus. For he holds that those same indivisible and solid bodies are carried downward by their own weight in a straight line, and that this is the natural motion of all bodies.

But while Epicurus despises dialectic, Torquatus — which alone contains both the whole knowledge of perceiving what is in each thing, and of judging of what kind each thing is, and of arguing by method and rule — he stumbles in speaking, as it seems to me at least, and distinguishes by no art the very things he wishes to teach, such as these very matters of which we were just now speaking. The highest good is by you called pleasure. We must, then, lay open what pleasure is; for otherwise what is sought cannot be explained. And had he laid it open, he would not be so at a loss. For he would either uphold that pleasure which Aristippus upholds — that is, by which the sense is sweetly and pleasantly moved, which even the beasts, if they could speak, would call pleasure — or, if he preferred to speak in his own fashion, rather than as 'all the Danai and the Mycenaeans, the youth of Attica,' and the rest of the Greeks who are summoned in this anapaest, he would call by the name of pleasure this not-being-in-pain alone, and despise that Aristippean kind; or, if he approved of both, as he does, he would join freedom from pain with pleasure, and use two ultimate goods.

The arts themselves too we think must be taken on for their own sake, both because there is in them something worthy of being taken on, and because they consist of cognitions and contain in them something established by reason and method. But from false assent they judge that we are more estranged than from the other things which are contrary to nature. Now of the limbs — that is, the parts of the body — some seem to have been given by nature for the sake of their use, as the hands, the legs, the feet, and those things which are within the body, whose usefulness, how great it is, is even disputed by the physicians; but others for no usefulness, but, as it were, for a certain adornment, as the tail to the peacock, the parti-coloured plumes to doves, breasts and beard to men.

And from the principles given by nature certain enlargements of goods were aroused, partly proceeding from the contemplation of more hidden things, because there was implanted in the mind a love of knowledge, from which followed also the desire of unfolding reason and of arguing; and because this creature alone was born sharing in shame and modesty and desiring the conjunctions of men for society, and observing in all things which it should do or say that nothing be done by it except honourably and becomingly — from these beginnings, as I said before, and these seeds given by nature, temperance, modesty, justice, and all honourableness was perfectly completed.

From these, others set out from those things which they name the first according to nature, among which they count the soundness and preservation of all the parts, health, the senses entire, freedom from pain, strength, beauty, and the rest of that kind; like to which are the first things in the mind, the little sparks, as it were, and seeds of the virtues. Since of these three some one is that by which nature is first moved either to seeking or to repelling, and nothing at all besides these three can be, it is necessary that the whole duty of fleeing or following be referred to some one of them, so that that prudence which we said is the art of life is concerned with some one of those three things, from which it draws the beginning of the whole life.

Then, in the same place, the acute fellow, when this difficulty met him — that if all things were borne straight down, and, as I said, in a straight line, no atom could ever touch another — brought in a fiction of his own devising: he said that the atom swerves a very little, by the least amount conceivable; and that thus are produced the entanglements and couplings and cohesions of atoms among themselves, from which arise the world and all the parts of the world and whatever is in it. Now this whole notion is a childish invention, and besides it does not even achieve what he intends. For the swerve itself is imagined arbitrarily — he says the atom swerves without a cause, than which nothing is more disgraceful in a natural philosopher than to say that anything comes to be without a cause — and that natural motion of all weights toward the lower region in a straight line, which he himself had laid down, he took away from the atoms without cause, and yet did not attain the end for which he had invented all this.

For many and great philosophers have made these ultimate goods composite: as Aristotle joined the exercise of virtue with the prosperity of a complete life; Callipho added pleasure to the honourable; Diodorus added freedom from pain to that same honourable. Epicurus would have done the same, had he joined this opinion, which is now Hieronymus's, with the old opinion of Aristippus. For these two disagree with each other. Therefore they use single ends, and, though each speaks Greek admirably, neither does Aristippus, who calls pleasure the highest good, place freedom from pain in pleasure, nor does Hieronymus, who sets the highest good as freedom from pain, ever use the name of pleasure for that painlessness — since indeed he does not even count pleasure among things to be sought.

These things are said, perhaps, rather meagrely; for they are, as it were, the first elements of nature, to which the richness of discourse can hardly be applied, nor indeed do I think of pursuing it. But yet, when you speak of grander matters, the things themselves snatch the words; so the discourse becomes both weightier and also more splendid.' 'It is as you say,' said I; 'but yet everything that is said clearly about a good matter seems to me admirably said. But to wish to speak ornately about such matters is childish; while to be able to expound them plainly and clearly is the mark of a learned and intelligent man.'

'You have, Cato,' said I, 'the form of those philosophers of whom I speak.
