This being set forth, I long to know what the cause is why Zeno departed from this ancient constitution; which of these things was not approved by him: that they said every nature is the preserver of itself, or that every creature is commended to itself, so that it should wish itself both safe in its own kind and unharmed; or that, since the end of all the arts was that which nature most sought, the same ought to be laid down about the art of life as a whole; or that, since we consist of mind and body, both these very things and their virtues are to be taken for their own sake. Or did that so great pre-eminence which was assigned to the virtues of the mind displease him? Or the things which are said about prudence, about the knowledge of things, about the conjunction of the human race, and the things said by these same men about temperance, about modesty, about greatness of mind, about all honourableness? The Stoics will confess that all these things were said admirably, and that this was not the cause for Zeno's departing.

But from that which a man shall have determined to be the thing by which nature is first moved, there will arise also the reasoning of the right and the honourable, which may agree with some one of those three — so that it is honourable either to do all things for the sake of pleasure, even if you do not attain it; or of not being in pain, even if you cannot attain it; or of attaining the things which are according to nature, even if you attain nothing. So it comes about that, as great as is the difference in the natural principles, so great is the unlikeness in the ends of goods and evils. Others again, from the same principles, will refer every duty either to pleasure, or to not being in pain, or to obtaining those first things according to nature.

For if all the atoms swerve, none will ever cling together; while if some swerve and others are borne straight by their own inclination, this will be, first, to assign as it were provinces to the atoms — which shall move straight and which obliquely; and second, that same turbulent collision of atoms (in which Democritus too is stuck) will not be able to produce this ordered beauty of the world. Nor is it the part of a natural philosopher to believe that there is any smallest thing — which assuredly he would never have supposed, had he chosen to learn geometry from his friend Polyaenus rather than to unteach the man himself. The sun seems large to Democritus, as to one learned and accomplished in geometry; to Epicurus perhaps a foot wide. For he thinks it just so big as it appears, or a little larger or smaller.

For there are two things here too, lest you think them mere words. The one is to be without pain, the other to be with pleasure. You try, out of these two things so unlike, to make not only one name — for that I should more easily endure — but even one thing out of two; which can in no way be done. This man, who approves of both, ought to have used both, as he does in fact, and yet does not divide them in words. For when he praises in very many passages that very pleasure which we all call by the same name, he dares to say that he cannot even suspect any good severed from that Aristippean kind of pleasure; and he says this where his whole discourse is on the highest good. But in another book, in which, with the gravest opinions briefly compressed, he is said to have published, as it were, the oracles of wisdom, he writes in these words — which are surely known to you, Torquatus, for who of you has not learned by heart the Kyriai Doxai of Epicurus, that is, his Authoritative Maxims, so called because they are the gravest opinions for living happily, briefly stated? Mark, then, whether I interpret this maxim rightly:

'Let us proceed, then,' said he, 'since we have departed from these principles of nature, with which the things that follow ought to agree. And this is the first division. They say that that is to be valued — for so, I think, let us call it — which is either itself according to nature, or produces some such thing, so that it is worthy of selection because it has some weight worthy of valuation, which they call axia; and, on the contrary, that is to be unvalued which is contrary to the former. The beginnings, then, being so established, that those things which are according to nature are to be taken for their own sake, and their contraries likewise rejected, the first duty — for so I call kathekon — is that one preserve oneself in the state of nature; next, that one hold those things which are according to nature and repel their contraries. And this selection and likewise rejection being found, there follows next selection joined with duty; then that selection continuous; then at last constant and consistent with nature; in which there first begins to be present, and to be understood, what it is that can truly be called good.

They will say, I suppose, that there were certain other great errors of the ancients, which that man, eager for investigating the truth, could by no means bear. For what is more perverse, what more intolerable, what more foolish, than to place good health, freedom from all pains, the integrity of the eyes and the other senses among goods — rather than to say that there is no difference at all between those things and their contraries? For all those things which they called goods are, he says, preferred, not good; and likewise those things which excel in the body, the ancients foolishly said are to be sought for their own sake; rather to be taken than to be sought. And finally, that whole life which consisted in virtue alone — that life which abounded also in the other things which were according to nature was not more to be sought, but rather to be taken. And although virtue itself produces a life so happy that it cannot be happier, yet certain things are lacking to the wise even when they are most happy; and so they do this, that they may repel from themselves pains, diseases, infirmities.

Six opinions, then, about the highest good having now been set forth, of the three nearest these are the chiefs: of pleasure, Aristippus; of not being in pain, Hieronymus; of enjoying those things which we said are the first according to nature, Carneades — not indeed as their author, but as their defender for the sake of argument. The three earlier were such as could be; of which one alone has been defended, and that vehemently. For that one should do all things for the sake of pleasure, when, even if we attain nothing, yet that very purpose of so acting is in itself to be sought, and honourable, and the only good — no one has said. Nor did anyone think that the avoidance of pain itself, for its own sake, is among things to be sought, unless one could also avoid it. But that to do all things, that we may attain the things which are according to nature, even if we do not attain them, is both honourable and the only thing to be sought for its own sake, and the only good — the Stoics say.

Thus what he alters he spoils, and what he keeps is wholly Democritus's: the atoms, the void, the images which they call eidola, by whose impact we not only see but also think; and that very infinity which they call apeiria comes entirely from him, as do the countless worlds that come to be and perish daily. These doctrines, though by no means approved by me, yet I should not wish Democritus, praised by all others, to be reviled by this man who alone followed him.

'If the things that produce the pleasures of the luxurious freed them from the fear of the gods, of death, and of pain, and taught them what the limits of their desires are, we should have nothing to blame, since they would be filled on every side with pleasures, and would have, on no side, anything either painful or distressing — which is the evil.' At this point Triarius could not contain himself. 'I beg you, Torquatus,' said he, 'does Epicurus say this?' — for he seemed to me, though he knew it, yet to wish to hear Torquatus confess it. But Torquatus was by no means alarmed, and answered confidently enough: 'In those very words,' said he; 'but you do not see what he means.' 'If he means one thing,' said I, 'and says another, I shall never understand what he means; but he says plainly what he understands. And if he says this — that the luxurious are not to be blamed, if they are wise — he speaks absurdly, just as if he should say that parricides are not to be blamed, if they are neither greedy, nor fear the gods, nor death, nor pain. And yet what is the point of granting any exemption to the luxurious, or of imagining some who, while living luxuriously, would not be blamed by the chief of philosophers on that score at least, provided they guarded against the rest?

For the first reconciliation of man is to those things which are according to nature. But as soon as he has gained intelligence, or rather a notion — which they call ennoia — and has seen the order of things to be done and, so to speak, their harmony, he values it much more than all those things which he first loved; and so by knowledge and reason he gathers that in this is placed that highest good of man which is to be praised and sought for its own sake — which, since it lies in that which the Stoics call homologia, and we, if you please, may call \"consistency\" — since, then, in this lies that good to which all things are to be referred, namely honourable deeds and the honourable itself, which alone is counted among goods, although it arises later, yet it alone is to be sought by its own force and worth; but of those things which are first in nature, none is to be sought for its own sake.

O great force of genius, and just cause why a new school should arise! Go on further. For there follow those things which you most learnedly embraced: that the folly, injustice, and other like vices of all men are equal, and that all sins are equal, and that those who by nature and teaching had advanced far toward virtue, unless they had plainly attained it, are supremely wretched, and there is nothing at all between their life and that of the most wicked — so that Plato, that great man, if he was not wise, lived no whit better or more happily than any most wicked man. This, forsooth, is the correction and emendation of the old philosophy — which can have no access at all into the city, into the forum, into the senate-house! For who could bear a man so speaking, who professed himself the author of a life to be led gravely and wisely, changing the names of things, and, while he held the same opinion as all men, imposing other names on the things to which he assigned the same force, changing only the words, taking nothing away from the opinions?

These six, then, are the simple opinions about the highest of goods and evils — two without a patron, four defended. But of the joined and double expositions of the highest good there were altogether three, nor indeed could there be more, if you look deeply into the nature of things. For either pleasure can be joined to honourableness, as it pleased Callipho and Dinomachus; or freedom from pain, as Diodorus; or the first things of nature, as the ancients, whom we have named both Academics and Peripatetics. But since all things cannot be said at once, these things must for the present be noted: that pleasure is to be set aside, since we are born for certain greater things, as will soon appear. About freedom from pain much the same things are wont to be said as about pleasure. Since, then, both about pleasure with Torquatus, and about honourableness, in which alone all good was placed, with Cato, it has been disputed, first, the things which were said against pleasure fall much the same against freedom from pain.

Now in the other part of philosophy, that of inquiry and discussion, which is called logic, this master of yours is, as it seems to me at least, plainly unarmed and naked. He does away with definitions; he teaches nothing about dividing and partitioning; he hands down no method by which a chain of reasoning is constructed and concluded; he shows no way by which captious arguments are solved and ambiguities distinguished; he places the judgment of things in the senses, holding that if once anything false is approved as true, all judgment of true and false is overthrown.

But still, would you not blame the luxurious, Epicurus, for this very cause — that they so live as to pursue pleasures of every kind — especially since, as you say, the highest pleasure is to feel no pain? And yet we shall find profligates, first, so irreligious that they eat off the sacred dish; then so unafraid of death that they have on their lips that line from the Hymnis: \"Six months of life are enough for me; the seventh I pledge to the grave.\" And now they will produce those Epicurean remedies for pain, as from a medicine-chest: \"If severe, short; if long, slight.\" One thing I do not know — how a man can have his desires limited, if he is a profligate.

But since those things which I have called duties proceed from the beginnings of nature, they must necessarily be referred to these, so that it can rightly be said that all duties are referred to this, that we may attain the first principles of nature — yet not so that this is the uttermost of goods, because honourable action is not present in the first reconciliations of nature; for it is consequent and arises later, as I said. It is, however, according to nature, and exhorts us to seek it much more than all the earlier things. But from this an error must first be removed, lest anyone think it follows that there are two uttermost goods. For if anyone's purpose were to aim a spear or an arrow at something, then, just as we say the uttermost in goods, so he, to do everything he can to take aim — in such a comparison everything must be done by him to take aim, and yet, though he does everything to attain his purpose, this is, as it were, his uttermost end, such as we call the highest good in life; but that he should hit it is, as it were, to be selected, not to be sought.

Would an advocate, pleading in his peroration for a defendant, deny that exile, the confiscation of goods, are evils? That these are to be rejected, not shunned? And that a judge ought not to be merciful? Or if he were speaking in an assembly — if Hannibal had come to the gates and hurled a javelin over the wall — would he deny that to be captured, to be sold, to be slain, to lose one's country are among evils? Or could the senate, when it decreed a triumph to Africanus, speak of 'his virtue' or 'his good fortune,' if neither virtue can be said to be in any but the wise man, nor good fortune truly? What sort of philosophy, then, is that, which speaks in the common manner in the forum, in its own little books? — especially since, in what they signify by their own words, nothing is made new, nothing about the things themselves is changed, the same things remaining in another fashion.

Nor indeed are other things to be sought against that Carneadean opinion. For in whatever way the highest good is so set forth that it lacks honourableness, neither duties nor virtues nor friendships can stand in that reasoning. But the joining of either pleasure or not being in pain with honourableness makes that very honourable thing which it wishes to embrace base. For to refer the things you do to those things, of which the one, if a man be free from evil, one would say he is in the highest good, the other is concerned with the lightest part of nature — this is to darken, not to say to defile, all the splendour of honourableness. There remain the Stoics, who, when they had transferred all things from the Peripatetics and Academics, pursued the same things under other names. These it is better to speak against one by one. But now, what we are about;

But he confirms above all the doctrine that Nature herself, as he says, decrees and approves — that is, pleasure and pain. To these he refers everything that we should pursue or shun. Though this is the teaching of Aristippus, and is better and more frankly defended by the Cyrenaics, yet I judge it to be of such a kind that nothing seems more unworthy of man. For to greater things, in my opinion at least, Nature begot and shaped us. And I may be mistaken; but I am wholly of this mind — that the Torquatus who first won this surname did not strip that torque from his enemy in order to derive from his body some bodily pleasure, nor fight against the Latins at the Veseris in his third consulship for the sake of pleasure; and as for his striking off his son's head with the axe, he seems even to have deprived himself of many pleasures, since he set the right of sovereignty and command above Nature herself and above a father's love.

What, then, is the point of saying, 'I should have nothing to blame, if they had their desires limited'? This is to say: I should not blame profligates, if they were not profligates. In that manner one would not blame the wicked either, if they were good men. This severe man does not think luxury itself, in and of itself, blameworthy; and indeed, Torquatus, to speak the truth, if the highest good is pleasure, he very rightly does not think so. For do not imagine to me profligates, as you are wont, who vomit at the table, who are carried away from banquets and, still gorged, the next day cram themselves again; who, as they say, have never seen the sun set or rise; who, their patrimonies spent, are in want. No one of us thinks that profligates of that kind live pleasantly. But men neat and elegant, with the best cooks, bakers, fishing, fowling, hunting, all these things choice; avoiding indigestion; for whom the wine, drawn from a full jar, is 'golden,' as Lucilius says, 'whom neither the strainer nor the little bag has yet robbed of anything'; men who employ entertainments, and what follows, those things which, if taken away, Epicurus cries that he does not know what good is; let there be present too handsome boys to wait at table; let the dress, the silver, the Corinthian bronze, the very place, the building answer to all this — such profligates, then, I should never say live well, or happily.

But since all duties proceed from the beginnings of nature, from these same it must be that wisdom itself proceeds. But just as it often happens that one who has been commended to someone esteems him to whom he is commended more than him by whom he was commended, so it is by no means strange that we are at first commended to wisdom by the beginnings of nature, but afterward wisdom itself becomes dearer to us than those things by which we came to it. And as the limbs were so given to us that they appear to have been given for a certain plan of living, so the appetite of the mind, which is called horme in Greek, seems to have been given not for any kind of life whatever, but for a certain form of living; and likewise reason, and perfected reason.

For what does it matter whether you call riches, resources, health goods or 'preferred things,' since he who calls them goods assigns no more to them than you who name those same things 'preferred'? And so a man most freeborn and grave, worthy of that intimacy of Scipio and Laelius, Panaetius, when he wrote to Quintus Tubero about the bearing of pain — what ought to have been the head of the matter, if it could be proved, namely that pain is not an evil — he nowhere set down, but what it was, and of what kind, and how much there was in it of alien, and then what the method of enduring it was; whose opinion, indeed, since he was a Stoic, seems to me to have condemned that emptiness of words.

of them, when we shall wish. But the unconcern of Democritus, which is, as it were, a tranquillity of mind, which they call euthymia, had to be set apart from this discussion, because that very tranquillity of mind is the happy life itself; but we are inquiring, not what it is, but whence it comes. Now the opinions of Pyrrho, Aristo, Erillus, hissed off and cast out — because they cannot fall within this circle which we have described — ought not to have been employed at all. For since this whole question about the ends and, as it were, the uttermost of goods and evils proceeds from that which we said is fitted and accommodated to nature, and which itself is first sought for its own sake, this whole thing both they take away, who in those matters in which there is nothing that is not either honourable or base deny that there is any cause why one thing should be preferred to another, and think there is no difference at all among those things; and Erillus, if he so felt that there is nothing good except knowledge, took away every cause of forming a counsel and the discovery of duty. The opinions of the rest being thus excluded, since there can be none besides, this opinion of the ancients must necessarily prevail. Therefore, by the institution of the ancients, which the Stoics too use, let us take our beginning here.

Again — when Titus Torquatus, who was consul with Gnaeus Octavius, used that severity toward the son whom he had given in adoption to Decimus Silanus, ordering him, when the envoys of the Macedonians accused him of having taken money as praetor in the province, to plead his cause before himself, and, after hearing both sides, pronounced that he did not seem to have shown himself in his command such as his ancestors had been, and forbade him to come into his sight — does he seem to you to have given any thought to his own pleasures? But to pass over the dangers, the toils, the pain too which every best man takes upon himself for his country and for his kindred — so that he not only seizes no pleasure but even passes by all pleasures, and would rather endure any pains whatever than abandon a single part of his duty — let us come to those things which declare this no less, but seem of lighter weight. What pleasure, Torquatus, do letters bring to you, or to Triarius here? Or history and the knowledge of affairs? Or the unrolling of the poets, or the holding in memory of so many verses?

From which it follows, not that pleasure is not pleasure, but that pleasure is not the highest good. Nor was that Laelius, who as a young man had heard the Stoic Diogenes and afterward Panaetius, called wise because he did not understand what was most delicious — for it does not follow that he whose heart is wise should not have a wise palate — but because he reckoned it of little worth. 'O sorrel,' as he says, 'how you boast, and are scarce well enough known for what you are!' In this knowing, that famous Laelius used to raise the cry, 'Wise!' — rebuking our gluttons one by one. Admirably said Laelius, and rightly 'wise'; and that too truly: 'O Publius, O whirlpool, Gallonius! you are a wretched man,' he says; 'never in your life have you dined well, who spend all that you have on that prawn and sturgeon with the great-sized fish.' This is said by a man who, placing nothing in pleasure, denies that the man dines well who places everything in pleasure; and yet he does not deny that Gallonius ever dined pleasantly — for that would be a lie — but that he dined well. So gravely and severely did he separate pleasure from the good. From which it follows that all who dine well dine pleasantly, but not that all who dine pleasantly dine well. Laelius always dined well.

For as to the actor his action, to the dancer his motion is given — not any whatever, but a certain definite one — so life must be led in a certain definite kind, not in any whatever; and this kind we call \"agreeing\" and \"consistent.\" For we do not judge wisdom to be like steering or medicine, but rather like that action which I just mentioned, and like dancing — so that the uttermost end, that is, the performance of the art, is in the art itself, not sought from without. And yet there is also some unlikeness between wisdom and these very arts, because in them the things rightly done do not yet contain all the parts of which they consist; whereas the things which we may call \"right\" or \"rightly done,\" if you please — but which they call katorthomata — contain all the numbers of virtue. For wisdom alone is wholly turned in upon itself, which does not happen in the other arts.

But that I may come nearer to those things, Cato, which were said by you, let us proceed more closely, and let us compare those things which you just now said with those which I set before yours. The things, then, which are common to you with the ancients, let us so use as if they were granted; the things which come into controversy, of these, if you please, let us discuss.' 'I, indeed,' said he, 'am pleased that we proceed more subtly and, as you yourself said, more closely. For the things which you have so far brought forward are popular; but I desire more elegant things from you.' 'From me?' said I. 'But yet I will strive, and, if not many things occur to me, I will not flee those popular ones.

Every living creature loves itself, and, as soon as it is born, does this, that it may preserve itself; because this first appetite for guarding its whole life is given it by nature — that it should preserve itself and be so disposed that it may be best disposed according to nature. This constitution it has at first confused and uncertain, so that it only guards itself, of whatever sort it be, but understands neither what it is, nor what it can do, nor what its own nature is. But when it has advanced a little, and has begun to perceive how far each thing touches it and pertains to it, then it begins gradually to advance, and to recognize itself and to understand for what cause it has that appetite of mind which we mentioned, and it begins both to seek the things which it feels are fitted to nature and to repel their contraries. Therefore for every living creature that which it seeks is placed in that which is accommodated to nature. So the end of goods arises — to live according to nature, so disposed that one can be best disposed and most accommodated to nature.

And do not tell me this: 'Why, these very things are a pleasure to me, and so were those deeds to the Torquati.' Never did Epicurus so defend his doctrine, nor Metrodorus, nor any of them who had either any wisdom or had learned these things. And as for the question often raised, why there are so many Epicureans — there are other causes too, but what most attracts the multitude is this: that they think Epicurus says that right and honourable deeds produce of themselves gladness, that is, pleasure. These excellent men do not understand that the whole theory is overthrown if the matter so stands. For if it were granted that those things are pleasant of their own accord and in themselves, even though nothing be referred to the body, then virtue too and the knowledge of things would be desirable in and for themselves — which is the very last thing he wishes.

What is 'well'? Lucilius will say: 'cooked and seasoned'; but give me the chief dish of the dinner: 'good conversation.' What follows from that? 'If you ask, pleasantly'; for he came to dinner to satisfy the demands of nature with a quiet mind. Rightly, then, does he deny that Gallonius ever dined well; rightly calls him wretched, especially since he spent all his zeal upon it — Gallonius, whom no one denies to have dined pleasantly. Why, then, not well? Because what is 'well' is rightly, frugally, honourably done; whereas he dined badly, crookedly, basely, shamefully — therefore not well. And Laelius did not prefer the sweetness of sorrel to Gallonius's sturgeon, but disregarded sweetness itself; which he would not have done, had he placed the highest good in pleasure.

But it is unskilful to compare the uttermost end of medicine and steering with the uttermost end of wisdom. For wisdom embraces both greatness of mind and justice, and judges all things that befall a man to be beneath itself — which does not happen in the other arts. But no one will be able to hold those very virtues of which I just made mention, unless he has determined that there is nothing which differs or is distinct, one thing from another, except things honourable and base.

But first let it be laid down that we ourselves are commended to ourselves, and that we have from nature this first appetite, that we preserve ourselves. This is agreed. There follows this — that we observe who we ourselves are, that we may keep ourselves such as we ought to be. We are, then, men. We consist of mind and body, which are of a certain kind; and we ought, as the first natural appetite demands, to love these and to establish from them that end of the highest and uttermost good. And this, if the first things are true, must be so established: to attain as many and as great as possible of the things which are according to nature.

But since each living creature has its own nature, it is necessary that the end too of all be this, that nature be filled out — for nothing forbids certain things to be common both among the other living creatures themselves, and to man with the beasts, since the nature of all is common — but those uttermost and highest things which we seek are distinct and divided among the kinds of living creatures, and each one has its own, fitted to that which the nature of each desires.

'These doctrines of Epicurus, then,' said I, 'I do not approve. For the rest, I could indeed wish either that he himself had been better equipped with learning — for he is, as you must needs admit, not sufficiently polished in those arts whose masters are called cultured — or that he had not deterred others from such studies. Though I see that you at least have by no means been deterred.' When I had said this, more to provoke him than to speak myself, Triarius, smiling gently, said: 'Why, you have nearly removed Epicurus altogether from the chorus of philosophers. What have you left him, except that, however he expressed himself, you understand what he meant? In physics he said what was borrowed, and not even those things which you would approve; whatever he tried to correct in them, he made worse. Of the art of reasoning he had none. In calling pleasure the highest good, he first saw too little in that very point, and then this too was borrowed; for Aristippus said it before, and said it better. At the end you added that he was unlearned as well.'

Pleasure, therefore, must be set aside, not only that you may follow what is right, but also that it may become you to speak with frugality. Can we, then, call it the highest good in life, when we seem unable to call it so even at dinner? But how does the philosopher speak? 'Three kinds of desires: natural and necessary; natural and not necessary; neither natural nor necessary.' First, he divided inelegantly; for he made three kinds out of what were two. This is not to divide, but to shatter. Those who have learned the things which he despises are wont to proceed thus: 'Two kinds of desires, natural and empty; of the natural, two — necessary and not necessary.' The matter would have been finished. For it is faulty, in dividing, to count a part among the kinds.

Let us now see how admirably those things follow which I have already laid down. For since this is the uttermost end — for you understand, I believe, that I have for some time been calling that which the Greeks say is telos now \"uttermost,\" now \"last,\" now \"highest\"; it will also be allowed to say \"end\" for \"uttermost\" or \"last\" — since, then, this is the uttermost end, to live agreeably and consistently with nature, it necessarily follows that all the wise always live happily, completely, prosperously, hindered by nothing, prevented by nothing, lacking nothing. And that which holds together no less this doctrine of which I speak than our life and fortunes — namely, that we judge that alone to be good which is honourable — this indeed can be amplified and adorned rhetorically, at length and copiously, with all the most choice words and weightiest sentences; but I am delighted by the brief and sharp corollaries of the Stoics. Their arguments, then, are concluded thus:

This end, then, those men held; and what I express in more words, they more briefly — to live according to nature — this seemed to them the uttermost of goods. Come now, let those men teach — or rather you, for who better than you? — in what way, setting out from the same principles, you bring it about that to live honourably (for that is to live either from virtue or agreeably with nature) is the highest good, and in what way, or at what point, you have suddenly deserted the body and all those things which, though they are according to nature, are not in our power, and finally duty itself. I ask, then, how those so great commendations, proceeding from nature, were suddenly abandoned by wisdom.

Wherefore when we say that the uttermost end of all living creatures is to live according to nature, it must not be taken as if we said that there is one uttermost end of all, but as it can rightly be said of all the arts that it is common to them to be concerned with some knowledge, but that the knowledge of each art is its own — so it is common to all living creatures to live according to nature, but their natures are diverse, so that one thing is from nature for the horse, another for the ox, another for man. And yet in all there is a common sum, and indeed not only in living creatures, but also in all those things which nature nourishes, increases, guards — among which we see that the things which are born from the earth do many things in a manner for themselves of their own accord, which avail for living and growing, so that they may in their own kind come to their uttermost; so that now it is allowed to embrace all things in one comprehension, and to say without hesitation that every nature is the preserver of itself, and has this set before it as, as it were, its end and uttermost — that it may guard itself in the best state of its kind; so that it must necessarily be that the end of all things which thrive by nature is like, but not the same. From which it ought to be understood that for man the uttermost of goods is to live according to nature, which we may interpret thus: to live from the nature of man perfected on every side and lacking nothing.

'It can in no way be, Triarius,' said I, 'that one should not state what he disapproves in the man from whom he dissents. For what would prevent me from being an Epicurean, if I approved what he said? — especially since to master those doctrines thoroughly would be mere play. Therefore the criticisms of those who differ among themselves are not to be blamed; but abusive speech, insults, then fits of anger, and obstinate wranglings and contentions in debate seem to me unworthy of philosophy.'

But let us grant him this. For he despises elegance in argument; he speaks confusedly. We must humour him, provided he thinks rightly. And yet that very thing I do not greatly approve, and only tolerate — a philosopher speaking of limiting the desires. Can desire be limited? It must be removed and torn out by the roots. For who is there in whom there is desire, who cannot rightly be called covetous? He will be, then, avaricious — but within limits; and an adulterer — but he will keep measure; and luxurious in the same way. What sort of philosophy is this, which brings not the destruction of depravity, but is content with a moderate amount of vice? Although in this division I wholly approve of the matter itself, I miss the elegance. Let him call these things the needs of nature, and keep the name of 'desire' for elsewhere, so that, when he speaks of avarice, of intemperance, of the greatest vices, he may arraign it as on a capital charge.

What is good is all praiseworthy; what is praiseworthy is all honourable; therefore what is good is honourable. Does this seem sufficiently concluded? Certainly; for what was produced from the two propositions that were taken, you see is concluded in it. But of the two from which the conclusion was produced, against the former it is wont to be said that not every good is praiseworthy. For that what is praiseworthy is honourable is granted. But this is most absurd — that anything should be good which is not to be sought; or to be sought, which is not pleasing; or, if that, not also to be loved; therefore also to be approved; thus also praiseworthy; and this is honourable. So it comes about that what is good is also honourable.

But if we were not seeking the highest good of man, but of some living creature, and that were nothing but mind — for let it be allowed to imagine something of that kind, that we may the more easily find the truth — yet to that mind this end of yours would not belong. For it would desire health, freedom from pain; it would also seek its own preservation and the guardianship of those things, and would establish for itself the end of living according to nature, which is, as I said, to have those things which are according to nature, either all or most and greatest.

These things, then, must be explained by us; but if rather plainly, you will pardon. For we must serve this man's age, and one now hearing these things perhaps for the first time.' 'Quite so,' said I; 'although the things which you have said so far might, even for his age, be rightly said in that manner.' 'The boundary of things to be sought being set forth, then,' said he, 'next it must be shown why that matter is so as I said. Wherefore let us begin from that which I put first, which is also in very deed first — that we may understand that every living creature loves itself. Although this has no doubt — for it is fixed in nature itself and is grasped by the senses of each so that, if anyone should wish to say the contrary, he would not be heard — yet, that we may pass over nothing, I think reasons too must be brought forward why this is so.

Then Torquatus said: 'I entirely agree; for one cannot argue without criticism, nor argue rightly with anger or obstinacy. But to all this, if it is not troublesome, I have something I should like to say.' 'And do you think,' said I, 'that I should have said these things unless I wished to hear you?' 'Do you prefer, then, that we run through Epicurus's whole system, or inquire only into the one question of pleasure, on which the whole contest turns?' 'That is for you to decide,' said I. 'I shall do so, then,' said he. 'I shall expound one matter, and that the greatest; physics another time — when I shall prove to you both that swerve of the atoms and the size of the sun, and the very many errors of Democritus criticized and corrected by Epicurus. Now I shall speak of pleasure — nothing new, of course, yet things which I am confident you yourself will approve.'

But these things, indeed, are said by him rather freely, and rather often. Which for my part I do not blame; for it befits so great and so renowned a philosopher to defend his decrees boldly. But still, from the fact that he seems often to embrace too vehemently that pleasure which all nations call by this name, he is at times in great straits — so that, if the consciousness of men be removed, there is nothing so base that he would not seem ready to do it for the sake of pleasure. Then, when he has blushed — for the force of nature is very great — he takes refuge in saying that nothing can be added to the pleasure of one feeling no pain. But that state of not being in pain is not called pleasure. 'I do not trouble,' says he, 'about the name.' What of the fact that the thing is wholly different? 'I shall find many — or rather countless — men, not so inquisitive nor so troublesome as you are, whom I shall easily persuade of what I wish.' Why, then, do we doubt that, if to feel no pain is the highest pleasure, not to be in pleasure is the greatest pain? Why is this not so? Because not pleasure is contrary to pain, but the privation of pain.

Next I ask, who can glory either of a wretched life or of one not happy? Of the happy life alone, then. From which it follows that the happy life is worthy of glorying, so to speak — which cannot rightly fall to any but an honourable life. So it comes about that the honourable life is the happy life. And since he to whom it falls to be rightly praised has something signal toward honour and glory, so that on account of things so great he can rightly be called happy, the same will most rightly be said of the life of such a man. So, if the happy life is discerned by honourableness, then what is honourable must be held the only good. But what then?

For of whatever kind of creature you establish, it must be — even if it be without a body, as we imagine — that there are yet in the mind certain things like those which are in the body, so that in no way, except as I have set forth, can the end of goods be established. But Chrysippus, setting forth the differences of living creatures, says that some of them excel in body, others in mind, and some are strong in both; then he discusses what end it is fitting to establish for each kind of living creature. But when he had placed man in that kind, so as to assign him excellence of mind, he established the highest good as that — not that the mind should excel, but that there should seem to be nothing besides the mind. But the highest good would be rightly placed in virtue alone in one way only: if there were a creature which consisted wholly of mind, and that mind itself yet such that it had nothing in itself which was according to nature, as health is.

And yet how can it be understood or conceived that there is any living creature which hates itself? For contrary things will clash. For when that appetite of mind shall have begun, with deliberation, to draw something to itself which harms it, because it is its own enemy, since it will do this for its own sake, it will both hate itself and at the same time love itself; which cannot be. And it must be that, if anyone is his own enemy, he thinks the things that are good evil, the things that are evil good on the contrary, and flees the things to be sought, seeks the things to be fled — which is, without doubt, the overturning of life. Nor indeed, if some are found who seek either nooses or other deaths, or, like that man in Terence, who 'resolved meanwhile to do less injustice to his own son,' as he himself says, 'until he should be made wretched,' is he to be thought his own enemy.

'Certainly,' said I, 'I shall not be obstinate, and shall gladly assent to you if you prove what you say.' 'I shall prove it,' said he, 'provided you keep the fairness you display. But I prefer to use continuous discourse rather than to question or be questioned.' 'As you please,' said I. Then he began to speak. 'First, then,' said he, 'I shall proceed as the author of this system himself prefers: I shall determine what the thing we are inquiring into is, and of what kind — not that I suppose you ignorant of it, but that my discourse may go forward by method and in due order. We are inquiring, then, what is the last and uttermost of goods, which in the opinion of all philosophers must be such that everything ought to be referred to it, but it itself to nothing else. This Epicurus places in pleasure, which he holds to be the highest good, and pain the highest evil; and he sets about to prove it thus:

But to fail to see this — that it is the strongest proof of that pleasure, on whose removal he denies he can understand at all what good is (and that pleasure he describes thus: such as is perceived by the palate, by the ears; the rest he adds, which, were you to name them, you must first beg pardon) — this, then, which alone the severe and grave philosopher knows as the good, he likewise fails to see is not even to be sought, since, on this same author's showing, we do not desire that pleasure when we are free from pain.

Can it be denied in any way that no one can ever be made of a stable and firm and great mind — whom we call a brave man — unless it be established that pain is not an evil? For as he who places death among evils cannot but fear it, so no one in any matter can fail to care about that which he has decreed to be an evil, and despise it. And this being laid down and approved by the assent of all, it is assumed that he who is of a great and brave mind despises all things that can befall a man and counts them as nothing. Since this is so, it is established that nothing is evil which is not base. And that lofty and excellent man, of great mind, truly brave, accounting all human things beneath himself — he, I say, whom we wish to produce, whom we seek — surely ought both to trust himself and his life, both past and to come, and to judge well of himself, determining that nothing evil can befall the wise man. From which is understood that same thing — that that alone is good which is honourable, and that this is to live happily: to live honourably, that is, with virtue.

But it cannot even be conceived of what kind this should be, so as not to be repugnant to itself. But if he says that certain things are darkened and do not appear because they are very small, we too concede this; for Epicurus says even of pleasure that the smallest pleasures are often darkened and overwhelmed. But the advantages of the body are not in that class — so great, so prolonged in time, so many. And so, in those things in which, on account of their smallness, a darkening follows, it often happens that we confess it makes no difference to us whether they are or are not — as, in the case of the sun, which was said by you, it makes no difference to bring a lamp, or to add a farthing to the money of Croesus.

But some are moved by pain, others by desire; many too are carried away by anger, and, when knowingly they rush into evils, then they think they take the best counsel for themselves. And so they say, and do not doubt: 'Such is my use; do you do as is needful for you.' And those who have declared war on themselves would wish to be tortured by day, tormented by night; nor indeed would they accuse themselves on this account, that they should say they had taken ill counsel for their own affairs. For this complaint belongs to those who are dear to themselves and love themselves. Wherefore, whenever it is said that someone deserves ill of himself and is his own enemy and foe, and finally flees life, let it be understood that there underlies some such cause that from that very thing it can be understood that each man is dear to himself.

that every living creature, the moment it is born, seeks pleasure and rejoices in it as the highest good, but spurns pain as the highest evil and repels it from itself so far as it can; and that it does this while still unspoiled, Nature herself judging without corruption and entire. Therefore he denies that there is need of reasoning or argument to show why pleasure is to be sought and pain shunned. These things, he thinks, are perceived, just as that fire is hot, snow white, honey sweet — none of which need be confirmed by elaborate arguments; it is enough merely to point them out. For there is a difference between the proof and conclusion of an argument and a mere noticing and pointing out. The one reveals certain hidden and, as it were, wrapped-up matters; the other judges things ready and open to view. For since, when the senses are taken away from a man, nothing is left, it must be Nature herself who judges what is according to or contrary to Nature. And what does she perceive, or what does she judge, whereby she seeks or shuns anything, beyond pleasure and pain?

How contradictory these things are! Had he learned to define, to divide, had he grasped the force of language, in short the usage of words, he would never have fallen into such ruts. As it is, you see what he does. What no one ever called pleasure, he calls so; what are two things, he makes one. This pleasure in motion — for so he calls these sweet and, as it were, honeyed pleasures — he sometimes so belittles that you would think Manius Curius was speaking; sometimes so praises that he denies he can even suspect what good there is besides. Now this is talk to be put down not by some philosopher, but by a censor; for the fault is not in the speech only, but also in the morals. He does not blame luxury, provided it be free from boundless desire and fear. Here he seems to be seeking pupils, so that those who wish to be profligates may first become philosophers.

Nor indeed am I ignorant that there have been various opinions of philosophers — I mean of those who placed the highest good, which I call the uttermost, in the mind. Although some have followed this faultily, yet not only to those three who separated virtue from the highest good — when they placed either pleasure, or freedom from pain, or the first things of nature among the highest goods — but also to the other three, who thought virtue would be maimed without some addition, and for that reason each added one of those three things which I mentioned above — yet to all these I prefer, of whatever sort they are, those who placed the highest good in the mind and in virtue.

But in those things in which so great a darkening does not occur, it can yet happen that that very thing which makes a difference is not great. As to him who has lived pleasantly for ten years, if a month equally pleasant be added, since the addition has some weight toward the pleasant, it would be a good; but if that be not granted, the happy life is not therefore at once done away with. But the goods of the body are more like to this, which I put last. For they have an addition worthy of one's labouring at it — so that in this the Stoics seem to me sometimes to jest, when they say thus: that if to that life which is led with virtue there be added a flask or a strigil, the wise man would take that life rather, to which these are added, nor yet would be happier on that account.

Nor indeed is it enough that there is no one who hates himself, but this too must be understood, that there is no one who judges that it is of no concern to him in what state he is. For the appetite of mind will be taken away, if, as in those things among which there is no difference, we are not more inclined to either part, so we shall judge that it is of no concern to us in what state we ourselves are. And also, if anyone should wish to say this — it would be most absurd — that each man is so loved by himself that the force of that loving is referred to some other thing, not to that very man who loves himself. When this is said of friendships, of duties, of virtues, in whatever way it is said, yet it can be understood what is said; but in ourselves it cannot even be understood, that we should love ourselves for the sake of some other thing — for example, for the sake of pleasure; for we love that for our own sake, not ourselves for the sake of it.

There are, however, some of our school who would hand these matters down more subtly, and who deny that it is enough to judge by sense what is good or evil, but hold that this can also be grasped by the mind and by reason — that pleasure itself is to be sought for its own sake and pain itself to be shunned for its own sake. And so they say that there is implanted in our minds a kind of natural and innate notion, whereby we feel that the one is to be sought and the other to be spurned. Others, however — and with these I agree — hold that, since many arguments are advanced by various philosophers as to why neither pleasure should be counted among goods nor pain among evils, we ought not to trust our case too much, but think it must be argued, discussed with care, and debated with reasonings sought out, concerning pleasure and pain.

From the first origin of living creatures, as I think, the source of the highest good is sought. As soon as a creature is born, it rejoices in pleasure and seeks it as a good, and spurns pain as an evil. And of evils and goods, he says, the best judges are those creatures which are not yet corrupted. So you too laid it down, and these are your words. How many faults are there here! For by which pleasure — the steady or the moving — will the wailing infant judge the highest good and evil? Since, if it please the gods, we learn to speak from Epicurus. If by the steady, then this clearly is what nature wishes — that the creature be safe; which we grant. If by the moving, which yet is what you say, then no base pleasure will exist that should be foregone; and at the same time that newly born creature does not set out from the highest pleasure, which is placed by you in not being in pain.

But yet they too are very absurd, both those who said that to live with knowledge is the uttermost of goods, and those who said there is no difference among things, and that thus the wise man will be happy, preferring nothing else to anything at any moment; and those who, as certain Academics are said to have laid down, hold that the uttermost of goods and the highest office of the wise man is to withstand appearances and firmly to sustain his assents. To these individually a copious reply is wont to be made; but things that are plain ought not to be long. And what is more plain than that, if there be no selection of the things that are according to nature from those that are contrary to nature, all that prudence which is sought and praised will be done away with? Those opinions, then, which I have laid down being circumscribed, and any that are like them, it remains that the highest good is to live applying knowledge of those things which happen by nature, selecting the things that are according to nature and rejecting those that are contrary to nature — that is, to live agreeably and consistently with nature.

Is this a likeness at last? Is it not rather to be cast out with laughter than with discourse? For whether a flask be or be not, who would not most justly be laughed at, if he should be troubled? But indeed if anyone should relieve a man from distortion of limbs and the torture of pains, he would win great gratitude; nor, if that wise man were compelled by a tyrant to go to the torturer's rack, would he have a like countenance as if he had lost a flask — but, as one entering a great and difficult contest, when he saw that he must fight it out with his deadly adversary, pain, he would rouse all the reasonings of fortitude and patience, by whose protection he would enter that difficult, as I said, and great battle. Next, we do not ask what is darkened or perishes because it is very small, but what is such that it fills up the sum. One pleasure out of many is darkened in that pleasurable life; but yet that pleasure, however small, is a part of that life which is placed in pleasure. A coin is darkened in the riches of Croesus; yet it is a part of the riches. Wherefore let these things too, which we say are according to nature, be darkened in the happy life; only let them be parts of the happy life.

And yet what is there more plain than that each man is not only dear to himself, but vehemently dear? For who is there, or how few, from whom, when death draws near, 'the blood does not flee in timid fear, and he grow pale with dread'? Although this indeed is a fault — to shudder so greatly at the dissolution of nature (which likewise is to be blamed in pain) — but because nearly all are so affected, it is argument enough that nature shrinks from destruction; and the more some do this so that they are even rightly blamed, the more must it be understood that these very excesses would not have been in some, unless certain things were moderate by nature. Nor indeed do I speak of the fear of death of those who flee death because they think themselves robbed of the goods of life, or because they dread certain terrors after death, or fear lest they die with pain; for in children, who think of none of these things, often, if at any time in play we threaten that they will be hurled from somewhere, they are terrified. Nay even 'wild beasts,' says Pacuvius, 'which lack the cunning of understanding for taking precaution,' when the terror of death is cast upon them 'shudder.' But who thinks otherwise of the wise man himself, but that, even when he has resolved that he must die, yet he is moved by the parting from his own and the very leaving of the light?

But that you may see whence this whole error arose, of those who accuse pleasure and praise pain, I shall lay the whole matter open, and set forth those very things which were said by that discoverer of truth and, as it were, that master-builder of the happy life. For no one rejects, hates, or shuns pleasure itself because it is pleasure, but because great pains befall those who do not know how to pursue pleasure by reason; nor again is there anyone who loves, pursues, or wishes to attain pain itself because it is pain, but because there sometimes come occasions of such a kind that through toil and pain a man seeks some great pleasure. To take the smallest example: which of us undertakes any laborious bodily exercise except to obtain some advantage from it? And who could justly blame either the man who wishes to be in that pleasure which no annoyance follows, or him who shuns that pain which gives birth to no pleasure?

And yet Epicurus did not derive this argument from infants, or even from the beasts, which he thinks the mirrors of nature, so as to say that by them, with nature for guide, this pleasure of feeling no pain is sought. For this state of not being in pain cannot stir the appetite of the mind, nor has it any stroke by which it may impel the mind; and so in this same point Hieronymus errs. But that which soothes the sense with pleasure does impel it. And so Epicurus always uses this, to prove that pleasure is sought by nature: that this pleasure which is in motion allures both infants and beasts to itself, not that steady pleasure, in which there is only the absence of pain. How, then, does it agree to say that nature sets out from one pleasure, but to place the highest good in another?

But in the other arts, when a thing is said to be done skilfully, it must in a certain way be thought subsequent and consequent, which they call epigennematikon; but when we say a thing is done wisely, it is most rightly said so from the very first. For whatever proceeds from wisdom ought at once to be complete in all its parts; for in this is placed that which we say is to be sought. For as it is a sin to betray one's country, to do violence to one's parents, to plunder temples — sins which are in the effect — so to fear, so to mourn, so to be in lust is a sin even without effect. But as these things are sins not in their later parts and consequences, but at once in their first, so the things which proceed from virtue are to be judged right by their first undertaking, not by their completion.

And yet if, as ought to be agreed between us, there is a certain natural appetite seeking the things that are according to nature, of all these some sum must be made. This being established, then it will be allowed to inquire at leisure into those matters — about the magnitude of things, about their excellence, how much there is in each toward living happily, about those very darkenings, which on account of their smallness scarcely, or scarcely even, appear. What of that about which there is no disagreement? For there is no one who has said otherwise than that that to which all things are referred — which is the uttermost of things to be sought — is like in all natures. For every nature is loving of itself. For what nature is there which ever deserts itself, or any part of itself, or the disposition or force of that part, or the motion or state of any of those things which are according to nature? But what nature has forgotten its own first constitution? Surely none, but every one retains its own force from the first to the last. How, then, did it come about that the nature of man alone was that which deserted man, which forgot the body, which placed the highest good not in the whole man, but in a part of man?

But most of all in this kind the force of nature is plain, since both many endure beggary that they may live, and men worn out by old age are distressed at the approach of death, and bear those things which we see Philoctetes bear in the plays. He, when he was tortured by unbearable pains, yet prolonged his life by fowling — 'slow, he pierced the swift with the stroke of his arrows, standing, the flying,' as it is in Accius — and made coverings for his body from the weaving of feathers.

But indeed we both accuse, and deem most deserving of righteous hatred, those who, softened and corrupted by the blandishments of present pleasures, do not, in their blindness of desire, foresee what pains and troubles await them; and equally to blame are they who desert their duties through weakness of mind — that is, through the avoidance of toils and pains. And the distinction of these matters is easy and ready. For in a free hour, when our choice is unhampered and nothing prevents us from doing what pleases us most, every pleasure is to be taken up and every pain repelled. But at certain times, through duties owed or through the necessities of circumstance, it will often happen that pleasures must be refused and troubles not declined. And so the wise man holds to this rule of selection: that by rejecting some pleasures he may gain greater ones, or by enduring some pains he may avert harsher ones. Holding this view, what reason have I to fear that I cannot fit our Torquati to it?

Of the beasts, indeed, I think there is no judgment. For although they are not corrupted, yet they can be crooked. As one little staff is bent and curved on purpose, another is so by birth, so the nature of wild beasts is not indeed corrupted by bad training, but is by its own nature. Nor does nature move the infant to seek pleasure, but only to love itself, to wish itself whole and safe. For every living creature, as soon as it is born, loves itself and all its parts, and embraces above all the two greatest — mind and body — and then the parts of each. For there are certain chief things both in the mind and in the body, which, when it has slightly recognized them, it then begins to distinguish, so as to seek the things first given by nature, and to spurn their contraries.

But the good, which has so often been used in this discourse, is also explained by a definition. But their definitions differ a very little among themselves, and yet look to the same point. I assent to Diogenes, who defined the good as that which is by nature complete. And following this, he said that which also profits — for so let us call ophelema — is a motion or state arising from what is by nature complete. And since notions of things arise in our minds, if something is known either by use, or by combination, or by likeness, or by comparison of reason, it is by this fourth, which I have placed last, that the notion of the good has been made. For when the mind ascends from the things that are according to nature by the comparison of reason, then it arrives at the notion of the good.

But how — which they themselves too confess, and is agreed among all — will it be preserved that that uttermost end about which the inquiry is made should be like in all natures? For then it would be like, if in the other natures too that were the uttermost for each which excelled in each. For such seemed to be the uttermost end of the Stoics.

Do I speak of the race of men, or of living creatures altogether, when the nature of trees and plants is almost the same? For whether, as it has seemed to the most learned men, some greater and more divine cause implanted this force, or it comes about thus by chance, we see that the things which the earth produces are kept strong by their bark and roots — which happens to living creatures by the distribution of the senses and a certain compacting of the limbs. About which matter, although I assent to those who think that all these things are governed by nature — which, if nature should neglect, could not itself exist — yet I grant that those who disagree about this may think what they will, and may even understand this, that, if ever I say 'the nature of man,' I mean 'man'; for this makes no difference. For each man will be able sooner to depart from himself than to lose the appetite for those things which are profitable to him. Rightly, then, did the gravest philosophers seek the beginning of the highest good from nature, and thought that that appetite for things accommodated to nature was inborn in all, because they are contained in that commendation of nature by which they love themselves.

— those whom you just now assembled with so good a memory, and with such friendly and kindly feeling toward us; yet you have not corrupted me by praising my ancestors, nor made me slower to answer. Their deeds — how, I ask, do you interpret them? Do you think they either charged an armed enemy or were so cruel toward their own children and their own blood with no thought at all of their advantages, no thought of their own interests? Why, not even wild beasts do this — to rush and fall on so blindly that we cannot understand to what end their movements and onsets tend; and do you think that such excellent men did such great deeds without a cause?

Whether pleasure is, or is not, in these first natural things, is a great question. But to think there is nothing besides pleasure — neither limbs, nor senses, nor the motion of the mind, nor the integrity of the body, nor the health of the body — seems to me the height of stupidity. And from this source must all reasoning about goods and evils flow. To Polemo, and to Aristotle before him, those things seemed the first which I named a little before. Thence arose the opinion of the old Academics and the Peripatetics, that they should call the end of goods 'to live according to nature' — that is, with virtue applied, to enjoy the things first given by nature. Callipho added nothing to virtue but pleasure; Diodorus, freedom from pain. To all these, whom I have named, there are ends of goods consequent upon their first principles: to Aristippus, simple pleasure; to the Stoics, agreement with nature, which they would have to be living from virtue — that is, honourably — which they interpret thus: to live with an understanding of those things which come to pass by nature, choosing the things that are according to nature, and rejecting their contraries.

But this very good we feel and call good not by addition, nor by growing, nor by comparison with other things, but by its own proper force. For as honey, although it is most sweet, is yet felt to be sweet by its own proper kind of taste, not by comparison with other things, so this good of which we treat is indeed to be valued most highly, but that valuation is strong by kind, not by magnitude. For since valuation, which is called axia, has been counted neither among goods nor again among evils, however much you add to it, it will remain in its own kind. The valuation of virtue, therefore, is a different and proper one, which is strong by kind, not by growing.

Why, then, do you hesitate to change the principles of nature? Why do you say that every living creature, as soon as it is born, is applied to loving itself and is occupied in preserving itself? Why do you not rather say thus, that every creature is applied to that which is best in it, and is occupied in the guardianship of that one thing, and that the other natures do nothing else but preserve that which is best in each? But how is it the best, if there is no other good besides? But if the other things are to be sought, why is not the uttermost of things to be sought concluded either from the appetite of all of them, or of most and greatest? As Phidias can begin a statue from the first and complete it, and can take it begun by another and finish it, to this wisdom is like; for it did not itself beget man, but received him begun by nature. Looking, then, to this nature, it ought to finish that statue, as it were, begun. Of what kind, then, has nature begun man?

Next it must be seen — since it is plain enough that each man is by nature dear to himself — what the nature of man is. For that is what we inquire about. And it is plain that man consists of body and mind, the mind being first, the body second. Then we see this too, that the body is so shaped that it excels the others, and the mind so constituted that it is both furnished with senses and has the pre-eminence of mind, to which the whole nature of man is subject, in which there is a certain wonderful force of reason and of knowledge and of science and of all the virtues. Now the things which are of the body have neither authority to be compared with the parts of the mind, and have an easier knowledge. And so let us begin from these.

What the cause was I shall see presently; meanwhile I shall hold to this: if for some cause they did those deeds which are beyond doubt glorious, virtue was not their cause in and of itself. — 'He stripped the torque from his enemy.' — Yes, and shielded himself, that he might not perish. — 'But he ran a great risk.' — Yes, before the eyes of the army. — 'What did he gain by it?' — Praise and affection, which are the firmest defences of a life lived without fear. — 'He punished his son with death.' — If without cause, I should not wish to be sprung from one so heartless and so cruel; but if it was to sanction by the son's suffering the discipline of military command, and to hold the army in check by the fear of punishment in a most grievous war, then he provided for the safety of his fellow citizens, in which he knew his own was bound up.

So there are three ends devoid of the honourable: one of Aristippus or Epicurus; a second of Hieronymus; a third of Carneades; and three in which the honourable comes with some addition — those of Polemo, of Callipho, of Diodorus; and one simple end, of which Zeno is the author, placed wholly in seemliness — that is, in the honourable. For Pyrrho, Aristo, and Erillus have long since been cast aside. The rest were consistent with themselves, so that the ends agreed with the beginnings: for Aristippus, pleasure; for Hieronymus, freedom from pain; for Carneades, the enjoyment of the first natural things, was the uttermost. But Epicurus, since in his first recommendation he had named pleasure, ought, if it were the pleasure of Aristippus, to hold the same as the uttermost of goods which Aristippus held; or, if it were that of Hieronymus, ought not to have done the same — that is, to put that Aristippean pleasure in his first recommendation.

Nor indeed are the perturbations of the mind, which render the life of the foolish wretched and bitter — which the Greeks call pathe — moved by any natural force. (I could, interpreting the very word, call them \"diseases,\" but that would not fit all cases; for who is wont to call pity, or anger itself, a disease? But they say pathos. Let it be, then, \"perturbation,\" which by the very name seems to be declared faulty.) And all these are of four kinds in genus, more in their parts: distress, fear, lust, and that which the Stoics call by the common name of body and mind, hedone — but I prefer to call it \"gladness,\" the pleasurable elation, as it were, of an exulting mind. But the perturbations are moved by no force of nature, and all these are opinions and judgments of levity. And so the wise man will always be free from these.

And what is the office, what the work of wisdom? What is it that ought to be finished and perfected by it? If there is nothing in it which is to be perfected except a certain motion of the mind, that is, reason, the uttermost end for this must be to act from virtue; for the perfection of reason is virtue. If there is nothing but body, those things will be the chief: health, freedom from pain, beauty, and the rest.

How fitted to nature, then, the parts of our body, and the whole figure and form and stature are, appears; nor is there any doubt that it is understood what brow, eyes, ears, and the rest of the parts are proper to man. But certainly they must be sound and vigorous and have natural motions and uses, so that none of them be lacking, nor diseased or weakened; for this nature desires. There is also a certain action of the body, which keeps the motions and postures agreeing with nature; in which, if there be a fault by some distortion and depravation, or by a deformed motion or posture — as if a man should walk on his hands, or not forward but backward — he would plainly seem to flee himself, and, putting off man from man, to hate nature. Wherefore certain sittings too, and bent and broken motions, such as are wont to be those of insolent or effeminate men, are against nature; so that, even if it come about by a fault of the mind, yet the nature of man seems to be changed in the body.

And this principle has a wide range. For the very theme on which your discourse is most wont to vaunt itself — yours above all, who eagerly pursue antiquity — namely, the commemorating of famous and brave men and the praising of their deeds not for any profit, but for the very beauty of honour itself, is wholly overthrown once that selection of things which I have just described is established: that pleasures be foregone for the sake of attaining greater pleasures, or pains undertaken for the sake of escaping greater pains.

For as to his saying that it is judged by the senses themselves that pleasure is a good and pain an evil, he grants more to the senses than our laws allow us when we are judges of private suits. For we can judge nothing except what falls within our jurisdiction — wherein judges vainly add, when they pronounce sentence, 'if it is within my jurisdiction'; for if it was not within their jurisdiction, the thing is no more judged for that addition being left out. What do the senses judge? Sweet, bitter; smooth, rough; near, far; standing, moving; square, round.

But that everything which is honourable is to be sought for its own sake is common to us with the opinions of many other philosophers. For except the three schools which exclude virtue from the highest good, by all the other philosophers this opinion must be maintained — yet most of all by these Stoics, who would have nothing else in the number of goods except the honourable. But this indeed is a very easy and very ready defence. For who is there, or who ever was, of avarice so burning or of desires so unbridled, that the very thing which he would wish to attain by any crime whatever, he would not by many degrees prefer to come to without crime, even with all impunity offered him, rather than in that other way?

Now the inquiry is about the highest good of man; why, then, do we hesitate to inquire in his whole nature what is brought to pass? For since it is agreed among all that every office and work of wisdom is occupied in the cultivation of man, some — that you may not think I speak against the Stoics alone — bring forward such opinions as to place the highest good in that kind which is outside our power, as though they spoke of something inanimate; others, on the contrary, as though there were no body of man, so care for nothing besides the mind — especially since the mind itself too is not some empty I-know-not-what (for that I cannot understand), but is in a certain kind of body, so that not even it is content with virtue alone, but seeks freedom from pain. Wherefore both do the same, as if they should neglect the left side and guard the right; or, as Erillus did, should embrace the cognition of the mind itself and abandon action. For of all these, who pass over many things while they choose some one thing to follow, the opinion is, as it were, curtailed; but perfect and full is that of those who, when they inquired about the highest good of man, left no part either of mind or of body without its guardianship.

And so, on the contrary, moderate and even habits, affections, and uses of the body seem to be fitted to nature. But now the mind ought not only to be, but also to be of a certain kind, so that it both have all its parts sound and lack none of the virtues. And in the senses there is the proper virtue of each, that nothing hinder each sense from discharging its office in perceiving quickly and readily those things which are subjected to the senses. But of the mind, and of that part of the mind which is the chief, and which is named the intellect, there are several virtues, but two first kinds: one of those which are implanted by their own nature and are called involuntary; the other of those which, being placed in the will, are wont to be called by a more proper name — of which there is an excellent pre-eminence in the praise of minds. Of the former kind is teachableness, memory; which are nearly all called by the one name of natural talent, and those who have these virtues are called gifted. But the other kind is of the great and true virtues, which we call voluntary, such as prudence, temperance, fortitude, justice, and the rest of the same kind. And in sum these were the things to be said about body and mind, by which is, as it were, sketched what the nature of man requires.

But of the illustrious and glorious deeds of famous men let this much be said in this place. For there will soon be a fitter place to discuss the bearing of all the virtues upon pleasure. Now, however, I shall explain what pleasure itself is and of what kind, so that all the error of the ignorant may be removed, and it may be understood how grave, how self-controlled, how austere is that doctrine which is reckoned voluptuous, soft, and effeminate. For we do not pursue only that pleasure which moves our nature itself with a certain sweetness and is perceived by the senses with a kind of delight; but we count as the greatest pleasure that which is perceived when all pain has been removed. For since, when we are freed from pain, we rejoice in the very release and emptiness of all annoyance, and since everything in which we rejoice is a pleasure, just as everything by which we are hurt is a pain, the removal of all pain has rightly been called pleasure. For just as, when hunger and thirst are driven off by food and drink, the very removal of the discomfort brings with it the attainment of pleasure, so in everything the taking away of pain produces the succession of pleasure.

A fair sentence, therefore, will be pronounced by reason — when there has been applied to it, first, the knowledge of things divine and human, which may rightly be called wisdom; and then the virtues joined to it, which reason would have to be mistresses of all things, but you the attendants and ministers of the pleasures. The verdict of all of these, then, will first pronounce of pleasure that there is no place for it — not only that it should be set alone in the seat of the highest good, which we seek, but not even in that fashion, that it be attached to the honourable.

And what usefulness or what fruit do we seek when we desire to know those things which are hidden from us — how the bodies that are in the heavens move, and by what causes? And who lives by manners so rustic, or who has hardened himself against the studies of nature so vehemently, that he shrinks from things worthy of knowledge, and seeks them not without some pleasure or usefulness, and counts them as nothing? Or who is there who, learning the deeds, words, and counsels of our ancestors — whether of the Africani, or of him whom you always have on your lips, my great-grandfather, and of the other brave men surpassing in every virtue — is affected in mind by no pleasure?
