But you, Cato — because virtue, as we all confess, holds the highest place in man and the most excellent, and because we think those who are wise are absolute and perfect — dazzle the edge of our minds with the splendour of virtue. For in every living creature there is something highest and best, as in horses, in dogs — to which yet it is needful both to be free from pain and to be healthy; so, then, in man this perfection is praised especially in that which is best, that is, in virtue. And so you do not seem to me to consider enough what the road of nature is, and what the progress of each thing. For what nature does in fruits — that, when it has brought them from the blade to the ear, it leaves the blade and counts it as nothing — the same it does not do in man, when it has brought him to the disposition of reason. For it always so takes on something that it does not desert the things which it first gave.

From which it is plain — since we are loved by ourselves, and wish all things both in mind and in body to be perfect — that those very things are dear to us for their own sake, and that there are in them the greatest weights toward living well. For he to whom the preservation of himself is set before him must necessarily hold the parts too of himself dear, and dearer the more perfect they are and the more praiseworthy in their kind. For that life is sought which is filled out with the virtues of mind and body, and in this the highest good must necessarily be placed, since it ought to be such that it is the uttermost of things to be sought. This being known, it cannot be doubted that, since men themselves are dear to themselves for their own sake and of their own accord, the parts too both of the body and of the mind, and of those things which are in the motion and posture of each, are cultivated by their own dearness and sought for their own sake.

And so Epicurus did not allow that there is any state midway between pain and pleasure; for that very thing which to some seems midway — being free from all pain — is not only a pleasure but the highest pleasure. For whoever feels how he is affected must of necessity be either in pleasure or in pain. But Epicurus thinks that the highest pleasure is bounded by the absence of all pain, so that afterwards pleasure may be varied and diversified, but cannot be increased or enlarged.

Of freedom from pain there will be the same verdict. Carneades too will be rejected, and no theory of the highest good will be approved which either shares in pleasure or in freedom from pain, or is devoid of the honourable. So reason will leave two, which it considers again and again. For either it will determine that nothing is good but the honourable, nothing evil but the base, and that the rest either have no weight at all, or so much only that they are neither to be sought nor shunned, but only to be chosen or rejected; or it will prefer that theory which it sees to be at once most richly adorned with the honourable, and also enriched with the very first principles of nature and the perfection of the whole life. And this it will do the more clearly if it perceives whether the controversy between these two is one of fact or of words.

And who, trained and brought up in an honourable family, is not offended by baseness itself, even if it be not about to harm him? Who looks with an even mind on the man whom he thinks lives impurely and shamefully? Who does not hate the sordid, the vain, the light, the worthless? And what can be said — if we shall determine that baseness is not in itself to be shunned for its own sake — why men, having found darkness and solitude, should abstain from no disgrace, unless baseness itself by its own foulness deter them? Countless things can be said to this purpose, but it is not necessary. For there is nothing about which it can less be doubted than that honourable things are to be sought for their own sake, and in the same way base things are to be shunned for their own sake.

And so it joined reason to the senses, and, reason being produced, it did not abandon the senses. As if the culture of vines, whose office is this, to bring it about that the vine with all its parts may be as well as possible — but let us understand it thus (for it is allowed, as your school too is wont, to imagine something for the sake of teaching): if, then, that culture of vines were itself in the vine, it would, I believe, wish the other things which pertain to the cultivating of the vine, as before, but would set itself before all the parts of the vine, and would determine that there is nothing better in the vine than itself. Similarly the sense, when it has come to nature, watches over it indeed, but also watches over itself; but when reason has been taken on, it is placed in so great a dominion that all those first things of nature are made subject to its guardianship.

These things being set forth, it is easy to conjecture that those things are most to be sought from among our own which have the most dignity — so that the virtue of each best part, which is sought for its own sake, is to be sought most. So it will come about that the virtue of the mind is set before the virtue of the body, and that the voluntary virtues of the mind surpass the involuntary — which indeed are properly called virtues, and much excel, because they are born from reason, than which there is nothing in man more divine. For of all the things which nature both creates and guards, which are either without mind or not much otherwise, the highest good is in the body — so that that saying about the pig does not seem unskilful, that a mind was given to that beast instead of salt, lest it should rot. But there are certain beasts in which there is something like virtue, as in lions, in dogs, in horses, in which we see, not of bodies only, as in pigs, but also of minds in some part certain motions. But in man the whole sum is in the mind, and in the mind in reason, from which comes virtue, which is defined as the completion of reason, which they think must be explained again and again.

But at Athens — as I used to hear from my father, who jested at the Stoics with wit and elegance — there is in the Ceramicus a statue of Chrysippus seated with hand outstretched, and the hand signifies that he took delight in this little question: 'Does your hand, affected as it now is, lack anything?' — 'Nothing at all.' — 'But if pleasure were a good, it would lack it.' — 'So I suppose.' — 'Pleasure, therefore, is not a good.' But this, my father said, not even the statue would have said, if it could speak. For the argument is concluded acutely enough against the Cyrenaics, but is nothing against Epicurus. For if that were the only pleasure which, so to speak, tickles the senses and flows in upon them with sweetness, then neither could a hand be content, nor any part, with freedom from pain unaccompanied by a pleasurable motion of pleasure. But if the highest pleasure is, as Epicurus holds, to feel no pain, then, first, the point was rightly granted you, Chrysippus, that the hand lacked nothing while it was so affected; but the second was not rightly granted — that, if pleasure were a good, it would have lacked it. For it would lack it for this very reason: that what is free from pain is in a state of pleasure.

Following now the authority of this reason, I shall do the same. For, so far as I can, I shall lessen the contentions, and shall think that all those simple theories of the ends, in which there is no addition of virtue, must be wholly removed from philosophy — first that of Aristippus and of all the Cyrenaics, who were not afraid to place the highest good in that pleasure which moves the sense with the greatest sweetness, scorning that freedom from pain.

But that being established of which we spoke before — that what is honourable is the only good — it must be understood that what is honourable is to be valued more than those middle things which are procured from it. But when we say that folly and timidity and injustice and intemperance are to be shunned on account of the things which result from them, we do not say it in such a way that our discourse seems to fight with that which has been laid down — that that alone is evil which is base — because these things are referred not to bodily disadvantage, but to base actions, which arise from vices. For what the Greeks call kakiai I prefer to name \"vices\" rather than \"malices.\"

And so it does not depart from the care of those things over which, set in charge, it ought to govern the whole life — so that I cannot wonder enough at the inconstancy of these men. For they would have the natural appetite, which they call horme, and likewise duty, and virtue itself even, to be the guardian of the things which are according to nature. But when they wish to arrive at the highest good, they leap over all things and leave us two tasks instead of one, so that we take some things and seek others — rather than concluding both within one end.

Of those things too which the earth produces, there is a certain nurture and perfection not unlike that of living creatures. And so we say both that a vine lives and dies, and that a tree is both young and old, and thrives and 'grows old.' From which it is not strange, as in living creatures, so in these too, to think both that certain things are fitted to nature and others alien, and that there is a certain cultivator for their increasing and nourishing — which is the science and art of farmers, which cuts round, prunes, raises up, lifts, props, so that they can go whither nature bears them; so that the vines themselves, if they could speak, would confess that they ought to be so handled and tended. And now indeed that which tends it — to speak especially of the vine — is something external; for in the vine itself there is too little force, that it may be as well as possible, if no culture be applied.

That pleasure is the uttermost of goods can most easily be perceived from this. Let us suppose someone enjoying great, many, and unbroken pleasures both of mind and of body, with no pain either hindering him or threatening; what state could we call more excellent or more to be desired than this? For there must needs be in one so affected a firmness of mind that fears neither death nor pain — since death is void of sensation, and pain, when long, is usually slight, and when severe, short, so that its greatness is consoled by its brevity, and its duration by its lightness.

These men did not see that, as the horse is born for running, the ox for ploughing, the dog for tracking, so man is born for two things, as Aristotle says — for understanding and for action — like a mortal god; whereas they would have it that this divine creature was brought into being like some slow and sluggish beast, for feeding and for the pleasure of procreation: than which nothing seems to me more absurd.

'Indeed, Cato,' said I, 'you use words illustrious and declaring what you wish! And so you seem to me to teach philosophy in Latin and to give it, as it were, citizenship. Which indeed hitherto seemed to sojourn at Rome as a stranger, and not to offer itself to our discourses, and that chiefly on account of a certain polished subtlety both of things and of words. For I know there are some who can philosophize in any language; for they use no partitions, no definitions, and they themselves say that they approve only those things to which nature silently assents. And so in matters not at all obscure there is among them not much labour of arguing. Wherefore I attend to you studiously, and whatever names you impose on those things of which here is the discourse, I commit to memory; for it will perhaps be necessary for me to use those very same. You seem to me, then, most rightly, and according to the usage of our speech, to have set the vices as contrary to the virtues. For what is in itself blameworthy I think is for that very reason named vitium (vice), or even is called blameworthy (vituperari) from \"vice.\" But if you had called kakia \"malice,\" Latin usage would carry us over to another single definite vice. As it is, to every virtue a vice is opposed by a contrary name.'

But now you say that virtue cannot be established, if those things which are outside virtue pertain to living happily. Which is wholly the contrary. For virtue can in no way be brought in, unless all the things which it shall choose and which it shall reject be referred to one sum. For if we shall altogether neglect [the natural things], we shall fall into the vices and sins of Aristo, and shall forget what principles we have given to virtue itself; but if we do not neglect them, nor yet refer them to the end of the highest good, we shall not stray far from the levity of Erillus. For we shall have to take up the institutions of two lives. For he makes two separate uttermost goods, which, that they might be true, ought to have been joined; as it is, they are so separated as to be disjoined — than which nothing can be more perverse.

But indeed if sense should come to the vine, so that it had a certain appetite and were moved of itself, what do you think it would do? Will it care for itself the things which before it attained through the vine-dresser? But do you see that care will come to it, that it may tend its senses too and their whole appetite, and any limbs that are joined to it? So to those things which it always had it will join those which shall afterward have come, nor will it have the same end which its cultivator had, but will wish to live according to that nature which shall afterward have been joined to it. So the end of good for it will be like to that which had been before, and yet not the same; for it will now seek not the good of a plant, but of an animal. What, if not only sense be given to it, but even the mind of a man? Must it not be both that those former things remain, so that they are to be tended, and that these which shall have come be much dearer, and that each best part of the mind be dearest, and that in this filling out of nature the end of the highest good consist, since mind and reason far and much excel? So that which is the uttermost of all things to be sought, and drawn from the first commendation of nature, ascends by many steps, so that it comes to the highest, which is heaped up from the integrity of the body and from the perfected reason of the mind.

And when there is added to this that he dreads no divine power, and does not suffer past pleasures to slip away but delights in the constant remembrance of them — what is there that could be added to this which would be better? Set up, on the contrary, someone broken by such great pains of mind and body as can fall upon a man at their greatest, with no hope held out that they will ever be lighter, and with no pleasure besides, neither present nor expected: what more wretched can be said or imagined than he? But if a life filled with pains is most of all to be shunned, then surely the highest evil is to live with pain; and to this view it is consonant that the uttermost of goods is to live with pleasure. For our mind has nothing on which it may rest as on an extreme; and all fears and distresses are referred to pain, nor is there besides any thing which can of its own nature either disturb or vex us.

And this against Aristippus, who holds that pleasure which we all call by the one name 'pleasure' to be not only the highest but the only good. But you hold otherwise. He, however, as I said, is in fault. For neither the shape of the body nor the excelling reason of the human mind signifies that man was born for this one thing — to enjoy pleasures. Nor indeed should Hieronymus be heeded, whose highest good is the same that you sometimes, or rather too often, name — to feel no pain. For if pain is an evil, it is not enough, in order to live well, to be free from that evil. Ennius rather might say this: 'Too much of good has he, to whom there is no evil.' But let us judge the happy life not by the repelling of evil, but by the attainment of good; and let us seek it not by idling — whether in rejoicing, like Aristippus, or in not being in pain, like this man — but by doing or contemplating something.

Then he: 'These things, then, being so laid down,' said he, 'there follows a great contention, which the Peripatetics handled rather softly — for their manner of speaking is not acute enough, on account of their ignorance of dialectic — but your Carneades, by a certain remarkable training in dialectic and the highest eloquence, brought the matter to the utmost crisis, because he did not cease to contend, in this whole question which is called \"of goods and evils,\" that there is no controversy of things between the Stoics and the Peripatetics, but of words. But to me nothing seems so plain as that these opinions of those philosophers differ among themselves more in fact than in words; I say that there is a much greater discrepancy of things between the Stoics and the Peripatetics than of words, since the Peripatetics say that all the things which they themselves call goods pertain to living happily, while our school does not think the happy life is filled out from everything that is worthy of some valuation.

And so it is the contrary of what you say; for virtue can in no way be established, unless it shall hold the things which are first in nature as pertaining to the sum. For virtue was sought, not such as should desert nature, but such as should guard it. But that virtue, as it pleases you, guards a certain part, deserts the rest. And the very constitution of man, if it could speak, would say this — that its first, as it were, beginnings of appetite were that it should preserve itself in that nature in which it had arisen. But it had not yet been sufficiently made plain what nature most wished. Let it, then, be made plain. What else, then, will be understood, except that no part of nature be neglected? In which, if there is nothing besides reason, let the end of goods be in virtue alone; but if there is also body, that explanation of nature will surely have brought it about that we abandon those things which we held before the explanation. Therefore this is to live agreeably with nature — to depart from nature.

Since, then, the form of nature is that which I have set forth, if, as I said at the beginning, each man, as soon as he were born, should recognize himself and could judge what the force was both of his whole nature and of the single parts, he would at once see what this is which we seek, the highest and uttermost of all things which we seek, nor could he err in anything. But as it is, at first indeed nature is wonderfully hidden, and can neither be perceived nor known. But as our ages advance, gradually, or rather slowly, we recognize, as it were, our very selves. And so that first commendation, which was made to us by nature of ourselves, is uncertain and obscure, and that first appetite of mind acts only so far that we may be safe and sound. But when we have begun to discern and to feel what we are, and in what we differ from the other living creatures, then we begin to pursue those things for which we are born.

Moreover, the beginnings of seeking and of avoiding, and indeed of all action, proceed either from pleasure or from pain. Since this is so, it is plain that all right and praiseworthy things are referred to this end — that life be lived with pleasure. And since this is either the highest or the last or the uttermost of goods — what the Greeks call telos — which itself is referred to nothing else, but to which all things are referred, it must be confessed that the highest good is to live pleasantly. Those who set this in virtue alone, and, captivated by the splendour of a name, do not understand what Nature demands, will be freed from a most serious error, if they are willing to hear Epicurus. For those eminent and beautiful virtues of yours — unless they produced pleasure, who would think them either praiseworthy or to be desired? For just as we approve the physician's science not for the art's own sake but for the sake of good health, and the pilot's art is praised for its usefulness, not for the art itself, because it possesses the method of sailing well, so wisdom, which must be reckoned the art of living, would not be sought if it produced nothing; but as it is, it is sought, because it is, as it were, the craftsman that searches out and

The same things may be said against that Carneadean highest good, which he brought forward not so much to prove it as to set it against the Stoics, with whom he waged war. It is of such a kind that, added to virtue, it seems likely to have weight and to fill up completely the happy life, on which this whole inquiry turns. For those who add to virtue either pleasure — which virtue values least — or freedom from pain — which, even though it lacks evil, is yet not the highest good — make use of an addition not very probable; and yet why they do it so sparingly and so narrowly I do not understand. For as though they had to buy what they add to virtue, first they add the cheapest things; then they add single things, rather than joining to the honourable all the things which the first nature had approved.

Or can anything be more certain than that, by the reasoning of those who place pain among evils, the wise man cannot be happy when he is tortured on the rack? But the reasoning of those who do not hold pain among evils certainly compels that in all torments the happy life be preserved to the wise man. For if those who undergo the same pains for their country endure them more tolerably than those who do so for a lighter cause, it is opinion, not nature, that makes the force of pain either greater or less.

As certain philosophers, when, setting out from the senses, they had seen certain greater and more divine things, deserted the senses, so these men, when from the appetite of things they had beheld the beauty of virtue, cast away all the things which they had seen besides virtue itself, forgetting that the whole nature of things to be sought lies so widely open that it should flow on from the principles to the ends; nor do they understand that they are withdrawing the foundations of those beautiful and admirable things.

Which likeness we see in the beasts, which at first do not move themselves from the place in which they were born, then each is moved by its own appetite. We see little snakes creep, little ducklings swim, blackbirds fly out, oxen use their horns, scorpions their stings, and finally that each one's own nature is its guide to living. Which likeness appears also in the human race. For little children at first lie, at their birth, as if altogether without mind. But when a little firmness has come, they use both mind and senses, and strive to raise themselves up, and use their hands, and recognize those by whom they are reared. Then they delight in their equals and gladly gather with them, and give themselves to play, and are led by the hearing of fables, and wish to gratify others with what they themselves have to spare, and observe more curiously the things which are done at home, and begin to think out something and to learn, and wish not to be ignorant of the names of those whom they see; and in those matters in which they contend with their equals, if they have won, they are uplifted with gladness, if conquered, they are unnerved and cast down. And nothing of these things is to be thought to happen without cause.

procures pleasure — and what I call pleasure you now see, lest my discourse be undermined by the odium of the word. For since human life is most of all vexed by ignorance of things good and evil, and through that error men are often robbed of the greatest pleasures and tormented by the harshest pains of the mind, wisdom must be called in, which, by removing terrors and desires and by stripping away the rashness of all false opinions, may offer itself to us as the surest guide to pleasure. For wisdom alone it is that drives sorrow from our minds and does not suffer us to shudder with fear; with her as our teacher we may live in tranquillity, the fire of all our desires quenched. For desires are insatiable, and they overthrow not only individual men but whole households, and often shake the entire commonwealth.

Because these things seemed to Aristo and Pyrrho altogether worth nothing — so that they said there was no difference at all between being in the best health and being most grievously sick — men long ago rightly ceased to argue against them. For while they wished all things to be so in virtue alone that they stripped it of the selection of things, and gave it nothing either from which it might arise or on which it might rest, they did away with virtue itself, which they embraced. Erillus, again, referring all things to knowledge, saw one good of a sort, but neither the best nor that by which life could be steered. And so this very man too has long since been rejected; for after Chrysippus there was no real arguing against him. You, then, remain; for with the Academics the struggle is uncertain, who affirm nothing, and, as though knowledge were despaired of, wish to follow whatever seems like the truth.

Nor indeed is that consistent — that if, since there are three kinds of goods (which is the opinion of the Peripatetics), each man is the happier the fuller he is of bodily or external goods, the same should be approved by us, namely that he who has more of those things which are highly valued in the body should be the happier. For they think the happy life is filled out by the advantages of the body; our school, by no means. For since it is our view that not even by an abundance of those goods which we may truly call goods is the happy life made happier, or more to be sought, or more to be valued, certainly the multitude of bodily advantages pertains still less to the happy life.

And so it seems to me that all those indeed erred who said that the end of goods is to live honourably, but one more than another — Pyrrho, of course, most of all, who, virtue being established, leaves nothing at all that is to be sought; then Aristo, who dared not leave nothing, but brought in, as the things by which the wise man should be moved to seek something, whatever should fall into his mind, and whatever should, as it were, present itself. He is better than Pyrrho in this, that he gave some kind of seeking; worse than the rest, because he wholly withdrew from nature. But the Stoics, because they place the end of goods in virtue alone, are like those men; but because they seek a principle of duty, they are better than Pyrrho; because they do not imagine those things as merely presenting themselves, they surpass Aristo; but because they do not join those things which they say are accommodated to nature and to be taken for their own sake to the end of goods, they depart from nature, and are in a manner not unlike Aristo. For he devised certain I-know-not-what things presenting themselves; but these men set down indeed the first things of nature, but separate them from the ends and from the sum of goods; and when they prefer them, so that there may be some selection of things, they seem to follow nature; but when they deny that they pertain at all to the happy life, they again desert nature.

For the force of man is so generated by nature that it seems made for perceiving every virtue; and on that account little children are moved, without teaching, by the likenesses of the virtues, of which they have the seeds in themselves; for these are the first elements of nature, which being increased, the germ, as it were, of virtue is produced. For since we are so born and made that we contain in ourselves the beginnings both of doing something, and of loving some persons, and of generosity, and of returning gratitude, and have minds fitted for knowledge, prudence, fortitude, and alien from their contraries, not without cause do we see in children those sparks, as it were, of the virtues which I mentioned, from which the reason of the philosopher ought to be kindled, that, following it as, as it were, a god for his guide, he may come to the uttermost of nature. For, as I have now often said, in the weak age and feeble mind the force of nature is discerned as if through a mist; but when, advancing, the mind is strengthened, it recognizes indeed the force of nature, but so that it may advance further, while it is by itself only begun.

From desires spring hatreds, quarrels, discords, seditions, and wars; nor do they only flaunt themselves abroad, nor only rush upon others with blind onset, but, shut up within the mind, they are at variance and at strife among themselves, from which the bitterest life must needs result; so that the wise man alone, having lopped and cut away all emptiness and error, content within the bounds of Nature, can live without distress and without fear.

But with Epicurus there is more business, because he is compounded of a double kind of pleasure, and because both he himself, and his friends, and many afterward, were defenders of his opinion; and somehow that party which has the least authority — the people — sides with them with the greatest force. Unless we refute these, all virtue, all honour, all true praise must be abandoned. So, the opinions of the rest set aside, there is left a contest, not between me and Torquatus, but between virtue and pleasure. And this contest a man both acute and careful, Chrysippus, does not despise, but thinks the whole question of the highest good lies in the comparison of these two. But I judge that, if I shall have shown something to be honourable which is in itself, by its own force and for its own sake, to be sought, all your doctrines lie prostrate. And so, having briefly determined, as the time demands, what its nature is, I shall come to all your points, Torquatus, unless my memory chance to fail.

For if both to be wise is to be sought, and to be healthy, the two joined together would be more to be sought than to be wise alone; and yet, though both be worthy of valuation, the two joined would not be worth more than wisdom itself taken separately. For we who judge health worthy of some valuation, yet do not place it among goods, are also of the opinion that there is no valuation so great that it should be preferred to virtue. The Peripatetics do not hold the same; for they must say that an action which is both honourable and without pain is more to be sought than if the same action were with pain. To us it seems otherwise — rightly or wrongly, hereafter; but can there be a greater disagreement of things?

And so far I have said the things for which Zeno had no cause why he should depart from the authority of his predecessors. Now let us see the rest — unless either you wish to say something to these things, Cato, or we are now too long.' 'Neither, indeed,' said he. 'For I both wish that disputation of yours to be finished, nor can your discourse seem to me long.' 'Excellently,' said I. 'For what can be more to be wished by me than to dispute about the virtues with Cato, the author of all the virtues?

We must enter, then, into the nature of things, and see thoroughly what it demands; for otherwise we cannot know ourselves. Which precept, because it was greater than that it should seem to come from a man, was on that account assigned to a god. The Pythian Apollo, then, bids us know ourselves. But this is the one knowledge of ourselves — that we know the force of body and mind, and follow that life which enjoys those very things. But since the appetite of mind was from the beginning such that we should have those things which I mentioned as perfect as possible by nature, it must be confessed that, when we have attained that which was sought, nature rests, as it were, in that as in its uttermost, and that this is the highest good; which, certainly, as a whole, must of its own accord be sought for itself and for its own sake, since it was before shown that even its single parts are to be sought for their own sake.

For what division is more useful, or better fitted for living well, than that which Epicurus employed? He laid down one class of desires that are both natural and necessary; a second, that are natural but not necessary; a third, that are neither natural nor necessary. Of these the principle is this: that the necessary ones are satisfied with little labour and little expense; the natural ones, too, do not demand much, since Nature herself has the riches with which she is content both easy to procure and limited; but for empty desires no measure or end can be found.

By 'the honourable,' then, we understand that which is of such a kind that, all usefulness removed, with no rewards or profits, it can rightly be praised for its own sake. What this is can be understood not so much by the definition I have used — though somewhat by it — as by the common judgment of all men, and by the pursuits and deeds of all the best men, who do very many things for this one cause: because it is becoming, because it is right, because it is honourable, even though they see that no profit will follow. For men, though they differ from the beasts in many other things, yet differ most in this one: that they have reason given by nature, and a mind keen and vigorous, swiftly turning many things at once, and, so to speak, sagacious — which sees both the causes of things and their consequences, transfers likenesses, joins things separate, links the future with the present, and embraces the whole state of the life that is to follow. And this same reason made man eager for the company of men, and in agreement with them by nature, by speech, and by intercourse, so that, setting out from love of his household and his own, he extends himself further, and binds himself first in the fellowship of his fellow citizens, then of all mortals; and, as Plato wrote to Archytas, remembers that he was born not for himself alone, but for his country and for his own, so that a very small part is left for himself.

For as the light of a lamp is darkened and overcast by the light of the sun, and as a drop of honey is lost in the magnitude of the Aegean sea, and as the addition of a farthing to the riches of Croesus, or one step in the road which leads from here to India, so, when the end of goods is that which the Stoics say, all that valuation of bodily things must needs be darkened and overwhelmed and perish in the splendour and magnitude of virtue. And just as opportuneness — for so let us call eukairia — is not made greater by a prolonging of time (for the things called opportune have their own measure), so right effecting — for so I call katorthosis, since a right deed is katorthoma — right effecting, then, and likewise consistency, and finally the good itself, which is placed in this, that it agree with nature, has no addition of growth.

But first see this, that that gravest opinion of yours, which leads the family — that what is honourable is the only good, and that to live honourably is the end of goods — will be common to you with all who establish the end of goods in virtue alone; and what you say, that virtue cannot be formed if anything be counted except what is honourable, the same will be said by those whom I just named. But it seemed to me more fair to see Zeno, disputing with Polemo, from whom he had received what the principles of nature were, advancing from common beginnings, where he first took his stand and whence the cause of controversy arose — not, standing with those who did not even say that their highest goods proceeded from nature, to use the same arguments which they used and the same opinions.

But in enumerating the advantages of the body, if anyone shall think that pleasure has been passed over by us, let that question be deferred to another time. For whether there be pleasure in those things which we said are the first according to nature, or there be not, makes nothing to what we are about. For if, as it seems to me at least, pleasure does not fill out the goods of nature, it has rightly been passed over; but if it be in them, as some would have it, this our comprehension of the highest good is in no way hindered. For to the things which are established as the first of nature, if pleasure shall have come, some one advantage of the body will have come, nor will it have changed that constitution of the highest good which has been set forth.

But if we see that the whole of life is thrown into confusion by error and ignorance, and that wisdom alone it is which can deliver us from the assault of lusts and the terror of fears, and teach us to bear with moderation the very injuries of fortune, and show us all the paths that lead to rest and tranquillity — why should we hesitate to say that wisdom is to be sought for the sake of pleasures, and folly to be shunned for the sake of its troubles?

And since the same nature has implanted in man a longing to see the truth — which appears most plainly when, free from cares, we yearn to know even what goes on in the heavens — led on by these beginnings, we love all that is true, that is, faithful, simple, constant; and we hate things vain, false, deceiving, such as fraud, perjury, malice, injustice. And this same reason has in it something ample and magnificent, fitted rather for commanding than for obeying, accounting all human things not merely bearable but even slight — something lofty and exalted, fearing nothing, yielding to no one, ever unconquered.

For as that opportuneness, so these things of which I spoke are not made greater by a prolonging of time; and for that cause the happy life does not seem to the Stoics more desirable nor more to be sought if it be long than if it be short. And they use a likeness: that, as if the praise of a buskin were to fit the foot aptly, neither would many buskins be preferred to few, nor larger to smaller, so, for those whose every good is bounded by consistency and opportuneness, neither will they prefer the more to the fewer nor the longer to the briefer. Nor indeed do they say acutely enough:

By no means do I approve that, when you have taught — as you think — that that alone is good which is honourable, then again you say that it is necessary that beginnings be set forth fitted and accommodated to nature, from the selection of which virtue can arise. For virtue was not to be placed in selection, so that that very thing which was the uttermost of goods should acquire something else. For all the things which are to be taken and which are to be chosen or wished ought to be present in the sum of goods, so that he who has attained it should desire nothing besides. Do you see how, for those whose highest good is in pleasure, it is plain what they must do or not do? So that no one doubts to what all their duties look, what they ought to follow, what to flee? Let this be the uttermost of goods which is now defended by me; it appears at once what are the duties, what the actions. But for you, who have nothing else proposed except the right and the honourable, you will not find whence the principle of duty, whence the principle of acting, may arise.

And so far indeed our reasoning has so advanced that it was all drawn from the first commendation of nature. But now let us follow another kind of arguing, that not only because we love ourselves, but because each part of nature, both in body and in mind, has its own force, on that account we are moved supremely in these things of our own accord. And, to begin from the body, do you see how, if there be anything in the limbs crooked or weakened or diminished, men hide it? How they even strive and labour, if they can bring it about, that the fault of the body either not appear, or appear as little as possible? And how they endure even many pains for the sake of cure, so that, if the very use of the limbs is to be not only not greater but even less, yet their appearance may return to nature? For indeed, since all by nature think themselves to be sought wholly, and that not for any other thing, but for their own sake, it must be that the parts too are sought for their own sake, since the whole is sought for its own sake.

And by the same reasoning we shall say that not even temperance is to be sought for its own sake, but because it brings peace to our minds and soothes and calms them, as it were, with a certain harmony. For temperance it is that warns us to follow reason in things to be sought or shunned. For it is not enough to judge what should be done or not done, but one must also stand fast in what has been judged. But most men, because they cannot hold to and keep what they themselves have resolved, overcome and weakened when the appearance of pleasure is set before them, surrender themselves to be bound by their lusts, and do not foresee what will come of it; and for that reason, for the sake of a pleasure both small and unnecessary, which might be procured otherwise and which they could even do without painlessly, they fall sometimes into grave diseases, sometimes into losses, sometimes into disgrace, and often even become liable to the penalties of laws and courts.

And when these three kinds of the honourable have been marked, a fourth follows, of the same beauty and fitted to those three, in which there is order and moderation. The likeness of this, perceived in the comeliness and dignity of forms, made the passage to the honourableness of words and deeds. For from those three praises which I named before, it shrinks from rashness, and dares not harm anyone by an insolent word or deed, and fears either to do or to utter anything that may seem too little manly.

if good health is to be valued more if long than if short, then the longest use of wisdom too should be valued most. They do not understand that the valuation of health is judged by its span, that of virtue by opportuneness — so that those who say that seem about to say this too, that a good death and a good birth are better long than short. They do not see that some things are valued more by brevity, others by length.

Seeking this, then, both those who shall say that they follow whatever comes into their mind or whatever presents itself, and you, will return to nature. To whom nature might rightly answer that it is not true that the end of living happily is sought from elsewhere, while the principles of action are sought from her; for there is one reason by which both the principles of things to be done and the uttermost goods are contained; and that, as the opinion of Aristo was hissed off the stage — who said that nothing differs from another, and that there are no things besides the virtues and vices among which there is any difference at all — so Zeno errs, who says that in no thing except in virtue or vice is there a propensity even of the least weight toward attaining the highest good, and, although the other things have no weight toward the happy life, yet says there are in them weights toward the appetite of things — as though, forsooth, this appetite did not pertain to the attainment of the highest good! But what is less consistent than what they say — that, the highest good being known, they return to nature, that from her they may seek the principle of acting, that is, of duty?

What? In the motion and posture of the body is there nothing which nature herself judges must be observed? In what manner one walks, sits; what is the cast of the mouth, the countenance in each? Is there nothing in these things which we count worthy or unworthy of a free man? Do we not think many worthy of hatred, who by a certain motion or posture seem to have despised the law and measure of nature? And since these things are derived from the body, why should not beauty too itself rightly be thought to be sought for its own sake? For if we think crookedness and diminution of the body is to be fled for its own sake, why should we not also, and perhaps more, pursue dignity of form for its own sake? And if we flee baseness in the posture and motion of the body, why should we not pursue beauty? And health too, strength, freedom from pain we shall seek not only for usefulness, but also for their own sake. For since nature wishes to be filled out in all its parts, it seeks for its own sake that state of body which is most according to nature, which is wholly disturbed if the body be either sick, or in pain, or lacking in strength.

But those who wish so to enjoy pleasures that no pains follow from them, and who keep their own judgment, lest, overcome by pleasure, they do what they feel ought not to be done — these gain the greatest pleasure by foregoing pleasure. The same men also often endure pain, lest, by not doing so, they fall into a greater. From which it is understood that intemperance is not to be shunned for its own sake, nor temperance sought for its own sake, but because the latter procures greater pleasures.

You have, Torquatus, the form of honourableness filled out and completed on every side, which is contained wholly in these four virtues, which were named by you also. This your Epicurus says he is altogether ignorant of — what, or of what kind, those wish it to be who measure the highest good by honourableness. For if they refer all things to honourableness, and do not say that pleasure is in it, he says they sound with an empty voice — for he uses these very words — and neither understand nor see what meaning is to be placed beneath this word 'honourable.' For, as usage speaks, that alone is called honourable which is glorious by popular report. 'And this,' he says, 'though it is often more pleasant than certain pleasures, yet is sought for the sake of pleasure.' Do you see how great a disagreement there is?

And so it is consistent with what has been said that, by the reasoning of those who think that the end of goods — which we call the uttermost, the last — can grow, the same men should hold that one man is wiser than another, and likewise that one sins or acts rightly more than another — which we are not allowed to say, who do not think the end of goods can grow. For as those who are sunk in water can no more breathe if they are not far from the top, so that at any moment they may emerge, than if they were still in the deep; nor does that puppy which is now near to seeing see more than one just born; likewise he who has advanced somewhat toward the disposition of virtue is no less in wretchedness than he who has advanced nothing. I understand that these things seem wonderful; but since the earlier things are surely firm and true, and these are consistent with and consequent upon them, not even of the truth of these is there any room for doubt. But although they deny that either virtues or vices grow, yet they think each of them is in a manner poured out and, as it were, spread wider. But Diogenes thinks that riches have only this force, that they may be, as it were, guides to pleasure and to good health;

For it is not the reason of action or duty that impels us to seek the things which are according to nature, but by them both appetite and action are set in motion. Now I come to those brief sayings of yours, which you said were corollaries; and first that one, than which nothing can be briefer: Every good is praiseworthy; but the praiseworthy is honourable; therefore every good is honourable. O dagger of lead! For who would grant you, first, that? — which being granted, there is no need of the second; for if every good is praiseworthy,

Let us look at the parts of the mind, whose aspect is more illustrious; which, the loftier they are, the clearer signs they give of nature. So great, then, is the love of knowledge and of science inborn in us, that no one can doubt that the nature of man is carried off to these things, invited by no profit. Do we not see how children are not deterred even by blows from contemplating and searching out things? How, when driven off, they run back? How they rejoice that they know something? How they are eager to tell it to others? How they are held by processions, games, and spectacles of that kind, and on that account endure even hunger and thirst? What of this? Those who delight in liberal studies and arts — do we not see that they have regard neither for health nor for household estate, and endure all things, captivated by knowledge and science itself, and compensate with the greatest cares and labours that pleasure which they take from learning?

The same reasoning will be found to hold of fortitude. For neither the discharge of toils nor the endurance of pains allures of itself, nor patience, nor perseverance, nor wakeful vigils, nor even that very industry which is praised, nor fortitude itself; but we pursue these in order to live without anxiety and fear, and to free mind and body, so far as we can, from annoyance. For as by the fear of death the whole state of a quiet life is disturbed, and as it is wretched to succumb to pains and to bear them with a lowly and feeble spirit — and through that weakness of mind many have utterly ruined their parents, many their friends, some their country, but most of all themselves — so a strong and lofty mind is free from all care and anguish, since it both despises death (for those who are touched by death are in the same case as before they were born), and is so prepared for pains that it remembers that the greatest are ended by death, the small have many intervals of rest, and of the middling sort we are masters — so that, if they are bearable, we bear them, and if not, we may depart from life, when it does not please us, with an even mind, as from a theatre. By all this it is understood that timidity and cowardice are not blamed, nor fortitude and patience praised, on their own account, but that the former are rejected because they breed pain, and the latter chosen because they breed pleasure.

A renowned philosopher, by whom not only Greece and Italy but even all the barbarian world was stirred, says he does not understand what the honourable is, if it be not in pleasure — unless perhaps it be that which is praised by the rumour of the multitude. But I, for my part, judge this often to be base too; and, if ever it be not base, then it is not base when that is praised by the multitude which is in itself, of its own nature, right and praiseworthy — yet not for that reason is it said to be honourable because it is praised by many, but because it is of such a kind that, even if men were ignorant of it, or had fallen silent, it would yet, by its own beauty and aspect, be praiseworthy. And so this same man, overcome by nature, which cannot be withstood, says in another place that very thing which was said by you too a little before — that one cannot live pleasantly unless one also lives honourably.

but that, even though they contain these things, they do not do the same in virtue, nor in the other arts, to which money can be a guide, but cannot contain them. And so, if pleasure or good health be among goods, riches too must be placed among goods; but if wisdom be a good, it does not follow that we should also say riches are a good. Nor can that which is among goods be contained by anything which is not among goods; and for this cause — because cognitions and comprehensions of things, from which the arts are produced, move appetite — since riches are not among goods, no art can be contained by riches.

every good is honourable. Who, then, will give you that, except Pyrrho, Aristo, or men like them, whom you do not approve? Aristotle, Xenocrates, that whole family will not give it, since they say that health, strength, riches, glory, and many other things are goods, but do not say they are praiseworthy. And these men indeed so think that the end of goods is not contained in virtue alone, that they yet set virtue before all things. What do you think those will do who have altogether separated virtue from the end of goods — Epicurus, Hieronymus, and those too, if any wish to uphold the Carneadean end?

So that to me indeed Homer seems to have seen something of this kind in those things which he feigned about the songs of the Sirens. For they are not represented as wont to call back those who sailed past by the sweetness of their voices or by a certain novelty and variety of singing, but because they professed that they knew many things, so that men should cling to their rocks from desire of learning. For thus they invite Ulysses — for I have translated, as some things of Homer's, so this very passage too: 'O glory of the Argives, why dost thou not turn thy ship, Ulysses, that thou mayest learn our songs with thine ears! For no one has ever sailed past these blue waters on his course, but he first stood still, captivated by the sweetness of our voices, and afterward, sated in his eager breast with our varied music, more learned glided back and came to his native shores. We hold the grievous struggle of war and the disaster which Greece, by the divine will, brought upon Troy, and all the traces of things upon the wide lands.' Homer saw that the fable could not be approved, if so great a man were held entangled by little songs; they promise knowledge, which it was no wonder should be dearer than country to one desirous of wisdom. And to wish to know all things, of whatever kind they be, must be thought the mark of the curious; but to be led by the contemplation of greater things to the desire of knowledge, the mark of the greatest men.

Justice remains, that the account of every virtue may be complete; but much the same may be said of it. For as I have shown wisdom, temperance, and fortitude to be bound up with pleasure, so that they can in no way be torn or separated from it, so must we judge of justice — which not only never harms anyone, but on the contrary always brings, by its own force and nature, this benefit, that it calms our minds, and besides gives the hope that none of those things will be lacking which a nature not corrupted desires. And just as rashness and lust and cowardice always torment the mind and always vex it and are full of turbulence, so wickedness, if it has settled in anyone's mind, is turbulent by this very fact, that it is present; and if it has contrived anything, however secretly it has done it, yet it will never be confident that it will remain forever hidden. For the most part suspicion first follows upon the deeds of the wicked, then talk and rumour, then the accuser, then the judge; many, indeed — as in your consulship — have even informed against themselves.

What does he now mean by 'honourably'? The same as 'pleasantly'? So, then: that one cannot live honourably unless one lives honourably? Or unless by popular report? Without that, then, he denies he can live pleasantly. What is more shameful than that the wise man's life should hang on the talk of the foolish? What, then, does he here understand by the honourable? Surely nothing but what can be rightly praised for its own sake. For if for the sake of pleasure — what is that praise, which might be sought from the meat-market? He is not such a man that, holding honourableness in such esteem that without it he denies one can live pleasantly, he should mean by 'honourable' that which is popular, and deny that one can live pleasantly without it, or understand by 'honourable' anything other than what is right and in itself, by its own force, its own nature, of its own accord, praiseworthy.

But if we should concede this of the arts, yet the case of virtue would not be the same, because virtue needs the most reflection and exercise — which is not so in the arts — and because virtue embraces stability, firmness, constancy of the whole life, and we do not see these same things to be in the arts. Next is explained the difference of things, which if we should say there is none — as Aristo did — all life would be confounded, nor would any office or work of wisdom be found, since among those things which pertain to the leading of life there would be no difference at all, nor would any selection need to be applied. And so, when it had been sufficiently established that that alone is good which is honourable, and that alone evil which is base, then among those things which had no force toward living happily or wretchedly they yet wished there to be something which differed, so that some of them were to be valued, others the contrary, others neither.

And now how will either Callipho or Diodorus be able to grant you that, who join to honourableness another thing which is not of the same kind? Does it please you, then, Cato, when you have assumed things not granted, to bring out of them what you wish? Then there is that sorites, than which you think nothing more faulty: what is good is to be wished; what is to be wished is to be sought; what is to be sought is praiseworthy; then the remaining steps. But here I make a stand; for in the same way no one will give you that what is to be sought is praiseworthy. But that other is least of all a corollary, but in the first place dull — theirs, of course, not yours — that the happy life is worthy of glorying, because it cannot fall to anyone without honourableness that he should rightly glory.

For what ardour of zeal do you think there was in Archimedes, who, while he was rather attentively drawing certain things in the dust, did not even feel that his country was taken? How great a genius of Aristoxenus do we see consumed in music? With what zeal do we think Aristophanes spent his life in letters? What shall I say of Pythagoras? What of Plato or of Democritus? By whom, from desire of learning, we see the uttermost lands were traversed. Those who do not see these things have never loved anything great and worthy of knowledge. And in this place, those who say that those studies which I mentioned are cultivated for the sake of the pleasures of the mind do not understand that on that very account they are to be sought for their own sake, because the minds delight when no usefulness is set before them, and rejoice in knowledge itself, even if it be about to bring disadvantage.

But if some seem to themselves sufficiently fenced and fortified against the knowledge of men, yet they dread the gods, and believe that those very anxieties by which their minds are gnawed night and day are sent upon them by the immortal gods for the sake of punishment. But what so great an addition toward lessening the troubles of life can come from wicked deeds, as toward increasing them — both from the consciousness of those deeds, and from the penalty of the laws and the hatred of fellow citizens? And yet in some men there is no measure of money, nor of office, nor of power, nor of lusts, nor of feasting, nor of the rest of their desires, which no booty ever wickedly won diminishes, but rather inflames — so that such men seem rather to need restraining than unteaching.

And so, Torquatus, when you said that Epicurus cries that one cannot live pleasantly unless one lives honourably, wisely, and justly, you yourself seemed to me to glory in it. So great was the force in the words, on account of the dignity of the things signified by them, that you rose higher, that at times you paused, that, looking at us, you bore witness, as it were, that honourableness and justice are sometimes praised by Epicurus. How well it became you to use those words, which, if philosophers did not use, we should have no need of philosophy at all! For it is from love of these words — which are very rarely uttered by Epicurus, the words 'wisdom,' 'fortitude,' 'justice,' 'temperance' — that men of the most surpassing genius have betaken themselves to the study of philosophy.

But of those which were to be valued, in some there was cause enough why they should be preferred to certain things — as in health, in the integrity of the senses, in freedom from pain, in glory, riches, and like things — but others were not of that sort; and likewise of those which were worthy of no valuation, some had cause enough why they should be rejected — as pain, disease, the loss of the senses, poverty, ignominy, and the like — but others not so. Hence arose that which Zeno named proegmenon, and on the contrary that which he named apoproegmenon, since he used, in a copious language, words yet made and new — which is not granted to us in this poor language; although you are wont to call even this the more copious. But it is not out of place, that the force of the word may be the more easily understood, to set forth Zeno's reason for making this word.

Polemo will grant this to Zeno — his master too, and that whole tribe, and the rest, who, setting virtue much before all things, yet join to it something in defining the highest good. For if virtue is worthy of glorying, as it is, and so far surpasses the other things that it can scarcely be said, both it will be possible to be happy endowed with virtue alone, lacking the rest; and yet that will not be granted you, that nothing besides virtue is to be counted among goods. But those whose highest good is without virtue will perhaps not grant that the happy life has that in which anyone can rightly glory — although they indeed even make pleasures sometimes glorious.

But what is the point of seeking more about things so plain? For let us ask of ourselves how the motions of the stars, and the contemplations of the heavenly things, and the knowledge of all those things which are hidden by the obscurity of nature move us; and what history delights us, which we are wont to pursue even to the uttermost, when we go back over what was passed over, and follow out what was begun. Nor indeed am I ignorant that there is usefulness in history, not only pleasure.

True reason, therefore, calls the sound of mind to justice, fairness, and good faith; nor do unjust deeds profit a man who is helpless or powerless, who can neither easily accomplish what he attempts, nor keep it if he has accomplished it. And resources, whether of fortune or of talent, are better suited to generosity, by the use of which men win for themselves goodwill and — what is most apt for living in peace — affection, especially since there is no cause at all for wrongdoing.

'The sense of the eyes,' says Plato, 'is the keenest in us'; yet with these we do not behold wisdom. What burning loves of itself would she kindle! Why, pray? Is it because she is so cunning that she can best contrive pleasures? Why is justice praised? Or whence comes this proverb, worn smooth with age: 'one with whom you would play in the dark'? This saying, in this one matter, has the widest application: that in all our deeds we should be moved by the thing itself, not by a witness.

'For as,' said he, 'no one in a royal court says that the king himself is, as it were, brought forward to dignity — for that is proegmenon — but those who are in some honour, whose rank comes nearest, so as to be second to the royal pre-eminence, so in life it is not those things which are in the first place, but those which hold the second place, that are named proegmena, that is, \"brought forward\"; which we may either call by that very word — that will be word for word — or \"promoted\" and \"removed,\" or, as we said a while ago, \"preferred\" and \"chief,\" and those others \"rejected.\" For when the thing is understood, we ought to be easy in the use of words.'

You see, then, that you either assume things which are not granted, or things which, even granted, help you nothing. For my part, in all those conclusions I should think this worthy of philosophy and of us, and most of all when we were seeking the highest good, that our life, our counsels, our wishes, not our words, should be corrected. For who can, on hearing those brief and sharp things which, as you say, delight you, depart from his opinion? For when they expect and long to hear why pain is not an evil, those men say that to be in pain is harsh, troublesome, hateful, contrary to nature, hard to endure, but that, because there is in pain no fraud, no wickedness, no malice, no fault, no baseness, it is not an evil. He who has heard these things, that he may not care to laugh, will yet depart no whit firmer to bear pain than he had come.

What, when we read feigned fables, from which no usefulness can be drawn, with pleasure? What, when we wish the names of those who have done anything to be known to us — their parents, their country, and many things besides by no means necessary? What of this, that men of the lowest fortune, with no hope of doing great things, in short craftsmen, delight in history? And we can see most of all those wish to hear and read of deeds done who are far from the hope of doing them, worn out by old age. Wherefore it must be understood that in the very things which are learned and known there are invitations by which we are moved to learning and knowing.

For the desires that proceed from Nature are easily satisfied without any wrongdoing; but to those that are empty we ought not to submit. For they crave nothing worth desiring, and there is more of loss in the wrongdoing itself than of gain in the things that are gotten by wrongdoing. And so one would not rightly call even justice desirable for its own sake, but because it brings the greatest measure of pleasantness. For to be loved and to be held dear is pleasant, because it makes life safer and pleasure fuller. And so it is not only on account of those disadvantages which befall the wicked that we think wickedness should be shunned, but much more because, in whosever mind it dwells, it never lets him draw breath, never lets him rest.

For the things you were saying are slight and very weak — that the wicked are tortured by the consciousness of their minds, and then too by the fear of punishment, by which they are either afflicted, or are always in dread lest they be afflicted at some time. One must not imagine the bad man timid, or of feeble mind, who tortures himself for whatever he has done and dreads everything; but rather one who refers all things cunningly to his own advantage — keen, crafty, an old hand — so that he may easily devise how to deceive secretly, without a witness, without anyone privy to it.

But since we say that everything which is good holds the first place, it must be that this which we name \"preferred\" or \"chief\" is neither good nor evil. And we define it thus: that which is indifferent with a middling valuation; for what they call adiaphoron, that occurred to me so that I should call it \"indifferent.\" For it could not be in any way that nothing should be left among the middle things which was either according to nature or contrary to it; nor, when that was left, that nothing should be placed among these which was worthy enough of valuation; nor, this being placed, that there should not be some things preferred. Rightly, then, has this distinction been made; and even, that the matter may be the more easily perceived, this likeness is set down by them:

But you deny that anyone can be brave who thinks pain an evil. Why should he be braver, if he shall think that thing — which you yourself grant — harsh and scarcely to be borne? For timidity is born from things, not from words. And you say that, if one letter be moved, the whole doctrine will totter. Do I seem to you, then, to move a letter, or whole pages? For even though there be in them, what was praised by you, the order of things preserved and all things fitted and connected among themselves — for so you said — yet we ought not to pursue them, if, set out from false principles, they agree with themselves and do not stray from their purpose.

And the old philosophers indeed feign, in the Isles of the Blessed, what the life of the wise will be like, whom, freed from all care, requiring no necessary support or preparation of life, they think will do nothing else but spend all their time in inquiring and learning, in the knowledge of nature. But we see that this is not only the delight of the happy life, but also the relief of miseries. And so many, when they were in the power of enemies or of tyrants, many in prison, many in exile, lightened their grief by the studies of learning.

But if not even the praise of the virtues themselves — on which the discourse of the other philosophers most exults — can find any issue unless it be directed toward pleasure, while pleasure alone is that which calls us to itself and allures us by its own nature, there can be no doubt that this is the highest and uttermost of all goods, and that to live happily is nothing else than to live with pleasure.

Or do you think I speak of Lucius Tubulus? — who, when as praetor he had held the court for assassins, took bribes for his verdict so openly that in the next year Publius Scaevola, tribune of the plebs, proposed to the people whether they wished an inquiry into the matter. By that plebiscite an inquiry was decreed by the senate to the consul Gnaeus Caepio. Tubulus went straight into exile, not daring to answer; for the matter was open. We are inquiring, then, not about the wicked man, but about the cunning wicked man, such as Quintus Pompeius was in denying the treaty of Numantia; and not about one who fears everything, but first about one who does not care for the consciousness of his mind — which, indeed, it is no trouble to suppress. For the man who is called secret and covered, so far is he from informing against himself, that he will even bring it about that he seems to grieve at another's wicked deed. For what else is it to be crafty?

'For as,' they say, 'if we should imagine this to be, as it were, the end and uttermost — to throw the die so that it stands upright — the die which shall have been so thrown that it falls upright will have something \"preferred\" toward the end, and one thrown otherwise the contrary; and yet that preferment of the die will not pertain to the end of which I spoke — so the things which are preferred are referred indeed to the end, but pertain nothing to its force and nature.'

In the first constitution, then, your Zeno withdrew from nature; and when he had placed the highest good in excellence of mind, which we call virtue, and had said that nothing else is good except what is honourable, and that virtue cannot stand if in the other things there be anything which is better or worse one than another — these things being set down, he held thoroughly the consequences. You say rightly; I cannot deny it. But the things which follow are so false that those from which these are born cannot be true.

A leader of this state, Demetrius of Phalerum, when he had been driven from his country by injustice, betook himself to king Ptolemy at Alexandria. He, since he excelled in this very philosophy to which we exhort you, and was a hearer of Theophrastus, wrote many excellent things in that calamitous leisure, not for any use of his own, of which he was bereaved, but that culture of his mind was to him, as it were, a certain food of humanity. For my part I often used to hear from Gnaeus Aufidius, a man of praetorian rank, learned, deprived of his eyes, when he said that he was moved by the longing for light more than for usefulness. And finally we should think that sleep was given us against nature, unless it brought rest to our bodies and a certain medicine for toil; for it takes away our senses and removes all action. And so if nature either did not seek rest, or could attain it by some other means, we should easily endure it — we who even now are wont, for the sake of doing or learning something, to take on wakeful vigils almost against nature.

What is bound up with this fixed and stable opinion I shall briefly explain. There is no error in the ends of goods and evils themselves — that is, in pleasure or in pain; but men err in this matter when they are ignorant of the sources from which these arise. Now we admit that pleasures and pains of the mind arise from the pleasures and pains of the body — and so I grant, as you were just saying, that the case goes against any of our school who think otherwise, of whom indeed I see there are many, but unlearned. Yet although pleasure of the mind brings us gladness and pain of the mind brings us trouble, I say that each of these both takes its origin from the body and is referred to the body; and yet not for that reason are the pleasures and pains of the mind not far greater than those of the body. For with the body we can feel only what is present and at hand, but with the mind both the past and the future. For though we feel pain equally in the mind when we feel pain in the body, yet a very great increase can occur, if we suppose some eternal and boundless evil hangs over us. The same may be transferred to pleasure, so that it is the greater if we fear no such thing.

I remember being present with Publius Sextilius Rufus, when he laid the matter before his friends thus: that he was the heir of Quintus Fadius Gallus, in whose will it was written that he had been asked by him that the whole inheritance should come to his daughter. Sextilius denied that this had been done. He could deny it with impunity; for who would refute him? None of us believed him, and it was more likely that he was lying, whose interest it was, than the dead man, who had written that he had asked what he ought to have asked. He added, too, that, having sworn to uphold the Voconian law, he did not dare to act against it, unless his friends thought otherwise. We were present as young men, but there were many of the most eminent men, of whom none thought that more should be given to Fadia than could come to her by the Voconian law. Sextilius kept the very large inheritance, from which, had he followed the opinion of those who set honourable and right things before all profits and advantages, he would not have touched a single coin. Do you think, then, that he was afterward anxious or troubled in mind? Nothing less; on the contrary, by that inheritance he was rich, and on that account glad. For he valued highly money gained not only not against the laws, but even by the laws. Such money is to be sought by you even with danger; for it is the producer of many and great pleasures.

There follows that division, that of goods some pertain to that uttermost end — for so I call those which are said to be telika; for let us establish, as was agreed, to say in several words what we cannot in one, that the matter may be understood — but others are productive, which the Greeks call poietika, others both. Of those that pertain, nothing is good except honourable actions; of those that are productive, nothing except a friend; but wisdom they would have to be both pertaining and productive. For because wisdom is a consistent action, it is in that pertaining kind which I mentioned; but because it brings and produces honourable actions, it can be called productive.

For the dialecticians teach us, as you know, that if the things which follow upon any matter are false, that very thing which they follow is false. So that conclusion is made not only true, but so evident that the dialecticians think no reason even need be rendered for it: if that, then this; but not this; therefore not even that. So, your consequences being taken away, the first things are taken away. What follow, then? That all who are not wise are equally wretched, all the wise supremely happy; all right deeds equal, all sins equal — which, when they seemed at first magnificently said, on consideration were less approved. For the sense of each man, and the nature of things, and the very truth, cried out in a manner that it could not be brought to think that, among those things which Zeno levelled, there was no difference.

But there are also clearer, or rather quite plain and least doubtful, signs of nature, especially of course in man, but in every living creature — that the mind seeks always to do something, and on no condition can endure perpetual rest. This is easy to discern in the first little years of children. For although I fear lest I seem too much in this kind, yet all the old philosophers, especially ours, come to the cradle, because in childhood they think they can most easily know the will of nature. We see, then, that not even infants can be at rest. But when they have advanced a little, they delight in games even laborious ones, so that they cannot be deterred even by blows, and that desire of doing something grows up together with their ages. And so, not even if we thought we should use the most pleasant dreams, would we wish the sleep of Endymion to be given us; and if it should happen, we should think it the likeness of death.

Now this at least is clear: that the greatest pleasure or trouble of the mind brings more weight toward a happy or a wretched life than either of them, if it last an equal time in the body. We do not hold, however, that when pleasure is taken away distress straightway follows, unless by chance pain has succeeded into the place of pleasure; but on the contrary, that we rejoice at the laying aside of pains, even though no pleasure that moves the sense has succeeded — and from this it can be understood how great a pleasure it is not to be in pain.

As, then, by those who hold that what is right and honourable is to be sought for its own sake, dangers must often be undergone for the sake of seemliness and honour, so by your school, who measure everything by pleasure, dangers must be undergone in order to attain great pleasures. If a great matter, a great inheritance is at stake, since by money very many pleasures are produced, your Epicurus, if he wishes to follow his own end of goods, will have to do the same as Scipio, when great glory was set before him if he should draw Hannibal back into Africa. And so how great a danger did he undergo! For he referred all that effort of his to honour, not to pleasure. Thus your wise man, moved by some great profit, will fight, if there be need, even with hemlock.

These things which we call \"preferred\" are partly preferred in and of themselves, partly because they produce something, partly both: in themselves, as a certain habit of the mouth and countenance, as posture, as motion, in which there are some things to be preferred and some to be rejected; others will be called preferred for this reason, that they produce something of themselves, as money; but others on account of both, as the integrity of the senses, as good health.

Afterward that little Carthaginian of yours — for you know that the Citians, your clients, set out from Phoenicia — that acute man, then, not gaining his cause against the resistance of nature, began to twist words, and first conceded to those things which we count good that they should be held to be valuable and accommodated to nature, and began to confess that to the wise man — that is, to the supremely happy — it was yet more convenient if he had those things too which he dared not call goods; he concedes that they are accommodated to nature, and denies that Plato, if he were not wise, was in the same case as the tyrant Dionysius; that for the latter it was best to die, on account of despair of wisdom; for the former, to live, on account of hope. But that sins are partly tolerable, partly in no way, because some sins passed over more, others fewer, as it were, numbers of duty. And further, that some of the unwise are such that they could in no way come to wisdom, others such that, if they had set about it, they could attain wisdom.
