Nay even, we see the most idle men, endowed with some I-know-not-what singular sloth, yet always moved both in body and in mind, and, when they are hindered by no necessary matter, either calling for a gaming-board, or seeking some game, or requiring some conversation; and, since they have not the freeborn delights from learning, they pursue certain little circles and gatherings. Nay, not even the beasts, which we shut up for the sake of delight, when they are fed more abundantly than if they were free, easily endure to be confined, and require the loose and roaming motions granted them by nature.

But as we are uplifted by the goods we expect, so we are gladdened by those we remember. Fools, however, are tormented by the memory of evils; the wise are delighted by past goods renewed in grateful recollection. And it lies within us both to bury our adversities, as it were, in perpetual oblivion, and to remember our prosperities pleasantly and sweetly. But when we gaze on the past with keen and attentive mind, then it comes about that distress follows if those things were evil, and gladness if they were good. O glorious, open, simple, and direct path to living happily! For since assuredly nothing can be better for a man than to be free of all pain and trouble and to enjoy to the full the greatest pleasures of mind and body, do you see how nothing is left out that may help our life, so that we may the more easily attain the proposed end, the highest good? Epicurus — the very man whom you say is too much given over to pleasures — cries aloud that one cannot live pleasantly unless one lives wisely, honourably, and justly, nor wisely, honourably, and justly unless one lives pleasantly.

If the crime can be secret, he will rejoice; if caught, he will despise every punishment. For he will be equipped to despise death, exile, even pain itself. This pain, indeed, you make unendurable when you propose it as punishment to the wicked, but endurable when you would have the wise man always have more of good. But imagine a man not only cunning in doing some wicked thing, but also very powerful, as Marcus Crassus was — who yet was wont to use his advantage well, as our Pompeius does today, to whom thanks are owed for acting rightly; for he could be as unjust as he pleased, justly, with impunity. But how many unjust things can be done which no one could blame! If your friend, dying, should ask you to restore the inheritance to his daughter, and should nowhere write it, as Fadius wrote, nor tell it to anyone — what will you do?

But concerning good repute — for that which they call eudoxia is more aptly called in this place \"good repute\" than \"glory\" — Chrysippus indeed and Diogenes used to say that, usefulness being taken away, not even a finger should be stretched out for its sake; with whom I strongly agree. But those who came after them, since they could not withstand Carneades, said that this good repute of which I spoke is itself preferred and to be taken on for its own sake, and that it is the mark of a freeborn man liberally educated to wish to be well spoken of by his parents, his kinsmen, and good men too, and that for the thing's own sake, not for its use; and they say that, as we wish our children to be provided for, even if they are to be born after our death, for their own sake, so there must be provision made, even after death, for our future fame, for the thing's own sake, even when use is taken away.

Here he spoke otherwise than all, but felt the same as the rest. Nor indeed did he hold those things which he himself denied to be goods to be of less value than they who said they were goods. What, then, did he mean for himself, who changed those things? At least he might have taken away something from their weight and valued them a little less than the Peripatetics, so that he might seem also to feel something other, not only to say it. What? Of the happy life itself, to which all things are referred, what do you say? You deny that it is that which is filled out with all those things which nature desires, and you place it wholly in virtue alone; and since every controversy is wont to be either about a thing or about a name, either of them arises if either the thing is not known or there is error in the name. If neither of these is the case, pains must be taken that we use words as customary and as fitting as possible, that is, declaring the thing.

And so, the better born and trained each man is, the less would he wish to be in life at all, if, bereaved of conducting affairs, he could feed on the readiest pleasures. For either they prefer to conduct something privately, or, those who are of a loftier mind, undertake the commonwealth in gaining honours and commands, or betake themselves wholly to the studies of learning. In which life so far are they from pursuing pleasures, that they even endure cares, anxieties, wakeful vigils, and enjoy the best part of man — which is to be thought in us divine — the edge of genius and mind, neither seeking pleasure nor fleeing labour. Nor indeed do they intermit either the admiration of those things which were discovered by the ancients, or the investigation of new ones. And since they cannot be sated with this zeal, forgetful of all other things, they think nothing abject, nothing low; and so great is the force in such studies, that we see even those who have set themselves other ends of goods, which they direct by usefulness or pleasure, yet spend their ages in seeking out and explaining the natures of things.

For neither can a state in sedition be happy, nor a house amid the discord of its masters; much less, then, can a mind at variance with itself and quarrelling within itself taste any part of pure and unhindered pleasure. And indeed, a man who is forever swayed by warring and conflicting purposes and counsels can see nothing of quiet, nothing of tranquillity.

You, indeed, will restore it; Epicurus himself perhaps would restore it, as Sextus Peducaeus, son of Sextus — he who left us this son of his, the image of his own humanity and uprightness, learned, and the best and most just of all men — when he knew that no one was aware that he had been asked by Gaius Plotius, a distinguished Roman knight of Nursia, of his own accord went to the woman, and, when she suspected nothing, set forth her husband's charge, and restored the inheritance. But I ask of you — since you too would surely have done the same — do you not understand that the force of nature is the greater for this, that you yourselves, who refer all things to your own advantage and, as you yourselves say, to pleasure, yet do things from which it appears that you follow not pleasure but duty, and that upright nature prevails more than crooked reasoning?

But since we say that what is honourable is the only good, it is yet consistent to discharge duty, although we place that duty neither among goods nor among evils. For there is something probable in these matters, and that so far that a reason for it can be given; therefore so that a reason for an action probably performed can also be given. But duty is that which is so done that a probable reason for the deed can be given. From which is understood that duty is something middle, which is placed neither among goods nor among their contraries. And since in those things which are neither among virtues nor among vices there is yet something which can be of use, it must not be done away with. And there is also some action of that kind, and indeed such that reason demands that one do and perform some of those things. But what is done by reason we call duty. Duty, therefore, is of that kind which is placed neither among goods nor among their contraries.

Is there any doubt, then, that, if nothing is erred in the thing itself by the earlier men, they use words more conveniently? Let us see, then, their opinions, then let us return to words. They say that the appetite of the mind is moved when something seems to it to be according to nature, and that all the things which are according to nature are worthy of some valuation, and are to be valued in proportion to the weight there is in each; and that of the things which are according to nature, some have in themselves nothing of that appetite of which we have now often spoken, which are called neither honourable nor praiseworthy; others have pleasure in every living creature, but in man reason also. Of this, the things which are fitted are honourable, are beautiful, are praiseworthy; but those former are named natural, which, joined with the honourable, perfect and complete the happy life.

Therefore this at least appears, that we are born for action. But there are several kinds of actions, so that even the lesser are darkened by the greater; but the greatest are, first, as it seems to me at least, and to those in whose reasoning we now are concerned, the consideration and knowledge of the heavenly things, and of those which reason can track out, hidden and lurking by nature; then the administration of commonwealths, or the science of administering; then the prudent, temperate, brave, just reason, and the rest of the virtues, and the actions agreeing with the virtues, which, embracing all in one word, we call honourable; to the knowledge and use of which, being now strengthened, we are led by nature herself going before. For the beginnings of all things are small, but, using their own progressions, they are increased, and not without cause; for in the first origin there is a certain tenderness and softness, so that they can neither see the best things nor do them. For of virtue and the happy life, which two are most to be sought, the light appears later, much later even, so that it be understood plainly what they are. For admirably says Plato: 'Happy is he to whom it has fallen, even in old age, to be able to attain wisdom and true opinions!' Wherefore, since enough has been said about the first advantages of nature, now let us see about the greater and consequent ones.

But if the pleasantness of life is hindered by the graver diseases of the body, how much more must it be hindered by the diseases of the mind! And the diseases of the mind are the boundless and empty desires for riches, glory, dominion, and even for lustful pleasures. There are added distresses, troubles, griefs, which gnaw at and waste away the minds of men with cares — men who do not understand that the mind ought to feel no pain that is severed from present or future pain of the body. Nor indeed is there any fool who does not labour under some one of these diseases; therefore there is no one who is not wretched.

'If you should know,' says Carneades, 'that an asp lies hidden somewhere, and that someone is about to sit down upon it unawares, whose death would be a profit to you, you would act wickedly if you did not warn him not to sit down — yet with impunity; for who could prove that you knew?' But this is too much. For it is plain that, unless fairness, good faith, and justice proceed from nature, and if all these things are referred to usefulness, no good man can be found; and on these matters enough has been said by Laelius in our books On the Commonwealth.

And this too is plain, that the wise man does something among those middle things. He judges, then, when he acts, that this is a duty. And since he is never deceived in judging, there will be duty among the middle things. Which is established also by this conclusion of reasoning: For since we see that there is something which we may call a right deed, and that is a perfected duty, there will also be an inchoate one — so that, if to restore a deposit justly is among right deeds, to restore a deposit is placed among duties; for by adding \"justly\" it becomes a right deed, but the restoring itself in itself is placed among duty. And since it is not doubtful that among those things which we call middle one thing is to be taken and another rejected, whatever is so done or said is all contained under duty. From which is understood that, since all men by nature love themselves, both the foolish and the wise will take the things that are according to nature and reject their contraries. So there is a certain duty common to the wise and the foolish; from which it follows that duty is concerned with those things which we call middle.

But of all those advantages, to which they who say they are goods assign no more than Zeno, who denies it, by far the most excellent is that which is honourable and praiseworthy. But if two honourable things be set before us, the one with health, the other with disease, there is no doubt to which of them nature herself will lead us. But yet the force of honourableness is so great, and it so surpasses and excels all things, that it can be moved by no punishments and no rewards from that which it has decreed to be right; and that all the things which seem hard, difficult, adverse can be crushed by those virtues with which we are adorned by nature — not, indeed, that those things are easy nor to be despised (for what then would there be in virtue so great?), but that we should judge this, that there is not placed in them the greatest part of living happily or otherwise.

Nature, then, both begot and formed the body of man so that it perfected some things at the first origin, others it shaped with advancing age, nor indeed used much aid from external and adventitious things. But the mind it so perfected as the body; for it adorned it with senses fit for perceiving things, so that they needed no aid, or not much, for their confirmation; but that which is in man most excellent and best, it left untended. Although it gave such a mind as could receive every virtue, and implanted, without teaching, small notions of the greatest things, and, as it were, set about to teach and introduced into the things which were within, as if the elements of virtue. But virtue itself it only began, nothing further.

There is added also death, which, like the rock over Tantalus, forever hangs above; and then superstition, with which whoever is imbued can never be at peace. Besides, they do not remember past goods, they do not enjoy present ones, they only await future ones; and because these cannot be certain, they are worn down by anguish and fear, and are tortured most of all when, too late, they perceive that they have striven in vain after money, or commands, or power, or glory. For they win no pleasures, in hope of gaining which, inflamed, they had undertaken many and great toils.

Transfer the same to modesty, or temperance, which is the moderation of the desires in obedience to reason. Does a man, then, consult modesty enough, if he obeys his lust without a witness? Or is there anything shameful in and of itself, even if no infamy attend it? What? Do brave men, having cast up the reckonings of their pleasures, enter battle, pour out their blood for their country — or are they driven by a certain ardour and impulse of the mind? Which, pray, do you think, Torquatus, that famous Imperiosus, if he could hear our words, would more gladly hear — your speech about him, or mine: when I said that he did nothing for his own sake and all for the commonwealth, you, on the contrary, that he did nothing but for his own? But if you should wish to explain it more openly, and say that he did nothing except for the sake of pleasure, how, pray, do you think he would have borne it?

But since from these all duties proceed, it is not without cause said that all our thoughts are referred to them — among these both the departure from life and the remaining in life. For he in whom there are more things that are according to nature, his duty is to remain in life; but he in whom there are, or seem likely to be, more contrary things, his duty is to depart from life. From which it appears both that it is sometimes the wise man's duty to depart from life, though he be happy, and the fool's to remain in life, though he be wretched.

In sum, the things which Zeno said are to be valued and taken and fitted to nature, these same those men call goods, and the happy life that which would consist of those things which I named, either most or weightiest. But Zeno calls that alone good which has its own and proper appearance why it should be sought, but the happy life that alone which is led with virtue. If we must dispute about the thing, there can be no disagreement between me and you, Cato. For there is nothing about which you think otherwise than I, if only, the words being changed, we compare the things themselves. And this he did not fail to see, but was delighted by the magnificence and glory of words. Who, if he felt the things he says as the words signify, what would there be between him and either Pyrrho or Aristo? But if he did not approve of them, what was the point of differing in words from those with whom he agreed in substance?

And so it is ours — what I call ours, belongs to art — to seek out the consequences to the principles which we have received, until that which we wish be brought to pass. Which indeed is by no little more valuable and more to be sought for its own sake than either the senses or those things of the body which we have mentioned, which the excelling perfection of the mind so far surpasses that it can scarcely be conceived what the difference is. And so all honour, all admiration, all zeal is referred to virtue and to those actions which are agreeable to virtue, and all those things which are either so in our minds or are so done are called by the one name 'honourable.' Of all which, what the notions are — those at least which are signified by the names of things — and what is the force and nature of each, we shall soon see.

But behold others — petty and cramped, either despairing always of everything, or malicious, envious, peevish, shunners of the light, slanderous, monstrous; others, again, given over to amorous follies; others wanton; others bold, shameless, and the same intemperate and cowardly, never abiding in one resolve — for which reasons there is in their life no respite from trouble. Therefore no fool is happy, and no wise man is not happy. And in this we are much better and truer than the Stoics. For they deny that there is any good except a kind of shadow which they call the honourable — a name more splendid than solid — and they hold that virtue, resting upon this honourable, requires no pleasure and is content with itself for living happily.

Be it so; let Torquatus have done it, if you will, for the sake of his own advantages — for I prefer to say that, rather than 'pleasures,' especially in so great a man. But did his colleague, Publius Decius, the first in that family to hold the consulship, when he had devoted himself and, giving his horse the rein, rushed into the midst of the Latin line, think anything of his own pleasures? Where, that he might take it, or when? — when he knew that he must die at once, and sought that death with a more burning zeal than Epicurus thinks pleasure should be sought. And had this deed of his not been rightly praised, his son would not have imitated it in his own fourth consulship; nor again would his son, born of him, warring with Pyrrhus, have fallen in battle as consul, and offered himself, the third victim of his line in unbroken succession, for the commonwealth.

For that good and evil, which has now often been spoken of, follows afterward; but those first things of nature, whether the favourable or the contrary, fall under the judgment and selection of the wise man, and are, as it were, the underlying matter of wisdom. And so all the reasoning both of remaining in life and of departing is to be measured by those things which I mentioned above. For neither is the wise man retained in life by virtue, nor is death to be sought by those who are without virtue. And it is often the duty of the wise man to forsake life, though he be most happy, if he can do it opportunely — which is to act consistently with nature. For so they hold, that to live happily is a matter of opportuneness. And so it is prescribed by wisdom that the wise man should, if there be need, leave wisdom itself. Wherefore, since vices do not have that force that they should furnish a cause for voluntary death, it is plain that it is the duty even of fools, who are likewise wretched, to remain in life, if they are in the greater part of those things which we call according to nature. And since one departing from life and one remaining are equally wretched, nor does length make life more to be shunned for the one, it is not without cause said that those who can enjoy more of the natural things ought to remain in life.

What if those pupils of Plato should come to life again, and in turn those who were their hearers, and should speak with you thus? \"We, when we heard you, Marcus Cato — most studious of philosophy, most just a man, the best of judges, the most religious of witnesses — wondered what the cause was why you preferred the Stoics to us, who held about good and evil things those views which Zeno had learned from this Polemo, but used names which at first appearance moved wonder, when the matter was explained, laughter. But you, if those things were approved by you, why did you not hold them in your own words? Or if authority moved you, did you prefer some unknown fellow to us all and to Plato himself? — especially when you wished to be a leader in the commonwealth, and could be most adorned and equipped by us, with the highest dignity, for maintaining it. For those things were sought out by us, by us described, noted, taught; and we have written out all the kinds of governance of commonwealths, their conditions, changes, and even the laws and institutions and manners of states. And of eloquence, which is both the greatest ornament to leaders, and in which we hear you are most strong, how much you would have added to yourself from our monuments!\" When they had said these things, what, pray, would you answer to such men?'

But in this place let us only explain that these honourable things which I speak of, besides that we love ourselves, are moreover by their own nature to be sought for their own sake. Children show it, in whom, as in mirrors, nature is discerned. How great are the zeals of those contending! How great the contests themselves! How they are uplifted with gladness when they have won! How ashamed are the conquered! How they wish not to be accused! How they desire to be praised! What labours do they not endure, that they may be the chiefs of their equals! What memory is there in them of the well-deserving, what desire of returning gratitude! And these things appear most in each best disposition, in which these honourable things, which we understand, are, as it were, sketched by nature.

But these things can in a certain sense be said with our not only not opposing but even approving. For thus is the wise man by Epicurus brought in as always happy: he has his desires limited; he disregards death; concerning the immortal gods he holds the truth without any fear; he does not hesitate, if it be better so, to depart from life. Equipped with these things, he is always in pleasure. For there is no time at which he does not have more pleasures than pains. For he both remembers the past with gratitude, and so possesses the present as to mark how great and how delightful those things are; nor does he hang upon the future, but awaits it while he enjoys the present, and is utterly removed from those vices which I gathered up a little while ago; and when he compares the life of fools with his own, he is filled with great pleasure. And if any pains befall him, they never have so great a force that the wise man does not have more in which to rejoice than in which to be vexed.

I refrain from examples. Among the Greeks this is a modest matter: Leonidas, Epaminondas, some three or four. But if I should begin to gather ours, I shall indeed accomplish that — to make pleasure surrender herself to be bound by virtue — but the day will fail me; and, as Aulus Varius, who was held a rather harsh judge, used to say to his fellow on the bench, when, witnesses having been given, others still were called: 'Either this is enough of witnesses, or I know not what is enough' — so by me enough witnesses have been given. For what? Did pleasure lead you yourself — most worthy of your ancestors — as a young man to snatch the consulship from Publius Sulla? And when you had reported it to your father, that bravest of men — what a man he was, both as consul and as citizen, always, and especially after his consulship! On whose advice we ourselves did such things that we took thought for all rather than for our very selves.

But they think it pertains to the matter that it be understood that it comes about by nature that children are loved by their parents. From which beginning we trace the common fellowship of the human race. Which ought first to be understood from the shape and the limbs of bodies, which themselves declare that nature has held a plan for procreation. Nor indeed could these things agree among themselves, that nature should both wish offspring to be procreated and yet not care that the procreated be loved. And even in the beasts the force of nature can be perceived; whose toil in bearing and rearing when we behold, we seem to hear the very voice of nature. Wherefore, as it is plain that we shrink from pain by nature, so it appears that we are impelled by nature herself to love those whom we have begotten.

'I should ask you,' said he, 'to speak for me yourself, who had dictated their speech to them — or rather to give me a little room, that I might answer them — were it not that I would now rather hear you, and that I shall yet answer those men at another time — namely, when I answer you.' And, if you wished to answer truly, Cato, these things were to be said: not that those men were not approved by you — men of such great genius and such great authority — but that you had observed that the things which they, on account of their antiquity, had seen too little, these were thoroughly perceived by the Stoics; and that about the same matters these men both argued more acutely, and felt more gravely and bravely — since, indeed, first they deny that good health is to be sought, but say it is to be chosen, and not because to be healthy is a good, but because it is to be valued at something — yet not at more than it seems to those who do not hesitate to call it a good — but that this you could not bear, that those ancients, as it were bearded men (as we are wont to say of our own), believed that for him who lived honourably, if he were also in good health, of good repute, and well supplied, the life would be more to be wished, and better, and more to be sought, than that of one who, though equally a good man, were in many ways, like the Alcmaeon of Ennius, 'beset by disease,

But these things are in children; but expressed in those ages which are now confirmed. Who is so unlike a man that he is not moved both by the offence of baseness and by the approval of honourableness? Who is there who does not hate a lustful, insolent youth? Who, on the contrary, does not love modesty, steadfastness in that age, even though it be of no concern to himself? Who does not hate Pullus Numitorius of Fregellae, the traitor, although he profited our commonwealth? Who does not most highly praise Codrus, the saviour of his city, who the daughters of Erechtheus? To whom is the name of Tubulus not hateful? Who does not love Aristides, though dead? Or do we forget how greatly we are moved in hearing and reading, when we learn that something was done piously, in friendship, with greatness of mind?

Excellently, too, did Epicurus say that fortune crosses the wise man but little, and that the greatest and gravest affairs are administered by his own counsel and reason; and that no greater pleasure can be perceived from an infinite span of years than is perceived from this, which we see to be finite. In your dialectic he thought there was no path either toward living better or toward arguing more conveniently. On physics he laid the greatest weight. By that science the force of words, the nature of language, and the relation of things consequent or contradictory can be discerned. And when the nature of all things is known, we are relieved of superstition, freed from the fear of death, not troubled by ignorance of things — out of which itself dreadful terrors often arise. Finally, we shall be better in character too, when we have learned what Nature requires. Then truly, if we hold fast a stable knowledge of things, and keep that rule which has, as it were, fallen from heaven for the knowledge of all things, by which all judgments of things shall be directed, we shall never, overcome by any man's discourse, abandon our conviction.

But how finely you seemed to speak, when on the one side you set a man heaped with the most and greatest pleasures, with no pain present or to come, and on the other one in the greatest torments throughout his whole body, with no pleasure joined or hoped for; and you asked who was either more wretched than this, or more blessed than that first; and then concluded that pain is the highest evil, pleasure the highest good! There was a certain Lucius Thorius Balbus, of Lanuvium, whom you cannot remember. He lived in such a way that no pleasure so choice could be found that he did not have it in abundance. He was both eager for pleasures, and a connoisseur of that kind, and well supplied; so little superstitious that he despised the many sacrifices and shrines of his own native town; so little afraid of death that he was slain in battle for the commonwealth.

From this it arises that there is also a natural commendation of men among men, so that it ought to be that a man should not seem alien to a man, for this very reason, that he is a man. For as among the limbs some are, as it were, born for themselves, as the eyes, as the ears, others also aid the use of the other limbs, as the legs, as the hands, so certain savage beasts are born for themselves alone; but that creature which is called the pina in its wide shell, and that which swims out of the shell, which, because it guards the pina, is called the pinoteres, and which, when it has betaken itself back into the same shell, is shut in — so that it seems to have warned the pina to beware — and likewise ants, bees, storks do certain things for the sake of others too. Much more closely is this so among men. And so by nature we are fitted for gatherings, assemblies, states.

by exile and want.' Those ancients, then, less acutely think that life more to be wished, more excellent, happier; but the Stoics only that it is to be preferred in choosing — not because that life is happier, but because it is more accommodated to nature. And that those who are not wise are all equally wretched — this, forsooth, the Stoics saw, but it had escaped those earlier men, who did not think that men polluted by crimes and parricides were no whit more wretched than those who, though they lived chastely and uprightly, had not yet attained that perfect wisdom.

What shall I say of ourselves, who were born, taken up, and trained for praise and for honour? What shouts of the crowd and of the ignorant are raised in the theatres, when these things are said: 'I am Orestes,' and, on the contrary, from the other: 'Nay, in truth, I, I say, am Orestes!' And when too the way out is given by each to the confused and wandering king — when they both pray that they be slain together — as often as this is acted, ever at any time except with the greatest admirations? There is no one, then, who does not approve and praise this affection of mind, by which not only is no usefulness sought, but even, against usefulness, good faith is preserved.

But unless the nature of things has been clearly perceived, we shall in no way be able to defend the judgments of the senses. Moreover, whatever we discern with the mind, all of it arises from the senses; and if these are all true, as Epicurus's theory teaches, then at last something can be known and grasped. Those who do away with the senses and say that nothing can be grasped cannot, when the senses are removed, even make out the very thing they are arguing. Besides, with knowledge and science taken away, all method both of conducting life and of carrying on affairs is taken away. Thus from physics is drawn fortitude against the fear of death, and steadfastness against the dread of religion, and calm of mind, when ignorance of all hidden things is removed, and moderation, when the kinds of desires have been set forth; and, as I just taught, the rule of knowledge and the judgment established by it hand down the distinction of true from false.

He limited his desires not by Epicurus's division, but by his own satiety. Yet he had regard for his health: he used such exercises that he came to dinner both thirsty and hungry; he took such food as was both most delicious and likewise easiest to digest; he used wine both for pleasure and so that it should not harm him. He employed all those other things, without which Epicurus says he cannot understand what good is. All pain was absent — which, had it been present, he would not have borne softly, and yet he would have used physicians rather than philosophers. His complexion was excellent, his health sound, his favour with men the greatest; his life, in short, was crammed with every variety of pleasures.

But they hold that the world is governed by the will of the gods, and that it is, as it were, a common city and state of men and gods, and that each one of us is a part of that world; from which it follows by nature that we should set the common advantage before our own. For as the laws set the safety of all before the safety of individuals, so a good and wise man, both obedient to the laws and not ignorant of civic duty, takes thought for the advantage of all more than for that of any one man or his own. Nor is the betrayer of his country more to be blamed than the deserter of the common advantage or safety for the sake of his own advantage or safety. From which it comes about that he is to be praised who meets death for the commonwealth, because it is fitting that our country be dearer to us than ourselves. And since that voice is held inhuman and wicked, of those who say they do not refuse that, when they themselves are dead, a burning-up of all lands should follow — which is wont to be expressed in a certain common Greek verse — it is certainly true that there must be provision made, for their own sake, even for those who shall at some time exist.

And in this place you brought forward those similes, which they are wont to use, most dissimilar. For who is ignorant that, if several should wish to emerge from the deep, those indeed would be nearer to breathing who already approach the surface of the water, but could no more breathe than those who are in the depth? Does it help nothing, then, to advance and make progress in virtue, that one should be less most wretched, before he has come to it — since in water it helps nothing? And, since puppies which are now about to see are equally blind with those just born, must Plato too, since he did not yet see wisdom, have been equally blind in mind with Phalaris?

With such examples not feigned fables only, but even histories are crammed, and indeed most of all ours. For we chose the best man to receive the Idaean sacred things; we sent guardians to kings; our commanders devoted their own heads for the safety of their country; our consuls warned even their bitterest enemy, already approaching the walls, that he should beware of poison; in our commonwealth was found a Lucretia, who atoned by a voluntary death for a defilement offered by force, and one who slew his daughter, that she might not be defiled. All which things, and countless besides, who is there that does not understand both that those who did them, led by the splendour of dignity, were unmindful of their own advantages, and that we, when we praise them, are led by no other thing than honourableness? These things being briefly set forth — for I have not pursued the abundance which I could, since there was doubt in nothing — but by these things it is surely concluded that both all the virtues and that honourable thing which arises from them and cleaves to them are to be sought for their own sake.

There remains a topic most necessary of all to this discussion, concerning friendship — which, if pleasure be the highest good, you assert can have no existence at all. Of this Epicurus indeed speaks thus: that of all the things which wisdom has provided for living happily, nothing is greater than friendship, nothing more fruitful, nothing more delightful. And this he proved not by his words only, but far more by his life, his deeds, and his character. How great a thing this is the feigned fables of the ancients declare, in which, though they are so many and so various and fetched from the remotest antiquity, scarcely three pairs of friends are found, so that, setting out from Theseus, you come at last to Orestes. But Epicurus, in one house — and that a narrow one — what great companies of friends, and joined by what great concord of love, he held! And this is done even now by the Epicureans. But let us return to our subject; there is no need to speak of individuals.

This man you call happy; your theory, at least, so compels you. But the man whom I should set above him I do not dare to name; virtue herself shall speak for me, and will not hesitate to set Marcus Regulus above this happy man of yours. Regulus, when of his own free will, compelled by no force except the good faith which he had given to the enemy, he had returned from his country to Carthage — at that very moment, when he was tortured with wakefulness and hunger, virtue cries that he was more blessed than Thorius drinking among the roses. He had waged great wars, had been twice consul, had triumphed; and yet he reckoned those earlier deeds of his not so great nor so glorious as that last calamity, which he had taken on himself for the sake of good faith and steadfastness — which to us, hearing of it, seems pitiable, but to him, enduring it, was full of pleasure. For it is not by mirth, nor wantonness, nor laughter, nor jesting, the companion of levity, but often men sad with firmness and steadfastness who are happy.

From this affection of mind arose the wills and commendations of the dying. And since no one would wish to lead his life in utter solitude, not even with an infinite abundance of pleasures, it is easily understood that we are born for the conjoining and gathering together of men, and for natural community. But we are impelled by nature to wish to benefit as many as we can, and chiefly by teaching and by handing down the methods of prudence.

Those similes are not alike, Cato, in which, however much you have advanced, yet that from which you wish to be absent is in the same case until you have escaped. For neither does that man breathe before he has emerged, and the puppies are equally blind before they have seen as if they were always going to be so. These are the like cases: someone's edge of sight is dull, another grows old in body; these, treatment being applied, are relieved day by day; the one is stronger every day, the other sees. Like to these are all who study virtue; they are relieved of vices, relieved of errors — unless perhaps you think that Tiberius Gracchus the father was not happier than the son, when the one strove to establish the commonwealth, the other to overthrow it. And yet that man was not wise — for who is, or when, or where, or whence? — but because he strove for praise and dignity, he had advanced much in virtue.

But in every honourable thing of which we speak, there is nothing so illustrious nor of wider reach than the conjunction of men among men, and, as it were, a certain fellowship and sharing of advantages, and the very affection of the human race. Which, born from the first begetting — because the begotten are loved by their begetters, and the whole house is joined by marriage and offspring — creeps gradually abroad, first by kinships, then by affinities, then by friendships, after by neighbourhoods, then by fellow citizens and those who are publicly allies and friends, then by the embrace of the whole human race. Which affection of mind, giving to each his own, and bountifully and equally guarding this fellowship of human conjunction which I speak of, is called justice; to which are joined piety, goodness, generosity, kindness, courtesy, and the things of the same kind. And these things are so proper to justice that they are common to the other virtues.

In three ways, then, I see that friendship has been discussed by our school. Some, while they denied that the pleasures which pertain to our friends are in themselves as much to be sought as we seek our own — a point at which the stability of friendship seems to some to totter — yet maintain that position and extricate themselves easily, as it seems to me. For they say that friendship, like the virtues of which we spoke before, cannot be separated from pleasure. For since solitude and a life without friends are full of treachery and fear, reason itself counsels us to procure friendships, by the winning of which the mind is strengthened and cannot be parted from the hope of gaining pleasures.

Lucretia, ravished by force by the king's son, having called the citizens to witness, slew herself. This grief of the Roman people, with Brutus as their leader and author, was the cause of liberty to the state; and for the memory of that woman both her husband and her father were made consul in the first year. The humble Lucius Verginius, but one of the many, in the sixtieth year after liberty was regained, slew his maiden daughter with his own hand, rather than that she should be given over to the lust of Appius Claudius, who was then in supreme command.

And so it is not easy to find one who does not himself hand on to another what he knows; thus we are inclined not only to learning, but also to teaching. And as it has been given by nature to bulls that they contend for their calves against lions with the utmost force and onset, so those who are strong in resources and able to do it — as we have heard of Hercules and of Liber — are incited by nature to the saving of the human race. And even when we call Jupiter Best and Greatest, and the same the Saviour, the Hospitable, the Stayer, we wish it to be understood that the safety of men is in his keeping. But it is by no means consistent, when we ourselves are vile and neglected among ourselves, to demand that we be dear to the immortal gods and loved by them. As, then, we use our limbs before we have learned for the sake of what usefulness we have them, so among ourselves we are by nature conjoined and associated for civil community. And if this were not so, there would be no place either for justice or for goodness.

Shall I compare your grandfather Drusus with Gaius Gracchus, nearly his contemporary? The wounds which the latter inflicted on the commonwealth, the former healed. If there is nothing that makes men so wretched as impiety and crime — so that even now all the unwise are wretched, as assuredly they are — yet he is not equally wretched who takes thought for his country and he who longs for it to be extinguished. The relief of vices, then, is great in those who have some progress toward virtue.

For since the nature of man is so generated that it has something inborn, as it were civil and popular, which the Greeks call politikon, whatever each virtue does will not shrink from that community and the affection and fellowship of men which I have set forth; and in turn justice, as it pours itself out into the other virtues, so it will seek them. For justice cannot be preserved except by a brave man, except by a wise one. Of such a kind, then, as is all this conspiration and consent of the virtues which I speak of, such is that very honourable thing — since the honourable is either virtue itself or a deed done by virtue; and a life agreeing with these things and answering to the virtues can be esteemed right and honourable and constant and agreeing with nature.

And just as hatreds, envies, and contempts are opposed to pleasures, so friendships are not only the most faithful supporters but also the producers of pleasures, both to our friends and to ourselves; and in these we not only enjoy the present, but are also uplifted by the hope of the time to come and after. And because we can in no way hold fast a firm and lasting pleasantness of life without friendship, nor indeed maintain friendship itself unless we love our friends equally with ourselves, for that reason this very thing is brought about in friendship, and friendship is linked with pleasure. For we both rejoice in the joy of our friends as much as in our own, and grieve equally at their distresses.

Either these things, Torquatus, are to be blamed by you, or the advocacy of pleasure must be renounced. But what advocacy, what case is that of pleasure, which can call no witnesses, no panegyrists, from among famous men? For just as we summon from the records of the annals, as witnesses, those whose whole life was spent in glorious toils, who could not bear to hear the name of pleasure, so in your discussions history is dumb. I never heard, in the school of Epicurus, Lycurgus, Solon, Miltiades, Themistocles, Epaminondas named — who are on the lips of all the other philosophers. But now, since we too have begun to treat of these matters, our friend Atticus will supply us from his stores — what great men, and how many! Is it not better to say something of these, than to talk, in so many volumes, of Themista?

And as they think there are bonds of right among men toward men, so they think man has no right with the beasts. For Chrysippus said admirably that the other things were born for the sake of men and the gods, but these for the sake of their own community and fellowship, so that men can use the beasts for their own advantage without injustice. And since the nature of man is such that there is, as it were, a civil right between him and the human race, he who preserves it will be just, he who departs from it unjust. But just as, though a theatre be common, it can yet rightly be said that the place which each man has occupied is his, so in a city or in the common world right is not opposed to each man's having his own.

But your school says that progress toward virtue takes place, but denies that relief of vices takes place. But what argument these acute men use for proving it, it is worth while to consider. \"Of those arts whose sums can grow,\" he says, \"the sum of their contraries too will be able to be increased; but to the sum of virtue nothing can be added; therefore not even the vices, which are the contraries of the virtues, will be able to grow.\" Which, then, pray — are doubtful things laid open by evident, or evident things taken away by doubtful? And yet this is evident, that vices are greater one in another; that is doubtful, whether to that which you call the highest good any addition can be made. But you, when you ought to illustrate doubtful things by evident, try to take away evident things by doubtful.

And yet this conjunction and blending of the virtues is by the philosophers distinguished by a certain reasoning. For although they are so coupled and connected that all share in all, and one cannot be separated from another, yet each has its own proper office: as fortitude is discerned in toils and dangers, temperance in the passing over of pleasures, prudence in the choice of goods and evils, justice in giving to each his own. Since, then, there is in every virtue a certain care, as it were, looking outward and seeking and embracing others, it comes about that friends, brothers, kinsmen, connexions, fellow citizens, and finally all men — since we would have there to be one fellowship of men — are to be sought for their own sake. And yet none of these is of that kind that it should be in the end and uttermost of goods.

Wherefore the wise man will be disposed toward his friend in the same way as toward himself, and whatever toils he would undertake for the sake of his own pleasure, the same he will undertake for the sake of his friend's pleasure. And whatever was said of the virtues — how they always cleave to pleasures — the same must be said of friendship. For Epicurus said admirably, in these very words almost: 'The same knowledge,' he says, 'that has strengthened the mind not to fear any eternal or lasting evil, has discerned that within this very span of life the surest defence is the protection of friendship.'

Let those things be the Greeks'; though from them we have philosophy and all the liberal disciplines. But still there is something which is not lawful for us, though it be lawful for them. The Stoics contend with the Peripatetics. The one deny that anything is good but what is honourable; the others say that they grant the most, and by far the most, to honourableness, but that there are yet certain goods both in the body and outside it. And an honourable contest it is, and a splendid discussion! For the whole contention is about the worth of virtue. But when you discuss with your school, you must hear much even about obscene pleasures, of which Epicurus speaks very often.

But since we see that man is born for the protection and preservation of men, it is consistent with this nature that the wise man should wish to take part in and administer the commonwealth, and, that he may live according to nature, should take a wife and wish to have children by her. Nor do they think that even holy loves are alien to the wise man. But the manner and life of the Cynics some say falls within the wise man, if some such chance should occur that it must be done; others, by no means.

And so again, by the same reasoning which I used a little before, you will be stuck. For if, on this account, vices are not greater one than another, because nothing can be added even to that end of goods which you make — since it is evident that the vices of all are not equal, your end of goods must be changed. For we must necessarily hold this, that, when some consequence is false, that thing of which it is a consequence cannot be true. What, then, is the cause of those straits? The glorious ostentation in establishing the highest good. For when it is affirmed that that alone which is honourable is good, the care of health, the diligence of household affairs, the administration of the commonwealth, the order of conducting business, the duties of life, in short that very honourable thing in which alone you would have all things to be, must be deserted. Which things are most diligently said against Aristo by Chrysippus. From that difficulty those 'falsely-speaking malices,' as Accius says, were born.

So it comes about that two kinds of things to be sought for their own sake are found: one, which is in those things in which that uttermost is filled out, which are either of the mind or of the body; but these which are external — that is, which are neither in the mind nor in the body, as friends, parents, children, kinsmen, the country itself — these indeed are dear of their own accord, but are not in the same kind as those. Nor indeed could anyone ever attain the highest good, if all those things which are external, though to be sought, were contained in the highest good.

But there are some Epicureans, a little more timid in the face of your reproaches, yet acute enough, who fear that, if we hold friendship to be sought for the sake of our own pleasure, the whole of friendship may seem, as it were, to limp. And so they say that the first meetings and couplings and the wishes to establish intimacies arise for the sake of pleasure; but when advancing intercourse has produced familiarity, then affection blooms forth so greatly that, even if there be no advantage from the friendship, yet the friends are loved for their own sakes. For if we are wont, by the habit of frequenting them, to grow fond of places, of shrines, of cities, of gymnasiums, of the Field of Mars, of dogs, of horses, of the sports of exercise or of hunting, how much more easily and more justly can this come about in our intercourse with men?

You cannot, then, uphold those doctrines, Torquatus — believe me — if you have looked closely at yourself and your thoughts and pursuits; you will be ashamed, I say, of that picture which Cleanthes used to paint quite aptly in words. He bade his hearers picture to themselves Pleasure painted on a tablet, in the loveliest raiment and with royal adornment, seated on a throne; and the Virtues present as her little handmaids, who did nothing else, accounted no duty their own, except to wait upon Pleasure, and only whispered in her ear — if only that could be shown in a picture — to take care that she did nothing unwary that might offend the minds of men, or anything from which some pain might arise. 'We Virtues were born to serve you; we have no other business at all.'

But that all fellowship, conjunction, and affection of man toward man may be preserved, they would have both profits and harms — which they call ophelemata and blammata — to be common; of which the one profit, the other harm. Nor only did they say that these are common, but also that they are equal. But disadvantages and advantages — for so I call euchrestemata and dyschrestemata — they would have to be common, but not equal. For those things which profit or which harm are either goods or evils, which must necessarily be equal; but advantages and disadvantages are in that kind which we have called preferred and rejected; these can be unequal. But profits are said to be common, while right deeds and sins are not held common.

For because wisdom had not where to set its foot, all duties being taken away — but duties were taken away when all selection and distinction was removed, which could not exist when all things were so levelled that there was no difference among them — out of these straits those things escaped, worse than Aristo's. Yet his are simple, yours crafty. For ask Aristo whether these things seem good to him: freedom from pain, riches, health; he would deny it. What? Are the things which are contrary to these evils? No more so. Ask Zeno; he would answer in the very same words. Wondering, let us ask of each how we can lead our life, if we think it makes no difference to us whether we are well or sick, whether we are free or tortured by pain, whether we can ward off cold and hunger or cannot. 'You will live,' says Aristo, 'magnificently and admirably; you will do whatever shall seem good; you will never be distressed, never desire, never fear.'

How, then, you will say, can it be true that all things are referred to the highest good, if friendships, kinships, and the rest of external things are not contained in the highest good? By this reasoning, forsooth: that we guard those things which are external by those duties which arise from each one's own kind of virtue. For both the cultivation of a friend and of a parent, to him who discharges his duty, is profitable in this very thing, that so to discharge duty is among right deeds, which arise from the virtues. And these indeed the wise pursue, with nature for their guide, as though seeing; but men not perfect, and yet endowed with excellent geniuses, are often stirred by glory, which has the appearance and likeness of honourableness. But if they should see deeply honourableness itself, perfect and complete on every side, the one most glorious thing of all and most to be praised, with what gladness would they be filled, when they so greatly rejoice in the sketched opinion of it?

There are others, however, who say that there is a kind of compact among the wise, that they should love their friends not less than themselves. This both we understand can come about, and we often see it, and it is plain that nothing can be found more fitted for living pleasantly than such a union. From all which it can be judged that the principle of friendship is not only not hindered if the highest good be placed in pleasure, but that without this the establishment of friendship cannot be found at all.

But Epicurus denies — for this is your guiding light — that anyone who does not live honourably can live pleasantly. As though I cared what he affirms or denies. This is what I ask: what it is consistent for him, who places the highest good in pleasure, to say. What do you bring forward to show why Thorius, why Gaius Postumius, why the master of all these, Orata, did not live most pleasantly? He himself denies, as I said before, that the life of the luxurious is to be blamed, unless they are plainly fools — that is, unless they either desire or fear. And since he promises a medicine for both these things, he promises licence for luxury. For with these things removed, he denies that he can find anything to blame in the life of the profligate.

But they think friendship is to be employed, because it is of that kind which profits. But although in friendship some say that the welfare of a friend is as dear to the wise man as his own, while others say that his own is dearer to each man, yet even these latter confess that it is alien to that justice for which we seem to have been born, to take something away from anyone that one may take it to oneself. But by no means is it approved by this school of which I speak that either justice or friendship should be taken on or approved for the sake of usefulness. For those same usefulnesses will be able to undermine and overthrow them. For neither justice nor friendship can exist at all, unless they are sought for their own sake.

What says Zeno? He says these are monstrous things, and that in that way one can in no wise live; that he says that between the honourable and the base there is an immense — I know not what — boundless difference, but among the other things none at all. The same so far;

For what man given over to pleasures, what man inflamed by the fires of desires, in attaining those things which he had most keenly desired, do we think is flooded with so great a gladness as either the elder Africanus when Hannibal was conquered, or the younger when Carthage was overthrown? Whom did the descent on the Tiber on that festal day affect with so great joy as Lucius Paulus, when he brought king Perses captive, sailing in upon the same river? Come now, our Lucius, build up in your mind the loftiness and excellence of the virtues:

Wherefore, if the things I have said are clearer and brighter than the sun itself; if I have said everything drawn from the fountain of Nature; if our whole discourse confirms all its credit by the senses — that is, by witnesses uncorrupted and entire; if speechless infants, and even the dumb beasts, all but proclaim, with Nature for their teacher and guide, that nothing is welcome but pleasure, nothing harsh but pain, and judge of these neither perversely nor corruptly — ought we not to feel the deepest gratitude to him who, having heard this, as it were, voice of Nature, so firmly and gravely grasped it that he led all the sound of mind into the path of a calm, tranquil, quiet, and happy life? As for your thinking him too little learned, the cause is this: that he reckoned no learning to be such except what helped the discipline of the happy life.

You cannot, then, directing all things by pleasure, either uphold or retain virtue. For neither ought a man to be held good and just who abstains from injustice for fear of getting harm. You know, I suppose, that line: 'No man is pious who—'; beware of thinking anything more true. For so long as he fears, he is not just; and surely, if he should cease to fear, he will not be. But he will not fear, if he can either conceal it, or by great power maintain whatever he has done; and assuredly he will prefer to be thought a good man, though he is not, than to be one, though he be not thought so. Thus, what is most certain, instead of true and sure justice you hand down to us a counterfeit of justice, and teach us, in a manner, to despise our own steadfast conscience and to hunt after the wandering opinion of others.

But right, which can be so called and named, is by nature; and it is alien to the wise man not only to do injustice to anyone, but even to harm him. Nor indeed is it right to join or associate injustice with friends or with the well-deserving; and it is most gravely and most truly maintained that fairness can never be separated from usefulness, and that whatever is fair and just is also honourable, and in turn, whatever is honourable is also just and fair.

hear the rest, and contain your laughter, if you can. 'Those middle things,' he says, 'among which there is no difference, are yet of such a kind that of them some are to be chosen, some to be rejected, some altogether to be neglected — that is, of them you wish some, do not wish others, care not for others.' But just now you had said there was nothing in those things that made a difference. 'And now I say the same,' he will say, 'but it makes no difference toward the virtues and the vices.'

now you will not doubt that men possessed of them, living with a great and uplifted mind, are always happy, who understand that all the motions of fortune and the changes of things and times will be light and feeble, if they come into the contest of virtue. For those things which were counted by us among the goods of the body do indeed fill out the happiest life, but so that without them the happy life can exist. For those additions of goods are so small and slight that, as the stars in the rays of the sun, so those are not even discerned in the splendour of the virtues. And as this is truly said, that those weights of bodily advantages are small toward living happily, so it is too violent to say that they are nothing;

Was he to spend his time in unrolling the poets, as I and Triarius do at your urging — in whom there is no solid usefulness, and all the delight is childish — or to wear himself out, like Plato, on music, geometry, numbers, and the stars, which, set out from false beginnings, cannot be true, and which, even were they true, would bring nothing whereby we might live more pleasantly — that is, better? Was he, I say, to pursue those arts and abandon the art of living, so great, so laborious, and likewise so fruitful? Not Epicurus, then, is unlearned, but those are unlettered who think that things which it is disgraceful for boys not to have learned ought to be learned even into old age. When he had said this, 'I have set forth my opinion,' he said, 'and with this purpose, that I might learn your judgment, since the opportunity of doing so at my own pleasure has, before this time, never been given me.'

The same things may be said of the other virtues, the foundations of all of which you place in pleasure as on water. For what? Can we call that same Torquatus brave? — for I am delighted, though I cannot, as you say, corrupt me, I am delighted, I say, both by your family and your name; and indeed there rises before my eyes that best of men and most loving of us, Aulus Torquatus, of whose zeal toward me — and how marked it was — in those times which are known to all, each of you must needs be aware. Which kindnesses would not be pleasing to me — who wish both to be and to be held grateful — unless I perceived that he was my friend for my sake, not his own; unless you call this 'his own,' that it is the interest of all to act rightly. If you say that, we have won. For this is what we wish, this is what we contend for: that the fruit of duty be duty itself.

And to those virtues of which we have argued they add also dialectic and physics, and both these they call by the name of virtue: the one, because it has the method of seeing to it that we assent to nothing falsely, nor are ever deceived by captious probability, and that we may be able to hold and maintain the things we have learned about goods and evils. For without this art they think that anyone can be led away from the truth and deceived. Rightly, then, if in all things rashness and ignorance are faulty, the art which removes these is named a virtue.

Who, pray, did not know that? But let us hear. 'Those things which you mentioned,' he says, 'to be healthy, to be rich, not to be in pain, I do not call goods, but I will call them in Greek proegmena, in Latin \"brought forward\" — but I prefer \"preferred\" or \"chief,\" let it be more tolerable and softer; but those things, disease, want, pain, I do not call evils, but, if you please, \"rejectable.\" And so I do not say I seek those things, but choose them; nor wish for them, but take them; and the contraries, again, I do not flee, but, as it were, set apart.' What says Aristotle and the rest of Plato's nurslings? That they call all the things which are according to nature goods, but those which are against it evils. Do you see, then, that your Zeno agrees in words with Aristo, but differs in substance; agrees in substance with Aristotle and those men, but differs in words? Why, then, since there is agreement about the thing, do we not prefer to speak in the customary way? Or let him teach that I shall be more ready to despise money if I count it among preferred things than if among goods, and braver in bearing pain if I shall say it is harsh and difficult to endure and against nature than if I shall call it an evil.

for those who so argue seem to me to have forgotten what principles of nature they themselves laid down. Something, then, must be assigned to these, provided you understand how much is to be assigned. For it belongs to a philosopher seeking not so much glorious as true things, both not to count as nothing those things which even those glorious men confessed to be according to nature, and to see that there is so great a force of virtue and so great, so to speak, an authority of honourableness, that the rest are not indeed nothing, but so small that they seem to be nothing. This is the discourse neither of one who spurns all things except virtue, nor of one who amplifies virtue itself with its own praises; in short, this is the explanation of the highest good, complete and perfect on every side. From this the rest, trying to snatch little parts, each wished to seem to bring forward his own opinion.

This that wise man of yours does not wish, but exacts pleasure, as it were a wage, from all things. But I return to him. If for the sake of pleasure he fought it out with the Gaul at the Anio, having been challenged, and from his spoils put on himself both the torque and the surname for any other cause than that such deeds seemed to him worthy of a man — then I do not think him brave. Now if modesty, if restraint, if chastity, if, in a word, temperance shall be kept in check by the fear of punishment or infamy, and shall not guard themselves by their own holiness — what adultery, what defilement, what lust will not break loose and fling itself forth, when concealment is offered, or impunity, or licence?

To physics also the same honour is not without cause assigned, because he who is to live consistently with nature must set out from the whole world and from its governance. Nor indeed can anyone judge truly about goods and evils unless all the system of nature, and the life of the gods too, be known, and whether or not the nature of man agrees with the universe. And those ancient precepts of the wise, who bid us yield to the time, and follow god, and know ourselves, and do nothing in excess — what force these have (and they have the greatest) no one can see without physics. And also, toward cultivating justice, toward maintaining friendships and the other affections, this knowledge alone can hand down what force nature has. Nor indeed can either piety toward the gods, or how much gratitude is owed to them, be understood without the explanation of nature.

Wittily did Marcus Piso, our friend, both in many other places and in this, mock the Stoics: 'For what?' he used to say. 'You deny that riches are a good, you say they are a preferred thing? How do you help? Do you lessen avarice? In what way? If we follow the word — first, the word \"preferred\" is longer than \"good.\"' — Nothing to the point! — 'Let it be so; yet certainly it is weightier. For whence \"good\" was named, I do not know; \"preferred,\" I believe, from this, that it is preferred to other things. That seems to me a great matter.' And so he used to say that more was assigned to riches by Zeno, who placed them among preferred things, than by Aristotle, who confessed that riches are a good — but neither a great good, and one to be despised and looked down on in comparison with right and honourable things, nor greatly to be sought; and altogether about all those words changed by Zeno he so argued, that the things which were denied by him to be goods and which to be evils were called by him by gladder names than by us, these by sadder ones. Piso, then, in this manner — a most excellent man, and, as you know, most loving of you. Let us, a few things being added to these, make an end at last; for it is long to answer to all the things which were said by you.

Often by Aristotle, by Theophrastus, the knowledge of things was wonderfully praised for its own sake; captivated by this one thing, Erillus maintained that knowledge is the highest good, and that no other thing is to be sought for its own sake. Many things were said by the ancients about despising and looking down on human things; this one thing Aristo held: he denied that there is any thing besides vices and virtues either to be fled or to be sought. It was laid down by our school that, among those things which are according to nature, is to be free from pain; this Hieronymus said is the highest good. But indeed Callipho and after him Diodorus, the one having fallen in love with pleasure, the other with freedom from pain, neither could lack honourableness, which is most highly praised by our school.

What of this, Torquatus — how, pray, does it seem? — that you, with that name, that genius, that glory, do not dare to say in an assembly to what you refer what you do, what you think, what you strive for; for what end you wish to accomplish what you attempt; in short, what you judge best in life? For what would you wish to deserve, now when you have entered upon a magistracy and gone up to address the assembly — for you must declare what you will observe in administering justice, and perhaps too, if it seem good to you, you will say something of your ancestors and of yourself, in the manner of our forefathers — what, then, would you wish to deserve, that you should say you will do everything in that magistracy for the sake of pleasure, and that you have done nothing in your life except for the sake of pleasure? 'Do you think me,' you say, 'so mad as to speak in that fashion before the ignorant?' But say those same things in a court of law; or, if you fear the bystanders, say them in the senate. You will never do it. Why, unless because the speech is base? Do you think, then, me and Triarius men before whom you may speak basely?

But now I feel that I have been carried further than the proposed plan demanded. But the admirable composition of the doctrine and the incredible order of things drew me on; which — by the immortal gods! — do you not wonder at? For what, either in nature, than which nothing is more fitting, nothing more orderly, or in works made by hand, can be found so composed and so compacted and joined together? What later thing does not agree with the earlier? What follows that does not answer to what went before? What is not so woven, one thing from another, that, if you move a single letter, all things totter? And yet there is nothing that can be moved.

For out of the same jugglery of words both kingdoms have been born to you, and commands, and riches, and those indeed so great that you say that all things which are anywhere are the wise man's. Besides, that he alone is beautiful, alone free, alone a citizen; the fools all the contrary, whom you would have even to be insane. These things they call paradoxa, let us call them 'wonders.' But what have they of wonder, when you have come near? I will compare with you what thing you place beneath each word; there will be no controversy. You say all sins are equal. I will not now jest with you as I did about these same matters, when I defended Lucius Murena while you accused. Those things were then said before the ignorant, something too was granted to the bystanders; now we must proceed more subtly. Sins are equal.

Nay even the votaries of pleasure themselves seek by-ways, and have the virtues on their lips all day long, and say that pleasure is sought at first only, then that by habit a kind of second nature, as it were, is produced, impelled by which they do many things seeking no pleasure. The Stoics remain. They indeed transferred not some one or other thing from us, but our whole philosophy to themselves; and as the rest of thieves change the marks of the things which they have taken, so they, that they might use our opinions as their own, changed the names, as if the marks of things. So there is left this doctrine alone, worthy of the studious of the liberal arts, worthy of the learned, worthy of famous men, worthy of leaders, worthy of kings. When he had said this and paused a little, 'What is it?' said he;

But be it so: the word 'pleasure' itself has no dignity, and perhaps we do not understand it. For this you say again and again, that we do not understand what you mean by pleasure. A difficult and obscure matter, no doubt! When you say 'indivisible atoms' and 'intermundane spaces,' which neither are nor can be, we understand; and pleasure, which is known to all the sparrows, cannot be understood by us? What if I bring it about that you confess that I know not only what pleasure is — for it is a pleasant motion in the sense — but also what you mean it to be? For at one time you mean that very thing which I just now described, and put a name upon it — that it be in motion and make some variety; at another, a certain other highest pleasure, to which nothing can be added, which is present, you say, when all pain is absent: this you call 'steady.'

But how grave, how magnificent, how constant is the person of the wise man brought to completion! Who, when reason has taught that what is honourable is the only good, must necessarily be always happy, and truly possess all those titles which are wont to be mocked by the ignorant. For he will more rightly be called a king than Tarquin, who could rule neither himself nor his own; more rightly master of the people — for that is the dictator — than Sulla, who was master of three pestilent vices, luxury, avarice, cruelty; more rightly rich than Crassus, who, had he not been in want, would never have wished to cross the Euphrates with no cause of war. All things will rightly be called his, who alone knows how to use all things; rightly too he will be called beautiful — for the lineaments of the mind are more beautiful than those of the body; rightly the only free man, obeying no one's domination and yielding to no desire; rightly unconquered, whose body, even if it be bound, yet no chains can be cast upon his mind; nor will he await any span of life, so that he be judged at last whether he was happy when he has finished the last day of life by death — which that one of the seven wise men unwisely advised Croesus;

— In what way? — Because nothing is more honourable than the honourable, nor baser than the base. — Go on further; for about that there is great disagreement. Let us see those proper arguments, why all sins are equal. — 'As,' he says, 'in several strings, unless none of them be so stretched with its cords that it can preserve the harmony, they are all equally out of tune, so sins, because they are discordant, are equally discordant; they are therefore equal.' — Here we are deceived by an ambiguity. For it happens equally to all the strings that they be out of tune; but it does not at once follow that they are equally out of tune. That comparison, then, helps you nothing. For neither, if we shall have said that all avarices are equally avarices, will it follow that we should also say they are equal. Here is another simile that is dissimilar.

'do I seem to you to have discoursed sufficiently, by my right, in your ears?' And I: 'You indeed, Piso,' said I, 'as often at other times, so today seemed so to know these things that, if the opportunity of you fell to us more often, I should not think we need much supplicate the Greeks. And this indeed I approved the more, because I remember that Stasea of Naples, that teacher of yours, a noble Peripatetic indeed, was wont to say these things somewhat otherwise, assenting to those who placed much in good or adverse fortune, much in the goods or evils of the body.' 'It is as you say,' said he; 'but these things are said by Antiochus, our friend, much better and more strongly than they were said by Stasea. Although I do not ask what has been approved by you of me, but by this our Cicero, whom I desire to lead away from you as my pupil.'

Let that, then, be pleasure. Say, in any assembly, that you do everything in order not to be in pain. If you think not even this is said amply enough, honourably enough, say that you will do everything, both in that magistracy and in all your life, for the sake of your own advantage; nothing but what is expedient; in short, nothing except for your own sake. What shout of the assembly, or what hope of the consulship — which is most ready for you — do you think there would be? Will you, then, follow that principle which you use with yourself and with your own, but dare not profess and bring forth into the open? But indeed those things which the Peripatetics, which the Stoics say are always on your lips, in the courts, in the senate — duty, fairness, dignity, good faith, the right, the honourable, things worthy of empire, worthy of the Roman people, all dangers for the commonwealth, to die for one's country: when you speak these things, we dolts stand agape, while you, of course, laugh within yourself.

for if he had ever been happy, he would have carried his happy life through even to that pyre built by Cyrus. But if it is so, that no one is happy unless he be a good man, and all good men are happy, what is more to be cultivated than philosophy, or what is more divine than virtue?

'For as,' he says, 'a pilot sins equally if he overturns a ship of chaff and if of gold, so he sins equally who beats a parent and who beats a slave with injustice.' — Not to see that of what kind the burden is which the ship carries pertains nothing to the pilot's art! And so whether it carries gold or chaff makes no difference to steering well or ill! But what difference there is between a parent and a little slave both can and ought to be understood. Therefore in steering it makes no difference, in duty the greatest, of what kind the thing is in which one sins. And if in the very steering the ship was overturned by negligence, the sin is greater in the gold than in the chaff. For we wish to be assigned to all arts that which is called common prudence, which all who are set over any craft ought to have. So not even in this way are sins equal.
