Then Lucius: 'Those things indeed are greatly approved by me, which I think is so with my brother too.' Then Piso to me: 'What then?' said he; 'do you grant the young man leave? Or do you prefer that he learn those things which, when he has thoroughly learned them, he will know nothing?' 'I indeed permit him,' said I. 'But do you not remember that it is allowed me to approve those things which were said by you? For who can fail to approve the things which seem probable to him?' 'But indeed,' said he, 'can anyone approve what he has not perceived, comprehended, known?' 'That is no great disagreement, Piso,' said I. 'For there is no other reason why nothing seems to me able to be perceived, except that the force of perceiving is so defined by the Stoics that they deny anything can be perceived unless it be true in such a way that it cannot be false. And so this is a disagreement with them; with the Peripatetics none at all. But let us pass over these things; for they have a rather long and quarrelsome enough discussion.

For among those words so magnificent and so splendid pleasure has no place — not that pleasure which you say is in motion, which all townsmen and countrymen, all, I say, who speak Latin, call pleasure; nor even this steady kind, which no one but you calls pleasure. See, then, whether you ought not to use our words and your own meanings. But if you were to feign your face, your gait, that you might seem graver, you would not be like yourself; and will you feign your words, and say what you do not mean? Or even, as with your dress, will you have one opinion for home and another for the forum, so that there is display on the surface, but the truth hidden within? Consider, I pray you, whether this be right. To me, at least, those opinions seem true which are honourable, which are praiseworthy, which are glorious, which can be professed in the senate, before the people, in every gathering and assembly — that one may not be ashamed to think what one would be ashamed to say. But where can there be a place for friendship, or who can be a friend to any man whom he does not love for his own sake?

Yet they press on and remit nothing. 'Since,' they say, 'every sin is of weakness and inconstancy, and these vices are equally great in all fools, it is necessary that sins be equal.' As though either it were granted that in all fools the vices are equally great, and that Lucius Tubulus was of the same weakness and inconstancy as that Publius Scaevola by whose bill he was condemned; and as though it made no difference among the very things in which one sins, so that, the greater or less these are, the things sinned in these matters should be either

That seemed to me said by you too hastily, that all the wise are always happy; somehow your discourse flew past it. But unless it be so brought about, those things which Theophrastus said about fortune, about pain, about the torture of the body — with which he thought the happy life could in no way be joined — I fear are true. For that vehemently fights against itself, that the same man be happy and oppressed by many evils. How these things agree I do not at all understand.' 'Does it not please you, then,' said he, 'that there is so great a force of virtue that it is content of itself for living happily? Or, if you approve that, do you deny that it can so come about that those who are possessed of virtue, even afflicted by certain evils, are happy?' 'I indeed wish there to be in virtue the greatest force possible; but how great it is, another time; now only whether it can be so great, if anything be held among goods outside virtue.'

And what is it to love — from which the name of friendship is derived — but to wish that someone be endowed with the greatest goods, even though nothing flow back from them to oneself? 'It profits me,' he says, 'to be of this mind.' Nay, perhaps to seem so. For you cannot be so, unless you are; and how can you be so, unless love itself has seized you? — which is wont to be produced not by a reckoning-up of usefulness, but arises of itself and is born of its own accord. 'But I follow usefulness.' Then friendship will last just so long as usefulness follows; and, if usefulness establishes friendship, the same will destroy it.

greater or less! And so — for now let the discourse be concluded — by this one fault chiefly your Stoics seem to me to be pressed, that they think they can hold two contrary opinions. For what is so repugnant as that the same man should say that what is honourable is the only good, who says that the appetite for things accommodated to living proceeds from nature? So when they wish to retain those things which agree with the former opinion, they fall into Aristo; when they flee that, they defend in substance the same things as the Peripatetics, while they hold their words with their teeth. And these again, while they will not have them plucked from their order, come out rougher, harsher, harder both in discourse and in manners.

'And yet,' said he, 'if you grant the Stoics that virtue alone, if it be present, makes life happy, you grant it to the Peripatetics too. For those things which they dare not call evils, but grant to be harsh and inconvenient and to be rejected and alien to nature, we call evils, but slight and almost least. Wherefore if he can be happy who is in harsh and rejectable things, he too can be who is in slight evils.' And I: 'Piso,' said I, 'if there is anyone who is wont to see acutely in causes what the matter at issue is, you are surely he. Wherefore attend, I pray. For so far, perhaps by my fault, you do not perceive what I am asking.' 'I am here,' said he, 'and I await what you will answer to that which I was asking.'

But what, pray, will you do, if usefulness shall have failed friendship, as often happens? Will you forsake it? What sort of friendship is that? Will you keep it? How does that agree? — for you see what you have determined about friendship, that it is to be sought for the sake of usefulness. 'I should incur hatred, if I ceased to maintain a friend.' First, why is that thing worthy of hatred, unless because it is base? But if, lest you incur some inconvenience, you will not forsake your friend, yet, that you may not be bound to no profit, you will wish that he die. What if he will not only bring you no usefulness, but losses of your estate must be incurred, toils undertaken, danger of life undergone? Even then will you not look to yourself, and consider that each man is born for himself and for his own pleasures? Will you give yourself as a hostage unto death to a tyrant for a friend, as that Pythagorean did to the Sicilian tyrant? Or, being Pylades, will you say that you are Orestes, that you may die for a friend? Or, if you were Orestes, would you refute Pylades, declare yourself, and, if you could not prove it, would you not entreat that you both be slain together?

Fleeing this gloom and harshness of theirs, Panaetius approved neither the bitterness of their opinions nor the thorns of their arguing, and was in the one kind milder, in the other more illustrious, and always had on his lips Plato, Aristotle, Xenocrates, Theophrastus, Dicaearchus, as his own writings declare. Whom indeed I greatly advise you to handle studiously and diligently. But since it both grows toward evening, and I must return to my villa, for now thus far;

'I shall answer,' said I, 'that I am not asking at this time what virtue can effect, but what is said consistently, and what disagrees with itself.' 'In what way, then?' said he. 'Because, when this is published by Zeno magnificently, as if from an oracle: \"Virtue is content of itself for living happily,\" and \"Why?\" says one, he answers: \"Because there is no other good except what is honourable.\" I do not ask now whether it be true; that I say, that the things which he says cohere admirably among themselves.

You, indeed, Torquatus, would do all these things; for I think there is nothing worthy of great praise which I could believe you would forgo through fear of death or pain. But the question is not what is consistent with your nature, but what is consistent with your doctrine. That theory which you defend, those precepts which you have learned and approve, utterly overthrow friendship, however much Epicurus, as he does, exalt it to heaven with praises. 'But he himself cultivated friendships.' Who, pray, denies that he was a good man, and courteous, and humane? It is of his genius, in these discussions, not of his morals, that we inquire. Let that perversity belong to the levity of the Greeks, who pursue with abuse those from whom they dissent about the truth. But however courteous he was in maintaining his friends, yet, if these things are true — for I affirm nothing — he was not acute enough. 'But he approved himself to many.'

but let us often do this same thing.' 'We will indeed,' said he; 'for what better can we do? And this first service I shall exact of you, that you hear me refuting the things which were said by you. But remember that you approve all the things which we feel, except that we use other words; while to me nothing of yours is approved.' 'You give a scruple to one departing,' said I; 'but we shall see.' When these things had been said, we departed.

Let Epicurus have said this same thing, that the wise man is always happy — which indeed he is wont sometimes to bubble forth — whom he says, when he is worn out by the greatest pains, will say: \"How sweet this is! How little I care!\"; I would not fight with the man as to why he should have so much good in his nature; this I would press, that he does not understand what he ought to say, when he has said that pain is the highest evil. The same now is my discourse against you. You say all the same things both good and evil which those say who never saw a philosopher even painted, as the saying is: health, strength, stature, beauty, the soundness of all the nails, goods; deformity, disease, weakness, evils.

And rightly, perhaps; but still the testimony of the multitude is not the weightiest. For in every art, or study, or any kind of knowledge, or in virtue itself, the best of each is the rarest. And to me, indeed, the fact that he himself was a good man, and that many Epicureans both have been and today are faithful in friendships, and in their whole life constant and grave, governing their counsels not by pleasure but by duty — this seems to me a greater force of honourableness and a less of pleasure. For some men so live that their life refutes their doctrine. And as the rest are thought to speak better than they act, so these seem to me to act better than they speak.

Now those external things you indeed treat sparingly; but since these of the body are goods, you will certainly count among goods their producers — friends, children, kinsmen, riches, honours, resources. Against this attend that I say nothing; this I say, that, if those things are evils into which the wise man can fall, then to be wise is not enough for living happily.' 'Nay indeed,' said he, 'for living most happily it is too little, but for living happily it is enough.' 'I noticed,' said I, 'that you laid it down in that way a little before, and I know that it is wont to be said so by our Antiochus; but what is less to be approved than that someone be happy and not happy enough? For that to which whatever is added is enough, is too much; and no one is too happy; so no one is happier than the happy.'

But these things have nothing at all to do with the matter; let us look at the things you said about friendship. Among them I seemed to recognize one as said by Epicurus himself: that friendship cannot be torn from pleasure, and is therefore to be cultivated, because, since without it one cannot live safely and without fear, one cannot even live pleasantly. Enough has been answered to this. You brought forward another, more humane, of these more recent men, never said by Epicurus himself, so far as I know: that at first a friend is sought for the sake of usefulness, but, when intimacy has grown, then he is loved for his own sake, even though the hope of pleasure be set aside. Although this can be censured in many ways, yet I accept what they give. For it is enough for me, though not enough for them. For they say that something can sometimes be rightly done with no pleasure expected or sought.

'Then,' said he, 'to you Quintus Metellus, who saw three sons consuls — of whom one even both a censor and triumphing, and a fourth a praetor — and left them safe, and three daughters married, when he himself had been consul, censor, even an augur, and had triumphed, supposing him to have been wise — was he not happier than Regulus, supposing him likewise to have been wise, who was put to death in the power of the enemy by wakefulness and starvation?'

You also set down that others say there is a kind of compact among the wise, that, in the same way as they are disposed toward themselves, in the same way they should be disposed toward their friends; and that this both can be done, and has often been done, and pertains most of all to the gaining of pleasures. If they were able to make this compact, let them make that other too — to love fairness, modesty, all the virtues, for their own sakes, freely. But indeed, if we shall cultivate friendships for the fruits and profits and advantages, if there shall be no affection to make friendship itself, of its own accord, by its own force, of itself and for its own sake, to be sought — is it doubtful that we shall prefer farms and tenements to friends?

'Why do you ask me that?' said I. 'Ask the Stoics.' 'What, then,' said he, 'do you think they will answer?' 'That Metellus is no whit happier than Regulus.' 'Thence, then,' said he, 'we must begin.' 'Yet we stray from our purpose,' said I. 'For I am not asking what is true, but what each man ought to say. Would indeed that they said one man happier than another! Already you would see ruins. For since the good is placed in virtue alone and in the honourable itself, and since neither virtue, as it pleases them, nor the honourable grows, and that is the only good, possessing which one must necessarily be happy — since that cannot be increased in which alone being happy is placed, how can anyone be happier than another? Do you see how these things harmonize? And, by Hercules — for I must confess what I feel — wonderful among them is the connexion of things. The last things answer to the first, the middle to both, all to all. They see what follows, what is repugnant. As in geometry, if you grant the first, all must be granted. Grant that nothing is good except what is honourable; it must be granted that the happy life is placed in virtue. See again backward:

You may here again rehearse the things said by Epicurus, in the best words, in praise of friendship. I do not ask what he says, but what he can consistently say in accord with his theory and opinion. 'Friendship has been sought for the sake of usefulness.' Do you think, then, that this Triarius can be more useful to you than if the granaries at Puteoli were yours? Gather up all the things you are wont to say: 'The protection of friends.' You have protection enough in yourself, enough in the laws, enough in ordinary friendships. Now you cannot be despised; and hatred and envy you will easily avoid — for precepts are given by Epicurus for these things. And yet, using such great revenues for generosity, even without this Pyladean friendship, you will excellently guard and fortify yourself by the goodwill of many. 'But with whom shall I share my jests and my serious matters, as the saying is — with whom my secrets, with whom all my hidden things?'

this being granted, that will have to be granted. This your school does not likewise. \"Three kinds of goods\"; the discourse runs down the slope. It comes to the end; it sticks in the rut. For it longs to say that nothing can be lacking to the happy life for the wise man. An honourable discourse, Socratic, even Platonic. \"I dare to say it,\" says he. You cannot, unless you unravel those things. If poverty is an evil, no beggar can be happy, however wise he be. But Zeno dared to say him not only happy, but even rich. Pain is an evil; he who is driven onto the cross cannot be happy. Children are a good; bereavement is wretched. Country is a good; exile is wretched. Health is a good; disease is wretched. The soundness of the body is a good; weakness is wretched. Unimpaired sight is a good; blindness is wretched. If he can relieve each of these singly by consoling, how will he sustain them all together? Let the same man be blind, weak, afflicted with the gravest disease, an exile, bereaved, in want, tortured on the rack: whom do you call this man, Zeno?' 'Happy,' says he. 'Even most happy?' 'Quite so,' he will say, 'since I have taught that that thing has no degrees, just as virtue, in which being happy itself is also placed.'

With yourself best of all; then also with a moderate friend. But grant that these things are not without their value; what is that to the usefulness of so great a sum of money? You see, then, that if you measure friendship by its own affection, nothing is more excellent; but if by profit, the closest intimacies are outdone by the rent of profitable estates. You must, then, love me myself, not my possessions, if we are to be true friends. But in matters most plain we are too long. For when it has been proved and concluded that there is nowhere a place for the virtues nor for friendships, if all things be referred to pleasure, there is nothing further that need be greatly said. And yet, lest any point should seem to be left unanswered, I shall now say a few things more in reply to the rest of your discourse.

'To you this is incredible, that he is most happy. What? Is yours credible? For if you call me to the people, you will never prove that he who is so affected is happy; if to the prudent, about the one thing they will perhaps doubt, whether there is so much in virtue that those endowed with it are happy even in the bull of Phalaris; about the other they will not doubt, but that the Stoics say things consistent with themselves, and you things repugnant.' 'Does, then,' said he, 'that book of Theophrastus on the happy life please you?' 'Yet we stray from our purpose; and, not to be longer, plainly, Piso,' said I, 'if those things are evils, it pleases me.' 'Do they not, then,' said he, 'seem to you evils?'

Since, then, the whole sum of philosophy is referred to living happily, and men, seeking this one thing, have betaken themselves to this study, but place living happily, some in one thing, some in another, you in pleasure, and likewise, on the contrary, all wretchedness in pain — let us first see what your 'living happily' is. And this you will grant, I suppose, if only there be such a thing as being happy, that it ought to lie wholly in the power of the wise man. For if the happy life can be lost, it cannot be happy. For who feels confident that what is frail and falling will always remain firm and stable for him? But he who distrusts the perpetuity of his goods must needs fear lest at some time, having lost them, he be wretched. But no one can be happy amid the fear of the greatest things. No one, then, can be happy.

'You ask that,' said I, 'in which, whichever I answer, you must turn yourself this way and that.' 'In what manner, pray?' said he. 'Because, if they are evils, he who is in them will not be happy; if they are not evils, the whole reasoning of the Peripatetics lies prostrate.' And he, smiling: 'I see,' said he, 'what you are about; you fear lest I lead away your pupil.' 'You indeed,' said I, 'may lead him, if he follow; for he will be with me, if he be with you.' 'Hear, then, Lucius,' said he; 'for my discourse must be set up with you. All the authority of philosophy, as Theophrastus says, consists in procuring the happy life; for we are all inflamed with the desire of living happily. In this I agree with your brother.

For the happy life is wont to be spoken of not in some part, but in the perpetuity of time; nor is it at all called a life, unless it be finished and complete; nor can anyone be at one time happy, at another wretched; for he who shall think he can be wretched will not be happy. For when once the happy life has been taken up, it remains as long as wisdom herself, the producer of the happy life, and does not await the last span of life — that which Herodotus writes was the precept given by Solon to Croesus. 'But,' you say, as you yourself said, 'Epicurus denies that length of time contributes anything to living happily, and that no less pleasure is perceived in a brief span of time than if it were everlasting.'

Wherefore this must be seen, whether the reasoning of the philosophers can give us this. It promises it, at least. For unless it did this, why did Plato traverse Egypt, that he might receive numbers and the heavenly things from the barbarian priests? Why, after that, did he go to Archytas at Tarentum? Why to the rest of the Pythagoreans — Echecrates, Timaeus, Arion, to the Locrians — that, when he had expressed Socrates, he might join the discipline of the Pythagoreans, and learn those things which Socrates rejected? Why did Pythagoras himself both survey Egypt and go to the magi of the Persians? Why did he travel over so great regions of barbarians on foot, cross so many seas? Why did Democritus do these same things? Who — whether truly or falsely, we forbear to ask — is said to have deprived himself of his eyes; certainly, that his mind might be as little as possible drawn away from his thoughts, he neglected his patrimony, left his fields untilled, seeking what else but the happy life? Which, even if he placed it in the knowledge of things, yet from that investigation of nature he wished to follow this, that he should be of good cheer. For that he calls the highest good euthymia, and often athambia — that is, a mind free from terror.

These things are said most inconsistently. For when he places the highest good in pleasure, he denies that pleasure becomes greater in an infinite span of time than in a finite and moderate one. He who places all good in virtue can say that the happy life is completed by the perfection of virtue; for he denies that the day brings increase to the highest good. But he who thinks the happy life is produced by pleasure — how will he be consistent with himself, if he denies that pleasure grows by length of time? Then neither does pain. Or is the longest pain the most wretched, while length does not make pleasure more to be wished? What reason is there, then, why Epicurus should always call god happy and eternal? For, eternity taken away, Jupiter is no whit happier than Epicurus; for each enjoys the highest good — that is, pleasure. 'But this one with pain too.' But he counts that as nothing; for he says that, if he were being burned, he would say, 'How sweet this is!'

But these things, though admirably, are not yet polished. For few things, and those not even clearly worked out, were said by him about virtue at least. For afterward these things first began to be inquired into in this city by Socrates, then were brought down to this place; nor was it doubted that in virtue all hope both of living well and likewise happily was placed. Which things when Zeno had learned from our school, as is wont to be prescribed in legal actions, he \"did the same thing in another manner.\" This you now approve in him. Forsooth, the names of things being changed, he escapes the charge of inconstancy; we cannot escape it! He says the life of Metellus is not happier than that of Regulus, yet to be preferred — not more to be sought, but more to be taken; and, if there were a choice, the life of Metellus to be chosen, that of Regulus to be rejected; I call that life, which he says is to be preferred and more to be chosen, the happier, nor do I assign by any least weight more to that life than the Stoics.

In what, then, is he surpassed by god, if he is not surpassed in eternity? In which what good is there, beyond the highest pleasure, and that everlasting? What is the point, then, of speaking grandly, unless you speak consistently? In bodily pleasure — I will add, if you will, 'of the mind,' provided that very thing, as you wish, be from the body — does living happily consist. What? Who can guarantee that pleasure perpetual to the wise man? For the things by which pleasures are produced are not in the wise man's power. For being happy is not placed in wisdom itself, but in those things which wisdom procures for pleasure. But all that is external, and what is external is in the power of chance. So fortune becomes the mistress of the happy life — fortune, which Epicurus says crosses the wise man but little.

What is the difference, except that I call known things by known words, while they seek new names by which to say the same? So, as in the senate there is always someone who demands an interpreter, so those men must be heard by us with an interpreter. I call good whatever is according to nature, what is contrary, evil; and not I alone, but you too, Chrysippus, in the forum, at home; in the school you cease. What then? Do you think men ought to speak one way, philosophers another? How much each thing is worth, the learned and the unlearned say differently; but when it has been agreed among the learned how much each thing is worth — if they were men, they would speak in the customary way — provided the things remain, let them coin words at their discretion.

'Come,' you will say, 'these are small things. Nature herself enriches the wise man, whose riches Epicurus has taught to be easily procured.' These things are well said, and I do not gainsay them; but they fight among themselves. For he denies that less pleasure is perceived from the meanest fare — that is, from the most contemptible food and drink — than from the most choice things for feasting. To him, if he should deny that it makes any difference to living happily what fare one uses, I would grant it, and even praise it; for he would say what is true; and Socrates, who reckons pleasure at no point, I hear saying that the seasoning of food is hunger, of drink, thirst. But the man who, referring all things to pleasure, lives like Gallonius, but talks like that frugal Piso — him I do not hear, nor think that he says what he means.

But I come to the charge of inconstancy, lest you say too often that I stray; which you place in words, I thought it placed in the thing. If this be sufficiently perceived — in which we have the Stoics as the best of helpers — that there is so great a force of virtue that all things, if they be placed on the other side, do not even appear, when all the things which they at least call advantages, and to be taken and to be chosen and preferred — which they so define that they are to be valued at a fairly great worth — these things, then, when I call them by so many names used by the Stoics, partly new and invented, like those \"brought forward\" and \"reduced,\" partly signifying the same — for what is the difference, whether you seek or choose? to me indeed that which is chosen, and to which choice is applied, seems even more elegant — but when I have called all those things goods, it matters only how great I say they are, when things to be sought, how strongly. But if I neither call them more to be sought than you to be chosen, nor value them at more, I who call them goods, than you who call them \"brought forward,\" all those things must necessarily be darkened and not appear and run, as it were, into the rays of virtue as into those of the sun.

He said that natural riches are easily procured, because nature is content with little. Certainly — unless you valued pleasure so highly. 'No less pleasure,' he says, 'is perceived from the cheapest things than from the most costly.' This is to have not only no heart, but not even a palate. For those who despise pleasure itself may say that they do not prefer sturgeon to sprat; but to him whose highest good is in pleasure, all things must be judged by sense, not by reason, and those things must be called best which are sweetest.

But, you say, that life in which there is something of evil cannot be happy. Then neither is a cornfield happy with rich and thick ears, if you see oats anywhere; nor merchandise profitable, if amid the greatest gains it has contracted a little loss. Or is this so everywhere, and otherwise in life? And will you not judge of the whole from the greatest part? Or is it doubtful that virtue so holds the greatest part in human affairs that it overwhelms the rest? I shall dare, then, to call the other things which are according to nature goods, and not to cheat them of their old name, nor now to seek out some new one rather, but to place the greatness of virtue, as it were, in the other scale of the balance.

But be it so; let him attain the highest pleasures not only at little cost, but, for all I care, at none, if he can; let there be no less pleasure in that cress on which Xenophon writes the Persians were wont to feed, than at Syracusan tables, which are gravely censured by Plato; let the obtaining of pleasure be, I say, as easy as you wish — what shall we say of pain? Its torments are so great that in them the happy life cannot exist, if indeed pain is the highest evil. For Metrodorus himself, almost a second Epicurus, describes the happy man in these words, more or less: 'when the body is well constituted, and it is assured that it will so remain.' But can it be assured to anyone how his body will fare — I do not say a year hence, but by evening? Pain, therefore — that is, the highest evil — will always be feared, even when it is not present; for it can be present at any moment. How, then, can the fear of the highest evil dwell within the happy life?

That scale, believe me, will press down both earth and seas. For always from that which contains the greatest parts and pours itself out most widely the whole thing is named. We say that someone lives cheerfully; if, then, he has once been made rather sad, is the cheerful life lost? But this did not happen in that Marcus Crassus, whom Lucilius says laughed but once in his life, that on that account he was called less 'unlaughing,' as the same man says. Polycrates of Samos they called happy. Nothing had happened to him which he did not wish, except that he had thrown into the sea a ring in which he delighted. Was he, then, unhappy by that one annoyance, and happy again, when that very ring was found in the entrails of a fish? But he indeed, if he was foolish — which certainly, since he was a tyrant — was never happy; if wise, not even then was he wretched, when he was driven onto the cross by Oroetes, the satrap of Darius. 'But he was afflicted with many evils.' Who denies it? But those evils were overwhelmed by the greatness of virtue.

'A method is handed down by Epicurus,' he says, 'for disregarding pain.' Now this very thing is absurd — that the greatest evil should be disregarded. But what, pray, is that method? 'The greatest pain,' he says, 'is short.' First, what do you call short? Then, which pain do you call the greatest? For what? Cannot the highest pain last several days? Take care lest it last months too! — unless perhaps you mean that pain which, the moment it has seized a man, kills him. Who fears that pain? I would rather you relieved the pain by which I saw a most excellent and humane man, Gnaeus Octavius, son of Marcus, my friend, worn down — and that not once, nor for a short time, but both often and plainly long. What torments, O immortal gods, did he endure, when all his joints seemed to be on fire! And yet he did not seem wretched, because that was not the highest evil — only toilworn; but he would have been wretched, had he, in a shameful and vicious life, abounded in pleasures.

Or do you not grant even this to the Peripatetics, that they may say that the life of all good men — that is, of the wise and adorned with all the virtues — always has, in all its parts, more of good than of evil? Who says this? The Stoics, of course. By no means; but those very men who measure all things by pleasure and pain — do they not cry that the wise man always has present more of what he wishes than of what he does not wish? Since, then, those men place so much in virtue, who confess that for virtue's sake, unless it produced pleasure, they would not turn even a hand, what ought we to do, who say that even the least pre-eminence of mind goes before all the goods of the body, so that they are not even left in sight? For who is there who would dare to say that this falls within the wise man — that, if it could be, he would cast away virtue forever, to be freed from all pain? Who of us would say — we whom it does not shame to call those things which the Stoics call harsh, evils — that it is better to do something basely with pleasure than honourably with pain?

But that you say great pain is short, long pain slight — what sort of thing that is, I do not understand. For I see pains both great and at the same time quite long, the truer endurance of which you cannot use, who do not love honourableness itself for its own sake. There are certain precepts, and almost laws, of fortitude, which forbid a man to be unmanned in pain. Wherefore it must be thought base — I do not say to feel pain, for that is sometimes necessary — but to defile that Lemnian rock with the cry of Philoctetes, 'which, resounding with his wailing, lament, groan, and roarings, gives back, all dumb, his tearful voice.' Let Epicurus chant his charm over this man, if he can — over him whom 'from the viper's bite the veins of his vitals, steeped with venom, rouse to ghastly torments!' Thus Epicurus: 'Hush, Philoctetes! the pain is short.' But he has lain in the cave now for the tenth year. 'If it is long, it is slight; for it gives intervals and slackens.'

To us that Dionysius of Heraclea seems shamefully to have deserted the Stoics on account of pain of the eyes. As though, forsooth, he had learned this from Zeno — not to be in pain when he was in pain! He had heard, but had not learned, that that was not an evil, because it was not base, and was to be borne by a man. Had he been a Peripatetic, he would have remained, I believe, in his opinion — those who say pain is an evil, but, about bearing its harshness bravely, give the same precepts as the Stoics. And indeed your Arcesilas, although he was rather obstinate in arguing, yet was ours; for he was of Polemo's school. He, when he was burning with the pains of the gout, and his very intimate friend Charmides the Epicurean had visited him and was going out sad, said: 'Stay, I pray, our Charmides; nothing comes from there to here.' He showed his feet and his breast. And yet he would have preferred not to be in pain.

First, not often; then, what is that slackening, when both the memory of past pain is fresh, and the fear of pain to come and impending torments him? 'Let him die,' he says. Perhaps that is best; but where is that 'always more of pleasure'? For if it is so, take care lest you commit a crime, when you advise a man to die. Rather, then, let these things be said: that it is base, that it is unworthy of a man, to be broken by pain, to be crushed, to give way. For those sayings of yours — 'if severe, short; if long, slight' — are mere copybook maxims. By the fomentations of virtue, of greatness of soul, of patience, of fortitude, pain is wont to be soothed.

This, then, is our reasoning, which seems to you inconstant: that, on account of a certain heavenly and divine and so great pre-eminence of virtue, that, where virtue is, and great things and supremely praiseworthy done by virtue, there wretchedness and tribulation cannot be — yet toil can be, annoyance can be — I do not hesitate to say that all the wise are always happy, but yet that it can come about that one be happier than another.' 'And yet that point, Piso,' said I, 'must be confirmed by you again and again; which if you hold, you may lead away not only my Cicero, but even me myself.'

Hear — not to go far afield — what Epicurus says as he is dying, that you may understand how his deeds differ from his words: 'Epicurus to Hermarchus, greeting. While we were passing,' he says, 'the happy and likewise the last day of our life, we wrote this. But such pains of the bladder and the bowels were upon us that nothing could be added to their greatness.' Wretched man! If pain is the highest evil, it cannot be said otherwise. But let us hear himself: 'Yet there was set against all these,' he says, 'a gladness of mind, which I took from the remembrance of our reasonings and discoveries. But do you, as is worthy of the goodwill you have shown, from your youth up, toward me and philosophy, see that you protect the children of Metrodorus.'

Then Quintus: 'To me indeed,' said he, 'this seems sufficiently confirmed, and I rejoice that that philosophy, whose furniture I formerly valued more than the possessions of the rest — so rich did it seem to me, that I could seek from it whatever I had desired in our studies — this philosophy, then, I rejoice has been found even more acute than the rest, which some said was lacking to it.' 'Not more, indeed, than ours,' said Pomponius, jesting; 'but, by Hercules, your discourse was most pleasing to me. For the things which I thought could not be said in Latin, those have been said by you in fitting words, and no less plainly than they are said by the Greeks. But it is time, if you please, and indeed straight to my house.' When he had said this, and it seemed to have been discussed enough, we all proceeded into the town, to the house of Pomponius.

I do not now set the death of Epaminondas, nor of Leonidas, before this death. Of these, the one, when he had conquered the Lacedaemonians at Mantinea, and saw himself dying of a grievous wound, as soon as he came to himself asked whether his shield was safe. When his weeping comrades answered that it was safe, he asked whether the enemy were routed. When he had heard this too, as he wished, he bade them draw out the spear by which he was pierced. So, with much blood poured forth, he died in gladness and in victory. And Leonidas, king of the Lacedaemonians, set himself and those three hundred whom he had led out from Sparta against the enemy at Thermopylae, when there was offered him either base flight or glorious death. Glorious are the deaths of commanders; but philosophers for the most part die in their beds. Yet it matters how. Epicurus seems to himself happy as he dies. Great praise! 'There was set against,' he says, 'the highest pains a gladness.'

I hear indeed the voice of a philosopher, Epicurus; but you have forgotten what you ought to say. For first, if those things are true at whose remembrance you say you rejoice — that is, if your writings and discoveries are true — you cannot rejoice. For you have now nothing which you may refer to the body; but it has always been said by you that no one rejoices except on account of the body, nor feels pain. 'I rejoice,' he says, 'in things past.' In what things past? If in such as pertain to the body, I see that you are setting your reasonings against those pains, not the memory of pleasures perceived by the body; but if in such as pertain to the mind, then it is false, which you deny — that there is any gladness of the mind which is not referred to the body. Why, next, do you commend the children of Metrodorus? What, in that excellent duty of yours, and so great a good faith — for so I judge it — do you refer to the body?

Turn yourselves this way and that, Torquatus, as you please; you will find nothing written in this admirable letter by Epicurus consistent and in agreement with his decrees. So is he refuted by himself, and his writings convicted by his own uprightness and morals. For that commending of the boys, the memory and affection of friendship, the keeping of the highest duties at the last breath, show that there is in man an inborn uprightness, gratuitous, not invited by pleasures nor called forth by the wages of rewards. For what greater testimony do we seek that things honourable and right are in themselves to be wished for their own sakes, when we see such duties in a dying man?

But as I think that letter praiseworthy, which I have just now interpreted in almost as many words — though it agreed in no way with his lofty philosophy — so I judge that his will is at variance not only with the gravity of a philosopher, but even with his own opinion. For he wrote, both in many words often, and briefly and closely, in that book which I just now named, that death is nothing to us; for what is dissolved is without sensation, and what is without sensation is nothing at all to us. This very thing might have been put more elegantly and better. For the statement, 'what is dissolved is without sensation,' is of such a kind that he does not say clearly enough what is dissolved. But still I understand what he means.

But I ask what it is that — when by dissolution, that is, death, all sensation is extinguished, and when there is nothing at all left which pertains to us — he so carefully and so diligently provides and ordains: that Amynomachus and Timocrates, his heirs, should, by the judgment of Hermarchus, give what is enough for keeping his birthday every year in the month Gamelion, and likewise on the twentieth day of the moon in every month should give for the feast of those who studied philosophy together with him, so that the memory both of himself and of Metrodorus might be honoured.

I cannot say that these are not the acts of a man, however agreeable and humane; but of a wise man by no means — especially of a natural philosopher, which he wishes to be — to think that anyone has a birthday at all. What? Can the same day be more than once, which was but once? Surely it cannot. Or one of the same kind? Not even that, unless many thousands of years intervene, so that there be a return of all the stars at one time to the point whence they set out. There is, then, no man's birthday. 'But it is kept!' And I, of course, did not know it! But granted that it be kept — shall it be kept even after death? And shall he provide for this by will, who gave us, as it were, an oracle, that nothing after death pertains to us? These were not the acts of one who had traversed in mind countless worlds and infinite regions, of which there was no shore, no boundary. Did Democritus do any such thing? — to pass over the rest, I appeal to him, whom alone Epicurus followed.

But if a day was to be marked, should it rather be the day on which he was born, or that on which he was made wise? 'He could not,' you will say, 'have been made wise, had he not been born.' And by that reasoning, not even if his grandmother had not been born. The whole thing, Torquatus, belongs not to learned men — to wish the memory of one's name celebrated with feasts after death. As to how you keep those days, and into how great a wit of merry men you run, I do not say — there is no need of quarrels — I only say this much: that it would have been more your part to keep the birthday of Epicurus, than for him by his will to provide that it be kept.

But to come to the point — for, while we were speaking of pain, we were carried off to that letter — now the whole matter may be concluded thus: he who is in the highest evil is not, while he is in it, happy; but the wise man is always happy, and is sometimes in pain; therefore pain is not the highest evil. And now, what sort of thing is this — that past goods do not slip away from the wise man, but that he ought not to remember evils? First, is it in our power what we remember? Themistocles, indeed, when Simonides or someone else promised him an art of memory, said, 'I would rather one of forgetting; for I remember even what I do not wish, and cannot forget what I wish.'

A man of great genius, this; but the matter is yet thus, that it is the part of too imperious a philosopher to forbid remembering. Beware lest these be your Manlian commands, or even greater, if you order what I cannot do. What if the memory of past evils is even pleasant? — so that some proverbs are truer than your dogmas. For it is commonly said, 'Pleasant are toils once done'; and Euripides says not amiss — I will conclude in Latin, if I can; for you all know this Greek verse — 'Sweet is the memory of toils gone by.' But let us return to past goods. If these were spoken of by you such as Gaius Marius could use — so that, banished, in want, plunged in a marsh, he might lighten his grief by the recollection of his trophies — I should listen, and quite approve. For the happy life of the wise man cannot be made complete, nor brought to its end, if all his first wise counsels and deeds are buried in his own forgetfulness.

But to you the recollection of pleasures perceived makes the happy life — and indeed of pleasures perceived by the body. For if there are any others, it is false that all pleasures of the mind are from fellowship with the body. But if bodily pleasure delights even when past, I do not understand why Aristotle so greatly derides the epitaph of Sardanapalus, in which that king of Syria boasts that he has carried away with him all the pleasures of his lusts. 'For what he could not,' he says, 'even when alive, feel longer than while he enjoyed it, how could that remain to him when dead?' Bodily pleasure, therefore, flows away, and each first one flies off, and more often leaves a cause for repentance than for recollection. And so Africanus is happier, speaking to his country in that fashion: 'Cease, Rome, your foes—' and the rest, admirably: 'For my toils have won you ramparts.' He rejoices in past toils; you bid men rejoice in pleasures; and he recalls himself to those things from which he never referred anything to the body, while you cleave wholly to the body. But that very thing — how can it be maintained which you say, that all pleasures and pains of the mind pertain to pleasures and pains of the body?

Does nothing ever delight you — I see with whom I am speaking — you yourself, then, Torquatus, does nothing delight for its own sake? I pass over dignity, honourableness, the very aspect of the virtues, of which I spoke before; I will put these lighter things: a poem, a speech, when you either write or read it; when you search out the history of all deeds, of all regions; a statue, a picture, a pleasant spot, games, hunting, the villa of Lucullus — for if I said your own, you would have a hiding-place; you would say it pertained to the body — but those things which I have named, do you refer them to the body? Or is there something that delights you of its own accord? Either you will be most obstinate, if you persist in this — that the things I have named are referred to the body — or you will desert the whole Epicurean pleasure, if you deny it. And as to your argument that the pleasures and pains of the mind are greater than those of the body, because the mind shares in the three times, but by the body only present things are felt — how can this be proved, that he who rejoices on my account at something should rejoice more than I myself?

Pleasure arises in the mind on account of pleasure of the body, and the pleasure of the mind is greater than that of the body. So it comes about that he who congratulates is gladder than he whom he congratulates. But while you wish to make the wise man happy, since he perceives the greatest pleasures in his mind, and in all parts greater than in the body, you do not see what occurs. For he will also perceive pains of the mind in all parts greater than those of the body. So it must needs be that he whom you would have always happy is at some time wretched; nor indeed, while you refer all things to pleasure and pain, will you ever bring it about that he is not.

Wherefore some other highest good of man, Torquatus, must be found; let us concede pleasure to the beasts, whom you are wont to use as witnesses about the highest good. But what if even the beasts do many things, each led by its own nature, sometimes lovingly, sometimes with toil, as in begetting and rearing — so that it very easily appears that something else is set before them, not pleasure? Some rejoice in running and roaming; others, by gathering together, imitate in a fashion the assembly of a state;

we see in a certain kind of birds some signs of natural affection, recognition, memory; in many we see also longings. Shall there be, then, in the beasts certain likenesses of the human virtues, severed from pleasure, and shall there be in men themselves no virtue except for the sake of pleasure? And shall we say that to man, who far excels all other living creatures, nothing has been given by nature in a special degree?

We, indeed, if everything is in pleasure, are by far and greatly surpassed by the beasts, to whom the earth itself pours forth from itself various and abundant feed while they toil not at all; but to us they scarcely, or scarcely even, suffice, though we seek them with much labour. And yet in no way can the highest good of beast and of man seem to me the same. For why is there need of so great equipment in acquiring the best arts? Why of so great a concourse of the most honourable studies, of so great a retinue of virtues, if these are sought for no other end than pleasure?

Just as, if Xerxes — when with such great fleets and such great forces of horse and foot, the Hellespont bridged, Athos pierced through, he had walked the sea and sailed the land — if, when he had come into Greece with so great an onset, someone should ask him the cause of such great forces and so great a war, and he should say that he had wished to carry off honey from Hymettus, he would surely seem to have attempted such great things without cause; so, if we shall say that the wise man, equipped and adorned with the most numerous and weighty arts and virtues — not, like Xerxes, traversing seas on foot and mountains with fleets, but embracing in his mind the whole heaven and the whole earth with the entire sea — seeks pleasure, we shall be saying that he toiled so greatly for the sake of honey.

For higher and more magnificent things, believe me, Torquatus, we are born; nor is this proved from the parts of the mind alone — in which there is the memory of countless things (in you indeed boundless), in which there is conjecture of things to come not far differing from divination, in which there is shame, the moderator of desire, in which there is the faithful guardianship of justice for human fellowship, in which there is, in enduring toils and undergoing dangers, a firm and steady contempt of pain and of death — these things, then, are in our minds; but do you also consider the very limbs and senses, which, like the other parts of the body, will seem to you not only companions but even ministers of the virtues.

What? If in the body itself many things are to be preferred to pleasure — strength, health, swiftness, beauty — what, pray, do you think in our minds? In which those most learned ancients thought there was something heavenly and divine. But if the highest good were in pleasure, as you say, it would be desirable to spend days and nights in the greatest pleasure, with no interval between, while all the senses were stirred, flooded, as it were, with every sweetness. But who is worthy of the name of man, who would wish to be one whole day in that kind of pleasure? The Cyrenaics, indeed, do not refuse it; your school speaks of these things more modestly, those perhaps more consistently.

But let us survey in our minds not these greatest arts — for lacking which men were by our ancestors called good-for-nothing — but I ask whether you think that — I do not say Homer, Archilochus, Pindar, but Phidias, Polyclitus, Zeuxis directed their arts to pleasure. Shall the craftsman, then, set himself a higher aim toward beauty of forms than the excellent citizen toward beauty of deeds? But what other cause is there of so great an error, spread so far and wide, except that he who decrees pleasure to be the highest good deliberates not with that part of the mind in which reason and counsel reside, but with desire — that is, with the lightest part of the mind? For I ask of you: if there are gods, as you too think, how can they be happy, since they cannot perceive pleasures by the body? Or, if they are happy without that kind of pleasure, why do you refuse that there is a like exercise of mind in the wise man?

Read the panegyrics, Torquatus — not of those who were praised by Homer, not of Cyrus, not of Agesilaus, not of Aristides or Themistocles, not of Philip or Alexander; read the panegyrics of our own men, read those of your own family; you will see no one so praised that he was called a cunning craftsman in procuring pleasures. The inscriptions of monuments do not signify this — such as this one at the gate: 'This one man very many nations agree to have been the chief man of the people.'

Do we think that very many nations agreed concerning Calatinus that he had been the chief man of the people because he had been most surpassing in the procuring of pleasures? Shall we, then, say that there is good hope and a great natural gift in those young men whom we shall judge likely to be slaves to their own advantages and to do whatever is expedient for themselves? Do we not see how great a confounding of all things follows, how great a confusion? Kindness is done away with, gratitude is done away with, which are the bonds of concord. For neither, when you do a service to anyone for your own sake, is that to be held a kindness, but a money-lending; nor does gratitude seem owed to him who has done a service for his own sake. But the greatest virtues must all lie prostrate, pleasure being mistress. There are also very many basenesses which, unless honourableness by nature prevails most, it is not easy to defend why they should not befall the wise man.

And, not to embrace more things — for they are countless — virtue, well praised, must needs shut off the approaches of pleasure. And this you must not now expect from me. Look into your own mind, and, going over it with all thought, ask yourself whether you would prefer, enjoying perpetual pleasures, to pass your whole life in that tranquillity which you often used to claim, without pain — adding too that thing which your school is wont to add, but which cannot be, without the fear of pain — or, while you deserved best of all nations, while you brought help and safety to the needy, to endure even the labours of Hercules. For so our ancestors called labours not to be shunned — yet by the saddest word — 'aerumnae,' even in a god.

I should draw it out of you and compel you to answer, did I not fear that you would say that Hercules himself did the things which he wrought for the safety of the nations, with supreme labour, for the sake of pleasure. When I had said this, 'I have those,' said Torquatus, 'to whom I may refer these matters; and, although I could do something myself, yet I prefer to find men better prepared.' 'You mean, I suppose, our friends Siro and Philodemus, men both excellent and most learned.' 'You understand rightly,' said he. 'Well, then,' said I; 'but it were fairer that Triarius should give some judgment on our disagreement.' 'I swear off as an unfair judge,' said he, smiling, 'on this matter at least; for you handle these things more gently, while this man harasses us in the Stoic manner.' Then Triarius: 'Hereafter, indeed,' said he, 'more boldly; for these very things which I have just heard will be ready to my hand, nor will I attack before I see you equipped by those whom you name.' When these things had been said, we made an end both of walking and of disputing.
